CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction method that projects high-dimensional vectors into lower dimensions via random measurements, enabling the exact recovery of sparse and structured vectors from compressed data. This paper investigates the resilience of CountSketch against adaptive inputs, where the vector components are selected by an adversary aware of CountSketch's random projection matrix. Our analysis of this scenario yields both positive and negative findings. On the negative side, we demonstrate that for any fixed CountSketch projection matrix, an adaptive adversary can identify a specific vector that creates an unresolvable collision, rendering perfect recovery impossible. On the positive side, we propose a new randomized CountSketch algorithm that remains resilient to adaptive inputs. This new algorithm achieves a constant relative error guarantee for a broad class of vectors, including those adaptive adversaries can produce. Furthermore, this algorithm is the first to successfully resolve the well-known "randomness vs. randomness" dilemma in randomized algorithms. Specifically, we prove that a single random matrix drawn from our proposed distribution can fool an adversary possessing access to $k$ independent random matrices from the standard distribution used in prior work. This finding establishes the first constant-factor separation between standard random matrices and those resistant to powerful adversaries. Finally, we extend this result to show that our algorithm is resilient against powerful adversaries even when the adversary has access to $k$ independent random matrices from its own distribution that it can query. These findings offer the first constant-factor separation between standard random matrices and those capable of foolling powerful adversaries. Collectively, these results provide the first complete resolution to the "randomness vs. randomness" problem in the context of CountSketch. Additionally, our work offers the first explicit, nearly optimal tradeoff between the number of random matrices required and the robustness against the power of the adversary. We present ipie, a Python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) code designed for many-fermion systems. The method utilizes a stochastic estimator derived from the "plus-minus" formulation of the auxiliary-field Green's function, where the Green's function is represented by the product of two Ginzburg-Landau wave functions. The stochastic sampling employs the Metropolis algorithm, incorporating the determinant of the inverse of the overlap matrix to calculate the trial trial-estimator-energy. ipie is highly adaptable, supporting diverse quantum systems, and is implemented in C++ for execution on both CPU and GPU architectures. We demonstrate the code's accuracy and efficiency through benchmark tests on the hydrogen chain, the paramagnetic Hubbard model, and the one-dimensional spin-1 Heisenberg model. Furthermore, ipie has been successfully applied to investigate the electronic structures of small molecules and the magnetic ground state of the two-dimensional Hubbard model. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/iee-group/ipie. We anticipate that ipie will serve as a valuable resource for the quantum Monte Carlo community. High-frequency trading (HFT) serves as a vital mechanism for market stability, where the speed of information dissemination is paramount. In this study, we introduce a quantum network framework for HFT, enabling the rapid transfer of information between distant nodes. This approach is particularly relevant for implementing quantum games, such as the famous Entangled Prisoner's Dilemma game, within network environments. Our findings demonstrate that this model can be realized using existing H3C switches and routers. Furthermore, we illustrate how this framework facilitates new winning strategies in quantum games that were previously unattainable, offering significant implications for both economic theory and quantum information science. Additionally, we will investigate the deployment of quantum networks in space and their impact on HFT. Creating concise summaries of lengthy documents is a difficult NLP challenge that also serves as a critical real-world skill for professionals like journalists and lawyers. Recently, large language models have demonstrated significant potential for generating high-quality summaries. However, current models often struggle to maintain coherence and fail to capture all essential information. This paper introduces an agent-based approach to abstractive summarization, where the agent first plans the summary's content using an external knowledge base and natural language comments, and then generates the text based on that plan. This method enables the agent to acquire information from the knowledge base and incorporate necessary details into the final output. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the method demonstrates a substantial improvement in generated text quality, enhancing both readability and fluency. Finally, we present a detailed analysis of the generated summaries. This note outlines the key findings from a co-authored research project that extended Rademacher's theorem on the differentiability of real-valued functions to higher dimensions. Specifically, we demonstrated that for an实-valued function $f$ defined on a subset $A$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a nonempty interior, if $f$ possesses partial derivatives that are differentiable almost everywhere within the interior, then $f$ itself is differentiable at a point $x$ (belonging to the interior's complement relative to $A$) provided these partial derivatives are differentiable at $x$. The primary contribution of this work is a novel concept: the differentiability of an $n$-variable function across an expanding sequence of subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$. This notion is equivalent to differentiability on the union of such sequences and constitutes a natural extension of point-wise differentiability. Furthermore, this construction yields a new, streamlined proof of the original theorem. The findings in this note are applicable to any real-valued function possessing partial derivatives, and they generalize to functions with a finite number of partial derivatives, resulting in a novel and distinct approach to the differentiability of multivariable functions. Additionally, it is established that differentiability on an expanding sequence of subsets is equivalent to differentiability on the union of those subsets. This observation facilitates a concise proof of a significant theorem by the second author, which characterizes the differentiability of an $n$-variable function based on the differentiability of an $(n-1)$-variable function. Finally, we present a straightforward application of these results to the theory of partial differential equations. In this application, we assume that for a function $f$ with all partial derivatives, the set of points where $f$ is partially differentiable in at least one direction is dense within the domain. We further assume that for each partial derivative $D_j f$, there exists a sequence $\{A_j^k\}$ of subsets of the domain such that the union of these sequences covers the entire domain, and the collection of all points where $D_j f$ is differentiable along every direction is dense within $A_j^k$. Under these conditions, we conclude that $f$ is partially differentiable in at least one direction at every point in the domain. This result underscores the significance of the differentiability of functions on expanding sequences of subsets, particularly when the union of these sequences forms the domain. This paper introduces a novel computational framework designed to model vocal entrainment within conversational dyads. The proposed method integrates acoustic features with conversation history to predict entrainment at the utterance level. Evaluated on Dialogue Corpus 1.9, the model demonstrates strong performance, surpassing both baseline approaches and prior state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, statistical analysis of the trained model reveals that it aligns with expert-defined metrics for vocal entrainment. The study also leverages these insights to identify key factors influencing entrainment in dyadic dialogues. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta12347/Entrainment.

This paper introduces a categorical model for a quantum manipulation scheme based on the lambda-calculus. We demonstrate that this model is sound and that the resulting system remains non-confluent. Furthermore, we outline several directions for future research.

We introduce a novel approach to compute two quasiparticle excitations within the fractional quantum Hall effect, achieving the first analytical calculation for two quasiparticles with arbitrary charges. Utilizing this new method, we have evaluated various energy configurations involving different charged quasiparticles and quasihole quanta across multiple channels. Our findings demonstrate that these precise analytical results align exceptionally well with exact computations, existing literature, and experimental data. Furthermore, we have identified several new exact analytical solutions for specific configurations. This study offers a fresh perspective on quasiparticle interactions in the fractional quantum Hall effect and introduces a practical technique for investigating multi-particle systems. Our proposed formula can be applied to explore the ground state properties of two quasiparticles in the FQHE. Additionally, this work offers a comprehensive overview of experimental and theoretical research on quasiparticle interactions within the fractional quantum Hall regime. Finally, our results provide a foundation for future experimental investigations into two quasiparticles in this context. This paper is dedicated to Professor Jie Yu on the occasion of his 60th birthday. Keywords: Fractional Quantum Hall Effect; Quasiparticle Excitation; Analytical Calculation.

This study addresses a Stokes variational inequality arising in glaciology, characterized by a degenerate, semicoercive bilinear form that models nonNewtonian viscous effects within ice. The analysis assumes a convex domain and employs a variational approach, treating the problem as a constrained optimization task subject to a convex constraint on the velocity field. Velocity is fixed at the boundary, while the stress tensor remains indeterminate. A penalty method is utilized to transform the constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one. Subsequently, the variational inequality corresponding to this penalized problem is analyzed using the Cea's lemma. Finally, an a priori error estimate is derived for a finite element approximation of this variational inequality, under the condition that the finite element mesh aligns with the Newtonian subdomain. The derivation relies on established elliptic regularity results for degenerate Stokes problems, specifically those formulated by Schaeffer. Furthermore, numerical experiments are presented to validate the theoretical findings. These simulations utilize triangular finite elements on unstructured meshes, with a Lagrangian approach applied to penalize finite element functions that violate the constraint. The resulting variational inequality is solved via a fixed-point algorithm. These numerical results confirm the theoretical error estimates, particularly in two dimensions. Additionally, a practical implementation in three dimensions is proposed, utilizing a primal-dual active set method to resolve the inequality. This numerical approach yields both velocity and stress fields. In both two and three dimensions, the numerical solutions demonstrate convergence at the anticipated rates. Finally, the three-dimensional solution is compared against a solution obtained from a commercial software package. The proposed implementation is available as an open-source package on GitHub. We report on the DUVET project, a multi-wavelength investigation of the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 253, which revealed a high-velocity outflow extending up to 1000 km/s. By combining new observations from the MUSE instrument with existing data, we examined the spatial relationship between star-forming regions and the outflow. Our findings indicate that the outflow originates from the most intense star-forming regions, which are located at the centers of the galaxy's spiral arms. This suggests that the outflow is driven by the most vigorous star formation activity. Additionally, we identified a large-scale, low-velocity outflow moving at approximately 100 km/s, composed of ionized gas and dust. This slower flow is likely powered by the outflow's ram pressure, which compresses the interstellar medium and triggers further star formation. These results are consistent with the "blow-in" scenario, where the outflow both suppresses and stimulates star formation. Finally, we present a new model for the outflow's origin, proposing that it is driven by the combined effects of stellar winds and supernovae. This model aligns with the observed correlation between the outflow and star formation, as well as the measured outflow mass-loss rate. Overall, our study demonstrates the value of MUSE for investigating galactic outflows, offering both a wide field of view and exceptional spectral resolution. The DUVET dataset is publicly accessible at http://duset.astro.ohio-state.edu/. Drawing upon the principles of swarm robotics, we introduce a new framework designed to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of individual service robots operating in service environments. This system leverages a communication and coordination framework that enables the simultaneous deployment of multiple robots to execute tasks while sharing environmental data. We present the theoretical underpinnings of this approach and outline its potential applications within the built environment. Specifically, we highlight two key technologies: the first enables the simultaneous delivery of multiple orders in a restaurant setting, while the second facilitates the simultaneous collection of waste from various locations in a waste management context. A detailed examination of these technologies is provided in our case study. Additionally, we describe the Simultaneous Robotic Framework (SRAF) and its core technologies, which were developed through a collaboration between the University of Oxford and leading industry partners. SRAF is currently being integrated into industry operations, with results expected to significantly improve service performance. The technology is also available for research purposes. Our objective is to foster a community of researchers dedicated to advancing robotic solutions for real-world applications. Pre-training deep neural networks on tasks that provide semantic context can enhance performance on downstream vision tasks. This study examines two specific pre-training approaches for semantic segmentation: pre-training on monocular depth estimation (MDE) and pre-training on categorization. Both methods offer semantic context but differ in granularity; depth estimation provides a continuous depth map, while categoration offers coarse object-level annotations. We evaluated these approaches across multiple semantic segmentation datasets using various deep convolutional architectures. Our findings indicate that the benefit of adding semantic context depends on both the specific downstream task and the image dataset employed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that pre-training on MDE yields superior results compared to categorization when utilizing the KITTI and NYUv2 depth datasets for training semantic segmentation on the Cityscapes dataset. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for future pre-training strategies in semantic segmentation. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/depth_vs_cat. Additional details can be found in our arXiv paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00210. Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation, offering robustness against outliers and alignment in time series. However, performing statistical inference on this metric is challenging due to the non-Gaussian nature of its sampling distribution. This difficulty is particularly pronounced in time series contexts, where the statistic suffers from a significant loss of efficiency compared to Pearson's correlation. This paper introduces a finite-sample bias-corrected estimator designed to mitigate the non-Gaussian bias. We establish the asymptotic normality of this corrected estimator and develop a multiple testing procedure to control the false discovery rate. Through simulations, we demonstrate that our procedure maintains the desired false discovery rate while exhibiting superior power relative to existing methods. Furthermore, we apply the procedure to financial data to analyze the relationship between market returns and various factors. The implementation is accessible via the {\tt ktau} R package. While cloud computing was the primary solution for years, the increasing latency, high energy consumption, and limited scalability of these systems have driven research toward more efficient alternatives. This paper introduces a novel, privacy-preserving edge intelligence framework designed for automotive networks. This framework integrates distributed machine learning, secure multi-party computation, and federated learning to ensure secure and privacy-aware model training on CVs and IoT devices. The proposed system is implemented using Python, PySyft, and Flower, with a case study focusing on a Linear Regression model. Experimental results demonstrate that the framework successfully trains a machine learning model while maintaining data privacy. Furthermore, the framework is highly scalable, capable of handling large datasets and models without compromising performance. Finally, the system offers robust security, effectively preventing both local and remote attacks. We present the Euler characteristic manifold, defined as the set of all possible values of the Euler characteristic across every possible manifold. We offer an initial description of this manifold's structure and provide a proposal for endowing it with a sense of orientation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any attempt to create a quantum phase space out of this manifold inevitably leads to a paradox. Additionally, we explore the concept of a "birth" within this framework, revealing that it possesses an unusual property. Finally, we investigate whether this unusual nature can be mitigated by adopting a more radical perspective on what constitutes a manifold. Throughout this paper, we employ a highly experimental approach to manifold theory, which we anticipate will evolve significantly in the future. We intentionally refrain from establishing any rigorous mathematical theorems, as we believe such a foundation is unnecessary for this particular line of inquiry. Instead, we aim to foster a more radical and imaginative form of mathematical thinking. We conclude by outlining several intriguing philosophical questions that arise from our discussion of the Euler characteristic manifold. This work serves as a sequel to the paper titled "The Value of a Unit Sphere." Unit spheres are fundamental to modern theories of spacetime, including both classical and quantum frameworks. Given this significance, we examine the phase space associated with the dimension of a unit sphere and the potential quantum spatial environment it might generate. We also investigate whether there exists a spatial analogue to the Euler characteristic manifold. However, our analysis indicates that this spatial environment is paradoxical, suggesting that the Euler characteristic cannot be interpreted as a spatial variable. Instead, we propose that the Euler characteristic manifold functions more akin to a phase space than to a spatial environment. We anticipate that this paper will inspire further research into the nature of the Euler characteristic manifold and its role in understanding spacetime and quantum mechanics. Our goal is to contribute to the broader understanding of the universe by exploring the more radical aspects of manifold theory. We hope this work will encourage others to think more creatively about the Euler characteristic and its implications for our comprehension of space and time. This study integrates a strong Allee effect into a classical Holling-Tanner predator-prey model. Through careful selection of model parameters, we identify multiple bifurcation points, including saddle-node, Hopf, and transcritical types. Our theoretical findings regarding the classical Holling-Tanner model with Michaelis-Menten type response function are confirmed by numerical simulations. These results provide valuable insights for understanding the dynamics of both species and developing effective conservation strategies. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the classical Holling-Tanner model with Michaelis-Menten type response function lacks a bistable region. Finally, we examine the persistence of the classical Holling-Tanner model under white noise intensity. The combined impact of the Allee effect and white noise significantly influences the long-term survival of both prey and predator populations. Specifically, the Allee effect reduces the long-term growth rate of the prey population, whereas it increases the long-term growth rate of the predator population. Additionally, we identify critical thresholds for the white noise parameter that determine the extinction or persistence of both species. We demonstrate that the facet rotation simplex method, a recent rotation-based approach to simplex algorithms introduced by Li, Sun, and Ye, features a polynomial iteration bound with respect to the problem size when applied to the polyhedral combinatorics of network design problems. This combinatorial application drives the development of the method, which is a variant of the original simplex algorithm that incorporates rotation steps. Specifically, we establish a linear iteration bound for this method in general $m \times n$ linear programming problems by leveraging a potential function that tracks changes in the Hamming distance to an optimal basis. This technique is primarily employed to prove polynomial complexity for the method's application to network design. The findings are presented in two parts; this article corresponds to Part II. In Part I, we demonstrated that the facet rotation simplex method possesses a polynomial iteration bound for the polyhedral combinatorics of network design problems. In this paper, we prove that the method has a linear iteration bound for linear programming problems where the constraint matrix is totally unimodular. This result confirms that the facet rotation simplex method maintains a linear iteration bound for such problems, consistent with the classical simplex method. Furthermore, this outcome establishes that the facet rotation simplex method possesses a polynomial iteration bound for any polyhedron whose vertices have polynomial size coordinates. The proofs in Part I and Part II rely on the same technique, which utilizes a potential function to measure variations in the Hamming distance to an optimal basis. This technique was originally developed by Jain and Vazirani. Additionally, the technique incorporates a logarithmic factor in the Hamming distance potential function to address issues arising from large coordinate values. Consequently, the technique is applicable to a broader class of linear programming problems than those considered in Part I. However, this paper does not explore applications beyond totally unimodular matrices, reserving such extensions for future research. The results in this paper are derived from an earlier version of the analysis by the authors, which is included in the authors' thesis. The thesis also addresses applications beyond totally unimodular matrices, including those for network design problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that neglecting these effects can result in a bias of approximately 1.5 GeV in the extracted mass value. The increasing sophistication of deep learning techniques has led to a rise in sophisticated presentation attacks, necessitating the development of effective countermeasures to prevent unauthorized face authentication. This paper introduces a zero-shot vision transformer approach to address this challenge. We demonstrate that a pre-trained, generic vision transformer can be adapted for zero-shot presentation attack detection without any task-specific training. The transformer captures high-level semantic features from a single modality, which are then processed through a small fully connected head to classify inputs as either real or spoofed. Our method surpasses state-of-the-art models in zero-shot presentation attack detection. Additionally, we examine the method's limitations, specifically regarding resolution and model size, and propose a novel hybrid architecture that combines a lightweight model with the pre-trained transformer. This hybrid approach effectively balances performance and efficiency, making it ideal for deployment on edge devices. Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs) are designed to shorten the runtime of standard Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) by utilizing multiple cores. Among various PEA configurations, asynchronous parallel EAs offer distinct advantages, such as ease of implementation and flexible control over the selection phase. However, this flexibility introduces specific challenges; for instance, asynchronous parallelization methods that choose parents based on accumulated fitness comparisons are prone to evaluation time bias. This occurs because EAs with faster evaluation speeds are more likely to be selected, potentially degrading solution quality. To address this issue, we introduce a new asynchronous parallel multi-objective PEA that employs frequency-based parent selection, which mitigates evaluation time bias more effectively than comparison-based approaches. Experimental results demonstrate that this frequency-based method achieves superior performance compared to the comparison-based approach. Additionally, we propose a novel method for measuring evaluation time bias, which was validated through extensive testing. This approach offers a straightforward and reliable metric for assessing bias, a feature that comparison-based PEA lack. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of asynchronous parallel EAs to offer readers a clear perspective on their applicability. By understanding these characteristics, researchers can make more informed decisions when selecting an appropriate PEA for their specific problems. To support this, we have released our code and data alongside a new Python library that facilitates the rapid development of custom PEA variants. This library includes a bias measurement module and a framework for comparing multiple PEA types, streamlining the process of identifying the most suitable algorithm for a given evaluation scenario. Our work is expected to assist researchers in developing new PEAs and in selecting the most appropriate one for their evaluations. All code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/leopoldo-garcia/pae-framework. For further details, please visit https://leopoldo-garcia.github.io/pae/. The microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 was identified in the OGLE.IV catalog, with follow-up photometry from the WISE and NEAT surveys confirming its lensing nature. Although the light curve initially appeared simple, suggesting a single lens, a detailed analysis revealed a caustic-crossing signature indicative of a binary lens. This configuration implies the presence of a planet with a minimum mass of 4.4 Earth masses, located at a projected separation of 1.4 AU from the host star. Given the host's low luminosity of 0.0011 L☉, the planet's equilibrium temperature is estimated at 17 K, making it the coldest super-Earth discovered to date. The planet's mass is likely 1.1 to 1.6 times its minimum mass, and its migration history remains uncertain. This system joins a growing collection of cold, low-mass planets identified via microlensing, offering valuable insights into planet formation and evolution. Furthermore, the successful recovery of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 using Keck/NIRC2 confirms the capability of modern adaptive optics to detect low-mass planets around low-luminosity hosts. This study underscores the complementary strengths of microlensing and adaptive optics for investigating the population of cold, low-mass exoplanets. The system is also a prime candidate for future observations using VLT/SPHERE and ELT/MICADO. We investigate the Lindblad generator for a quantum system under rapid oscillation, employing high-frequency expansion techniques to analyze the slow evolution. Specifically, in the low-dissipation regime, we demonstrate that the slow-time master equation can be derived via a time-averaging principle. Furthermore, within this low-dissipation context, we establish the mathematical well-posedness of the slow equation and provide numerical evidence of its validity. Additionally, we present findings from numerical simulations in the dissipative regime. These findings indicate that while the method remains applicable, it requires modifications to the Hamiltonian term in the slow equation to ensure unitarity. Finally, we offer a numerical examination of this adjusted approach for the second highest-order sideband limit. Our numerical results suggest that this modified equation remains well-posed and valid in the low-dissipation limit, even when a time-averaging principle is inapplicable. We conclude by discussing these findings in the broader quantum engineering domain. Notably, our work provides the first mathematical proof of the validity of high-frequency expansions in the weak-dissipation limit. Moreover, the numerical methods employed can be utilized to investigate quantum engineering problems in general time-oscillating scenarios. The topological Kramers degeneracy of Ce 5d states in the heavy fermion metal CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ is disrupted by exchange fields generated by the ordered Ce 4f moments and by spin freezing within the paramagnetic phase. This depolarization is detected via neutron depolarization, which indicates that the Ce moments order ferromagnetically along the [110] direction for x = 0.15 and 0.20. The onset of this depolarization aligns with the magnetic transition observed in specific heat data. Additionally, measurements on the paramagnetic phase of CePd$_{0.8}$Rh$_{0.2}$ show that the neutron depolarization length increases with rising temperature, suggesting a frozen spin system. This behavior is attributed to the presence of Ce 4f moment clusters, which also account for the anomalous specific heat and resistivity trends in this composition. The depolarization results further suggest that the Ce moments in CePd$_{0.8}$Rh$_{0.2}$ exhibit local ferromagnetic correlations. These findings are consistent with the emergence of a Weyl semimetal state in the antiferromagnetic phase of CePd$_{0.8}$Rh$_{0.2}$. The implications of these observations for the topological properties of the material are discussed. The study concludes that depolarization measurements offer a valuable method for investigating the magnetic structure of rare-earth elements in complex magnetic systems. The technique's sensitivity to magnetic order in the [110] direction is particularly advantageous for studying the magnetic properties of topological materials. This work demonstrates that depolarization measurements can yield valuable insights into the magnetic structure of complex materials, thereby advancing our understanding of their electronic and topological characteristics. Furthermore, the results suggest that depolarization measurements can be utilized to investigate the dynamics of spin freezing in paramagnetic systems. Overall, this study highlights the potential of depolarization measurements as a versatile tool for studying a wide range of magnetic phenomena in complex materials. The findings have significant implications for the field of neutron scattering and may inspire further research into novel measurement techniques for investigating the magnetic properties of materials. We report the detection of narrow-line 21 cm self-emission from neutral hydrogen (HI) toward the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20, observed using the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope. This HI self-emission is identified as a signature of ionized neutral gas, generated by electron scattering within the HII region. Our findings indicate that the electron density in this area is approximately $10^3$ cm$^{-3}$, and the total ionized mass is estimated at $\sim 10^5 M_{\odot}$. These results suggest a significant discrepancy between the ionizing photon budget derived from the ionized mass and that predicted by the stellar population synthesis model. Furthermore, the data imply the presence of an additional ionizing source, likely a compact cluster of massive stars with a total mass of $\sim 10^4 M_{\odot}$. This study represents the first detection of HI self-emission from an HII region in the Galactic plane. Our results support the hypothesis that the intensity of this emission correlates with ionized gas density, offering a valuable tool for investigating the physical properties of HII regions. Additionally, this detection demonstrates that the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope is capable of observing the narrow-line self-emission of ionized neutral gas in HII regions. Future observations of similar regions will help clarify the relationship between ionized neutral gas and the starburst process. Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across various image processing tasks, including classification, object detection, and segmentation. However, these models frequently struggle to generalize to unseen data due to discrepancies between training and testing datasets. This paper offers a systematic evaluation of multiple self-supervised and semi-supervised domain adaptation methods for image classification. The experiments were conducted on a large-scale dataset comprising 11 pairs of training and testing sets. Our findings indicate that domain adaptation methods are highly effective in enhancing the generalization capabilities of deep neural networks to novel data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a simple ensemble of self-supervised approaches yields superior performance compared to individual methods. The study also provides a detailed analysis of the advantages and limitations of these techniques, along with recommendations for future research. The dataset used in this work is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/Domain-Adaptation-and-Generalization-in-Deep-Neural-Networks.

This note presents an elementary proof utilizing induction, which derives a closed-form expression for the number of curves satisfying a given set of degree constraints. The findings are generalized to count algebraic curves within $\mathbb F_q^2$. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a leading machine learning approach for processing graph data, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. Asymmetry is a defining characteristic of many natural systems, such as the human brain, river channels, and hurricane paths. While most existing research on quantum-induced asymmetry has focused on classical wave systems, this study explores how quantum light properties can generate optical asymmetry in linear media. Specifically, we demonstrate that an intrinsically symmetric light source, like a standard Gaussian beam, can develop an asymmetric intensity profile upon transmission through a nonlinear Drude metal if it was sufficiently squeezed in the quadrature perpendicular to its propagation direction. This phenomenon, termed quantum squeezing-induced optical asymmetry, is validated by a comprehensive theoretical framework combining quantum electrodynamics with classical Maxwell theory, supported by numerical simulations. Furthermore, we show that this asymmetry can be manipulated by adjusting the squeeze angle and magnitude, as well as the incident angle and metal parameters. This effect holds promise for diverse applications, including the quantum generation of optical vortices, imaging, and sensing. Additionally, we highlight a fundamental distinction between quantum and coherent asymmetry regarding their coherence length scales. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting this asymmetry using a single-photon camera. Our findings reveal a novel class of quantum Drude metals that exhibit unique optical properties, including quantum-enhanced transmission, scattering, and absorption. These quantum asymmetric metals could have broad applications in quantum information processing, sensing, and imaging. Our work establishes a new pathway for quantum manipulation of light using nanomaterials and offers a fresh perspective on the fundamental interaction between quantum and classical electrodynamics. Cholesterol's addition to a lipid bilayer can either increase or decrease the bending modulus, contingent upon the specific lipid and concentration levels. This behavior is governed by a competition between cholesterol's effect on the bilayer thickness and its coupling with the lateral modulus. This spectrum, when plotted against the quantized horizon area spectrum, aligns closely with the Planck spectrum. Furthermore, the calculated horizon temperature matches the Planck temperature. These findings indicate that loop quantum gravity can explain black hole thermodynamics, specifically the area spectrum and temperature, without requiring the mid-point rule approximation. Additionally, the horizon radius corresponds to the Planck length, and the model successfully avoids the singularity. These outcomes are consistent with the holographic principle and the Bekenstein-Hawking formula. This study presents a catalog detailing the composition and anisotropy of matter generated by ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) that reached Earth with energies ranging from 2 to 100 EeV, as observed by the first phase of the Pierre Auger Observatory between 2003 and 2019. The dataset comprises 2,712 events, categorized into 1,253 primary protons, 1,004 primary helium nuclei, and 455 primary heavy nuclei. Analysis reveals that the arrival directions of these UHECRs are not isotropic; rather, they exhibit clustering in specific regions of the sky, with the most prominent concentration located in the direction of the Centaurus A radio galaxy. Furthermore, the data indicates that, on average, the primary nuclei associated with events arriving toward Centaurus A are heavier than those of events from other directions. The paper also examines the potential influence of large-scale magnetic fields on the propagation of UHECRs and their correlation with known astrophysical sources. Additionally, the study addresses the propagation of UHECRs in the intergalactic medium, specifically the attenuation caused by the extragalactic background light, and explores the possibility of UHECR deflection by magnetic fields within the Milky Way and nearby galaxies. Finally, the observed correlation between UHECR arrival directions and the distribution of nearby radio galaxies may suggest a link between UHECR sources and active galactic nuclei. These findings are intended to facilitate future research into the origin and nature of UHECRs. The catalog can be accessed at http://www.pierreauger.org/data. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous applications, yet their inability to provide uncertainty estimates hinders their deployment in critical fields like medicine and autonomous driving. To address this, we introduce BayesOD, a novel Bayesian framework designed to quantify detection uncertainty using state-of-the-art detectors. BayesOD operates by running detectors multiple times with varied initial conditions to generate different predictions, which are then aggregated into a probability distribution to yield a final result along with an associated uncertainty metric. We evaluate this framework using popular detectors, including Faster R-CNN and RetinaNet. Experimental results demonstrate that BayesOD effectively and rapidly produces uncertainty estimates for both bounding boxes and class labels. Furthermore, these estimates correlate strongly with actual performance, indicating their utility in identifying and rectifying detector errors. Additionally, we show that BayesOD can enhance uncertainty estimation in medical imaging by effectively modeling class-specific variations in detector performance. Overall, our findings suggest that this framework offers a straightforward and effective approach for uncertainty quantification in deep object detectors. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/BayesOD.

Forecasting traffic flow at the segment level offers a more detailed and actionable view of future conditions compared to link-level predictions, which is crucial for applications like autonomous driving and advanced driver assistance systems. However, this task is difficult because traffic data exhibits significant spatial and temporal correlations, and anomalies are common. To address these challenges, we introduce Traffic Prediction on Traffic Moving Snippets (T4M), a deep learning framework that learns to forecast traffic flow by analyzing dynamic moving snippets. These snippets are derived from raw link-level data and capture the traffic state within a specific road section along with its immediate surroundings. We validate the effectiveness of T4M using two deep learning models: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms various state-of-the-art link-level prediction techniques. Furthermore, we apply the model to predict traffic congestion for small areas, generating binary maps that serve as a valuable tool for visualizing future traffic conditions. Finally, we discuss the model's potential utility for providing route guidance to drivers. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/zhongtao1201/T4M}. Within this framework, we demonstrate a variant of Rebocho's theorem applying to extensible families of incoherent type constructors and derive a proof-theoretic formulation of the factorization lemma. Furthermore, we illustrate the proof of Rebocho's theorem within a more granular granule of granule proof theory, a structure that also facilitates the development of a version of the empty type. Finally, we show that our methodology extends to establishing a proof-theoretic variant of Martin-Löf's reduction theory. This study introduces a multiple convolutional neural networks (CNNs) approach designed to segment the hippocampus in 3D T1-weighted MRI scans for patients suffering from Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy. The proposed framework integrates three distinct CNN architectures: 3D U-Net, 3D-ResNet, and 3D-ResNeXt, subsequently fusing their individual output predictions into a single final segmentation. Evaluated on the ADNI and International School of Biomedical Engineering (ISBE) epilepsy datasets, the method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, it achieves Dice similarity coefficients of 0.790 and 0.802 for Alzheimer's and epilepsy cases, respectively, while yielding DICE distances of 0.209 and 0.197. These results indicate that the proposed method enhances hippocampus segmentation accuracy across both disease states. We examine the mapping of single photons from one set of waveguide modes to another set of modes that exhibit transversal variations. This phenomenon, akin to the well-known holephong event where most input-output correlations are lost due to hole-to-hole mismatches, is typically viewed as undesirable. However, in waveguide-based integrated photonics, this is not always the case. By employing an input-output analysis, we demonstrate that this so-called "phenomenon" can be advantageous, effectively functioning as a mode cleaner. Furthermore, we show that this mechanism can be readily implemented using a single input-output configuration and can be universally realized through a specific class of non-unitary, non-singular coupling matrices. These findings hold significant implications for both fundamental research and practical applications. Specifically, they suggest that this mechanism could serve as a universal tool for quantum error correction within bosonic codes, a topic of current fundamental interest. Additionally, our approach offers a viable solution for designing output-holephong devices capable of acting as broadband holephong holephong systems. Finally, we propose that this mechanism could facilitate the construction of a universal quantum gate using only two beamsplitters. These proposals underscore the critical role of "phenomena" in advancing the field of integrated photonics. This study presents a Monte Carlo simulation designed to evaluate the potential for detecting low-energy cosmic rays trapped in Earth's magnetic field at low altitudes. The research details a model for magnetic field-guided cosmic ray dynamics and incorporates a simplified representation of atmospheric interactions. By analyzing 10 million trajectories of protons and electrons within the energy range of 100 MeV to 10 GeV, the authors investigate the relationship between particle energy and altitude. The results indicate that protons can be observed as low as 100 km, whereas electrons are trapped down to approximately 200 km. These findings suggest a promising method for observing previously inaccessible, low-energy cosmic rays. Additionally, the simulation successfully replicates the observed energy distributions of the Van Allen radiation belts. A key outcome is the prediction of a new, easily observable source of trapped cosmic rays, which could significantly aid in understanding the solar modulation of cosmic rays. The associated software is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/COSMIC-RAYS. Future research will refine the current model and expand the analysis to include heavier nuclei. This work was conducted as part of the 2020 Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) program at the University of Notre Dame. Keywords: Cosmic Rays, Monte Carlo Simulation, Low-Energy Electrons and Protons, Van Allen Belts.

The efficacy of Deep Graph Neural Networks (DGNNs) relies heavily on the interplay between deep neural networks and graph structures. However, current research often overlooks this synergy, leading to limited performance gains and a lack of interpretability. This paper introduces a novel framework that begins with random graphs and DGNNs, then iteratively refines both components to enhance accuracy. The process involves three key steps: 1) creating a pyramid-like shrinkage skeleton to capture the global structure, 2) optimizing graph topology to align with the DGNN's computational graph, and 3) conducting ablation studies to reveal hidden insights. Experimental results on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that this framework consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we provide interpretability by exposing the graph shrinkage skeleton skeleton and re-wiring decisions, offering valuable guidance for future research. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1998/DGNN-Skeleton}. Finally, we release a high-performance baseline implementation, \textit{GraphSAGE++}, which surpasses the original \textit{GraphSAGE} by 1.5% on real datasets and 2.5% on synthetic datasets. This work offers a comprehensive reference for advancing graph deep learning. Our findings indicate that global and local graph skeleton optimizations are essential for graph neural networks. Recent years have seen significant interest in private low-rank matrix completion, a technique designed to fill missing values in large data matrices while safeguarding user privacy. This study introduces the first differentially private algorithm for this task, leveraging the well-known Huber loss function. We demonstrate that this approach guarantees differential privacy and offer a novel analysis of its statistical performance, specifically regarding user utility. Our experiments indicate that the proposed method is competitive with non-private solutions when applied to matrices that are sufficiently low-rank. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on the average squared error for any differentially private low-rank matrix completion algorithm, providing a corresponding reduction from the Planted Clique problem. This bound proves that, given a sufficiently small number of missing entries, our algorithm achieves optimal statistical performance. Additionally, we derive a lower bound on the average squared error for a broader class of algorithms that are not strictly differentially private but maintain $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy. These results are supported by a theoretical analysis of the distribution of missing entries and empirical findings. Finally, we discuss extensions of our algorithm to handle missing data patterns and missing value rates that are not necessarily small. Overall, this work provides the first comprehensive analysis of differentially private low-rank matrix completion, supported by both theoretical and empirical evidence. The method is implemented in Python and made available on GitHub. The source code includes fully reproducible experiments and theoretical proofs, and our algorithms are benchmarked against existing non-private completion methods. We introduce a unified model that describes the extinction, emission, and polarization of linearly polarized light produced by dust in the "sparse" phase of the interstellar medium (ISM). This phase is defined as the diffuse ISM, characterized by low density ($n_H \lesssim 0.3$ cm$^{-3}$), high temperature ($T \gtrsim 8000$ K), and short dynamical timescales ($t \lesssim 10^7$ yr). The model relies on a representative dust population termed "Astrodust," which is assumed to be ubiquitous across all Galactic environments. Astrodust grains are randomly oriented within a turbulent magnetic field and are described by a size distribution of randomly oriented, randomly shaped, non-crystalline grains. The framework is built upon a collection of dust grains with fixed chemical and mineralogical compositions, varying sizes, and random shapes. Polarization is modeled using the Monte Carlo method, while extinction and emission are calculated via the method of moments. By applying this model to the Galactic plane, we derive a mean polarization fraction of 0.0015 for the diffuse ISM, which aligns with observational data. Furthermore, the model predicts a mean polarization fraction of 0.0025 for the diffuse ISM, representing a factor of approximately 1.7 times the polarization observed in the Galactic plane. We also predict that dust emission from the diffuse ISM is enhanced by a factor of roughly 1.5 compared to the emission expected if the ISM were entirely cold and dense. These predictions are consistent with available observations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the astrophysical significance of the ratio between Galactic polarization and the polarization fraction of the diffuse ISM is approximately 1.1, indicating a strong correlation between these two quantities. Finally, we show that the ratio of Galactic extinction to Galactic emission is about 1.3, with a standard deviation of 0.2, suggesting a robust correlation between these two observables. Overall, our findings suggest that the astrophysical significance of the ratios between polarization, extinction, and emission is approximately 1.1, 1.7, and 1.5, respectively, for the diffuse ISM. These results support the hypothesis that dust in the diffuse ISM is structurally homogeneous, composed of grains with fixed chemical and mineralogical compositions, sizes, and shapes. We report the detection of a massive planet within the protoplanetary disk of CIDA 1, a young, low-mass star with a mass of 0.18 solar masses. This system was previously identified as a candidate for a disk warping event, a phenomenon typically associated with higher-mass stellar hosts. Our analysis of ALMA 1.3 mm continuum data reveals a disk inclined at 60 degrees, exhibiting a clear warp and a prominent gap at approximately 100 au. The system's total mass is estimated at 0.2 solar masses, with a gas-to-dust ratio of 100. By integrating ALMA observations with ALMA and VLA data at longer wavelengths, we determined that the dust is vertically settled and concentrated in the disk's midplane. We propose that the gap was carved by a massive planet, which also induces the disk's warp. Our planet-disk interaction models indicate that a planet with a mass between 1 and 1.5 Jupiter masses, located at 90 to 110 au, can reproduce the observed disk structure. This finding is significant because it demonstrates that giant planets can form around very low-mass stars, and it represents the first instance of a disk warp being explained through planet-disk interactions. Furthermore, the system's low gas-to-dust ratio suggests that the gas mass is negligible, implying that the planet formed via core accretion in a gas-depleted environment. This system offers a valuable opportunity to investigate the link between planet formation and the initial conditions of the natal disk.

While [1] addresses tap optimization by limiting the solution space to symmetric vectors, we propose a more general approach. By relaxing the symmetry constraint to allow for symmetry within a specific subspace, we enable the tap-optimized vector to exist outside a symmetric orientation. Our technique, termed the Most Taps Problem, is demonstrated through the analysis of the $3 \times 3 \times 3$ Lights Out game. In this context, we examine most-tap vectors across different symmetry assumptions, comparing their corresponding tap counts and solution lengths. Finally, we present a conjecture regarding the existence of a most-tap vector for the $n \times n \times n$ game.

In our preliminary investigation, we sought to determine the tap count for the $3 \times 3 \times 3$ Lights Out game under the assumption that the light-up vector possesses symmetry in one of its three orthogonal orientations. We denote the tap count for a game with a light-up vector of a specific orientation as $T_{tap}$. Our findings revealed that $T_{tap}$ varies depending on the orientation of the light-up vector. Consequently, we established that the minimum number of taps required to solve the $3 \times 3 \times 3$ game is 4, achieved when the light-up vector exhibits plane symmetry.

To investigate the existence of a most-tap vector under the assumption of orthoradial symmetry, we analyzed the set of all possible tap counts. We observed that this set contains multiple distinct values, indicating that tap count is not invariant under orthoradial symmetry. Furthermore, we demonstrated that for any specific tap count, the number of corresponding solutions is not zero. This implies that a most-tap vector exists when orthoradial symmetry is assumed. We also examined the relationship between tap counts and solution lengths, proving that the most-tap vector does not necessarily yield the shortest solution length.

To explore the existence of a most-tap vector without assuming any specific symmetry, we analyzed the set of all possible tap counts. We found that this set also contains multiple values, confirming that tap count remains non-invariant without symmetry assumptions. Additionally, we showed that the number of solutions for a given tap count is non-zero, thereby establishing the existence of a most-tap vector in the absence of symmetry constraints.

This paper introduces a new two-stage segmentation framework that integrates image restoration techniques. The initial stage employs a fast segmentation method utilizing a speed-up strategy to handle difficult cases, while the subsequent stage applies a restoration process to refine the results. Specifically, the recovery module is designed to correct minor artifacts, improve edge sharpness, and enhance color fidelity. The research focuses on implementing a variety of well-known restoration methods, including deconvolution, blind deconvolution, blind super-resolution, and deblurring. Experimental results demonstrate that the models incorporating these restoration steps yield superior segmentation quality compared to the baseline approach that excludes any restoration procedure. Additionally, the study highlights specific advantages and limitations of each implementation, offering insights to guide future research efforts. Overall, the research aims to provide valuable insights for enhancing current segmentation models and establishing a robust foundation for developing high-performance algorithms. Abstract Interpretation is a well-established framework for creating static analysis tools that are both sound and scalable. Soundness ensures that no false negatives are missed, while scalability is achieved through the use of a lattice that is more abstract than the program's concrete semantics. Traditionally, the phases of program exploration and phase lifting are tightly coupled, meaning the choice of lattice directly influences how quickly and effectively analysis results are produced. This paper introduces a novel approach to scalability that decouples these phases, allowing program exploration to occur in a highly abstract domain while lifting into the target lattice for soundness in a relatively abstract domain. We demonstrate this new method through various decision procedures for properties concerning inter-procedural control and data flow. Our experimental results indicate that this technique can significantly enhance the scalability of static analysis. Specifically, our approach successfully analyzes large industrial programs, such as the Linux kernel, that were previously intractable. Furthermore, our methods outperform existing techniques for deciding property questions. Finally, we show that our approach effectively handles challenging cases, including the analysis of recursive functions and the evaluation of pointer aliasing. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of decision procedures grounded in SMT solvers to the problem of scaling static analysis. Our method effectively separates phase lifting from phase exploration, enabling the exploration phase to utilize a more abstract lattice that does not need to closely approximate the program's concrete semantics. This flexibility allows for the use of more aggressive approximations during exploration, thereby improving scalability. Our decoupling technique is implemented within the software tool COSY, which we have extended with new decision procedures. These procedures use the program's concrete semantics to answer queries about inter-procedural control and data flow. We have applied COSY to analyze large programs, such as the Linux kernel, and compared our approach against other techniques for deciding properties related to program properties. Our results demonstrate that using decision procedures to lift between lattices significantly outperforms other lifting strategies. Additionally, our method effectively addresses difficult analysis challenges, such as handling recursive functions and pointer aliasing. Crucially, the decision procedures allow for the use of a more abstract lattice during program exploration without compromising overall analysis precision. This capability is essential for achieving the scalability gains observed in our results. We conclude that our method offers a new perspective on scaling static analysis, one that separates phase lifting from phase exploration. By allowing the exploration phase to operate in a more abstract setting, we can employ more aggressive approximations, thus enhancing the scalability of static analysis. Topological materials have recently attracted significant attention due to the novel physical phenomena they exhibit, such as protected surface and edge states. While most oxide perovskites display strong electron-phonon coupling, making the topological classification of these insulators complicated, this study investigates single-crystal BaTiO$_3$ under ultrashort laser excitation. We report the emergence of topological phonon edge modes in the excited state, characterized by a gap between the topological index and time-reversal symmetry breaking. These topological phonon edge modes are anticipated to influence the material's electronic properties, thereby opening a new avenue for controlling the topological characteristics of oxides through optical excitation.

Identifying outliers is a critical challenge across numerous data mining domains, including anomaly detection, data cleaning, and feature selection. This paper introduces a novel, rapid, and exact algorithm for outlier detection within metric spaces. Our approach leverages proximity graphs, utilizing their hierarchical structure of low-degree, high-diameter, and low-dimension to efficiently explore the input space. We propose a new method for outlier score calculation that integrates both local and global properties of the score space. Our algorithm is designed to be tunable, allowing users to adjust sensitivity to varying degrees. We validate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, comparing it against existing state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms competing algorithms in terms of speed. Furthermore, we show that our method can significantly accelerate outlier detection in high-dimensional spaces. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm's effectiveness in feature selection by applying it to a real-world image classification task. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/PASOD. This work was presented at the 2020 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM). The quantum motion of an atom near a thin membrane can trigger dipole-dipole interactions between the atom and the membrane, a phenomenon known as motion-induced stimulation. This effect is linked to the coherent coherent scattering (CS) of electromagnetic radiation, which occurs when an incident photon is elastically scattered by a matter system without exciting internal transitions. The CS amplitude is determined by the product of the incident field and the matter's induced dipole moment. In a local response model, this amplitude is the product of the incident field and the dipole moment of individual atoms. Consequently, if an atom is in a superposition state capable of inducing a dipole moment, it can stimulate the membrane's motion. This induced motion, in turn, generates electromagnetic radiation through the inverse process of coherent scattering, termed motion-inhibition de-stimulation. This phenomenon is significant for understanding radiation from matter near membranes and for investigating quantum correlations between atoms and phonons in coupled light-matter systems. The paper also examines the conditions required to observe this effect experimentally. Furthermore, the study explores the impact of finite membrane thickness on de-stimulation and analyzes the impact of electromagnetic radiation generated by the membrane on the atom. These factors are crucial for the practical realization of motion-induced stimulation and de-stimulation. Finally, the paper addresses the issue of energy conservation in this process, highlighting the role of the vacuum. The findings may have broader applications in quantum optics, nanophotonics, and related quantum technologies. The discussion of these effects may also be relevant to understanding radiation from matter adjacent to other types of boundaries. We examine the kinetic equation governing reversible enzyme reactions involving $N$ substrates and products, which can be viewed as a constrained, non-equilibrium non-linear non-ideal gas. The equation's right-hand side describes a non-linear non-ideal chemical interaction between molecules, a phenomenon that can be decomposed into an infinite series of non-linear kinetic kernels. These kernels represent non-linear kinetic forces that drive the system's evolution toward reversible quasi-equilibrium states. By applying the Adomian-Polya decomposition method, we construct an iterative sequence of kinetic kernels to solve this kinetic equation. This approach yields analytical approximate solutions that correspond to the first few terms of the iterative sequence, enabling the calculation of the system's distribution function and verification of the kinetic kernels' non-linearity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Adomian-Polya method is applicable to a broad class of non-linear non-ideal gas kinetic equations, including those for irreversible enzyme processes and reversible reactions with $N$ substrates and products featuring arbitrary stoichiometric coefficients. Finally, we illustrate that the Adomian-Polya decomposition method is a valuable tool for solving non-linear non-ideal gas kinetic equations and for developing non-linear kinetic forces for such gases. Additionally, we show that the iterative sequence of kinetic kernels represents a non-linearization of the non-linear integral equation derived from the non-linear Fokker-Planck equation for enzyme reaction processes. This non-linearization facilitates the solution of the non-linear integral equation and the derivation of an iterative sequence of probability density functions for the non-linear kinetic forces acting on enzyme reaction gas molecules. The probability density functions are expressed as the first few terms of the iterative sequence, providing approximate solutions to the non-linear Fokker-Planck equation for the specified enzyme reaction processes. We also discuss the application of the Adomian-Polya decomposition method to solving non-linear integral equations. Specifically, we derive an iterative sequence of probability density functions for the non-linear integral equation, where the zeroth term is the solution to the linear integral equation and subsequent terms are defined recursively. This discussion highlights the applicability of the Adomian-Polya decomposition method to non-linear integral equations and the development of iterative sequences for probability density functions of the non-linear Fokker-Planck equation for enzyme reaction processes. Finally, we emphasize that the Adomian-Polya decomposition method is a useful tool for solving non-linear integral equations and for constructing iterative sequences for probability density functions of non-linear Fokker-Planck equations. This study presents a search for natural supersymmetry (nATLAS) and divided natural supersymmetry (d-nATLAS), utilizing proton-proton collision data from the CMS experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis targets simplified models characterized by a compressed chargino-neutralino mass spectrum, compressed squark masses, and soft signatures. A significant discrepancy between the observed and expected data was detected in a dedicated region designed to isolate d-nATLAS signals, resulting in a local significance of 4.1 sigma. This discrepancy corresponds to a global significance of 3.0 sigma. The observed event counts in the primary signal regions align with background predictions. Additionally, limits on the cross sections for natural and divided natural supersymmetry are established. The maximum excluded neutral chargino mass is determined to be 125 GeV for a compressed scenario with a 125 GeV Higgs boson, and 115 GeV for a scenario featuring a 125 GeV Higgs boson alongside a 120 GeV Higgs boson. Furthermore, squark masses up to 1.5 TeV are excluded in the compressed scenario. These exclusion limits are contingent upon specific assumptions regarding the masses of other particles within the model. This work represents the first search for d-nATLAS conducted by the CMS collaboration. The results are consistent with prior searches for compressed, simplified supersymmetry models. No signals were found in this or any other region sensitive to the Higgs boson production associated with neutral charginos. Consequently, the study concludes that no evidence for natural or divided natural supersymmetry was found in this analysis. The exclusion limits for natural supersymmetry models are also reported. This study presents a new econometric framework designed to identify rational expectation asset price bubbles. Within this model, the price series is modeled as a stochastic process that switches between a mean-reverting regime and a unit root regime. The transition from mean-reversion to a unit root signifies the onset of a bubble, while the return to mean-reversal marks its conclusion. Unlike prior models, the duration of the bubble is stochastic. The switching mechanism is governed by an intensity function that depends on an unobserved "shadow" bubble state, which fluctuates over time between active and inactive phases. We develop a non-linear state-space model to estimate the price series and detect bubble episodes. Using a Bayesian approach, we derive the posterior distribution of the intensity function and apply a threshold to classify shadow signals as positive or negative. Finally, we apply this methodology to historical data to examine bubble episodes in the S&P 500 and other major stock indices. The empirical analysis demonstrates the model's effectiveness in pinpointing bubbles and accurately capturing their dynamic characteristics. Furthermore, the results indicate that bubbles within major stock indices are not permanent; they exhibit a mean-reverting intensity with a specific mean time to reversion. This finding contradicts the common assumption that bubble intensity follows a simple Markovian process. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of this result for financial economics. We present a straightforward numerical method for calculating the partition function and expectation values in quantum systems via path integrals using time-slicing. This approach is demonstrated through an exact solution for a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to a driving force, as well as a highly accurate approximation for the same system under constant coordinate or momentum constraints. Results for the constant coordinate case align perfectly with the exact solution, while the constant momentum results correspond to the well-known RPA approximation. The method involves evaluating the functional integral numerically through ordinary integrals utilizing a Monte Carlo algorithm. Specifically, we employ a Metropolis algorithm to estimate both the partition function and expectation values, which are derived from a single set of Monte Carlo paths. This paper serves as a pedagogical introduction to Monte Carlo techniques within the context of quantum field theory. Furthermore, we provide a computer program implementing this method, which can be adapted for more intricate models. The program is written in Fortran 77 and includes features to compute the partition function and various expectation values. It is available upon request. Finally, we outline several directions for future research. For instance, the method could be extended to finite temperature field theory by applying a Monte Carlo algorithm to evaluate the partition function of a scalar field with self-interaction, thereby enabling the investigation of phase transitions. Additionally, the technique can be utilized to determine the ground state wave function of a many-body system. In this scenario, the imaginary time is constrained to a very small range, and the ground state wave function is approximated by the normalized path integral probability distribution. This is achieved by collecting numerous path integral configurations and employing a Monte Carlo algorithm to estimate the probability density. We also address the issue of the sign problem, which arises in this method when the potential energy is complex. Such complexity occurs in the constant momentum case and in field theories with self-interactions when the chemical potential exceeds the mass. In these scenarios, the partition function becomes complex, rendering its real part meaningless. However, the probability distribution remains well-defined as the real part of the partition function divided by its absolute value. Consequently, we can compute the real and imaginary components of the partition function and other quantities of interest. The real part of the partition function is then expressed as an average over all possible phase configurations of the complex weight factor. Since these phases are uncorrelated, the average phase factor approaches zero as the number of configurations increases, causing the real part of the partition function to vanish. In recent years, Item Recommendation (IR) has garnered significant research interest. While existing approaches primarily leverage user behavior data, they often overlook the rich information contained within text reviews. To address this, we introduce a new model designed to enhance recommendation quality by effectively integrating reviews with other behavioral features. We propose the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SiFN), which simultaneously injects both global and local review context into user behavior data. Furthermore, to better capture the connection between user preferences and review content, we developed two embedding strategies: one for review text and another for sentiments. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines. To address this, we present a data augmentation strategy for Arabic-English mixed social media text that leverages lexical substitutions using social and political Twitter hashtags. This approach is designed to expand existing datasets and enhance the quality of co-speaker identification models. Our methodology involves mapping and collecting relevant hashtags, translating them into the target text dataset, and validating the resulting distribution through word clouds. We subsequently evaluate the augmented dataset using two classification models: a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model pretrained on 14 Arabic and 11 European languages, and a Character-level Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that operates without any pretrained components. Finally, we incorporate these augmented datasets into co-speaker identification experiments, demonstrating that they yield a substantial improvement in classification accuracy. Furthermore, our results indicate that the combination of a CNN model with BERT-captured social and political hashtags surpasses the performance of a BERT model alone. We demonstrate that a uniform precompactness property known as Roelcke precompactness fails for collections of homeomorphisms acting on uniformed surfaces. Specifically, our failure criteria are the absence of Roelcke precompactness within the underlying uniform spaces and the quasi-boundedness of the homeomorphism collections. Furthermore, these conditions are adequate to prevent the existence of Roelcke uniformly continuous extensions from the given homeomorphism collections to their respective closure groups. The remaining portion of this study is dedicated to defining and investigating Roelcke precompactness. This concept is significant because it allows the application of combinatorial compactness arguments to precompact sets that are not Roelcke precompact. Additionally, we provide examples of Roelcke precompact sets that are not precompact in the standard Hausdorff sense. The theory of Roelcke precompactness is closely linked to concepts found in the theory of uniform random walks and in a prior work by the authors concerning combinatorially compact sets. The findings in this paper can be extended to establish analogous results regarding the non-Roelcke precompactness of homeomorphism sets on uniformed n-manifolds. To achieve this, the necessary conditions are the lack of Roelcke precompactness in the underlying uniform n-manifolds and the (locally) quasi-boundedness of the homeomorphism sets. In this extended context, precompactness refers to precompactness within the space of uniformly continuous homeomorphisms. The closure groups are defined as the groups generated by the closures of the respective homeomorphism sets. The proof for the n-manifold case relies on the fact that the group of all uniformly continuous surface homeomorphisms is Roelcke precompact. This fact is established by constructing an appropriate ultrafiltration of the homeomorphism set and proving that the ultrafilter limit of any homeomorphism remains Roelcke precompact. The methodology for this proof is also applicable to the surface case. However, an additional argument is required to ensure that the closure group of the surface homeomorphisms is amenable. This argument involves constructing a family of surface partitions that are quasi-invariant under the action of the closure group and exhibit specific combinatorial characteristics. The existence of such a family of partitions serves as a necessary condition for the Roelcke precompactness of the set of all uniformly continuous surface homeomorphisms. We investigate the integrability of integrable membranes within $\lambda$-deformed backgrounds following the methodology established by Delduc, Magro, and Taronn for integrable strings. These membranes exist as membranes of minimal area spanning a two-dimensional base manifold $\Sigma$ and embedding into a six-dimensional manifold $G/\!/\!H$, which arises from the double coset $G^{\mathbb{C}}_{\sigma}$ of a simple complex Lie group $G$. The background geometry is defined by the generalized $\lambda$-deformation of Poisson–Lie T-duality. We demonstrate that the equations of motion governing the membrane are equivalent to the stationarity conditions of an action that is both Poisson–Lie covariant and covariant under area-preserving diffeomorphisms of $\Sigma$. This action is constructed from the components of the non-local current algebra, mirroring the structure of the integrable string in two dimensions. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a canonical Lax connection for membranes in these backgrounds and prove its flatness. Additionally, we outline the construction of an infinite set of non-local charges for integrable membranes. As an application, we derive the equations of motion for membranes in a five-dimensional background formed by the generalized $\lambda$-deformation of the product of two three-dimensional groups. We also provide an application to four-dimensional backgrounds created by the generalized $\lambda$-deformation of the product of two four-dimensional Lie algebras.
