We introduce a new algorithm for solving Hex meshes, achieving UP to 58 Tets/Hex performance, representing a significant speedup over the current state-of-the-art. Our approach relies on a novel method for identifying the initial split hexagon, which we find within 100 hexagons from the center in 99% of cases. By integrating this technique with an existing algorithm, we enable the rapid and reliable conversion of large Hex meshes into high-quality, variable-size finite element grids. This process maintains robust element quality even near boundaries, with the resulting elements being substantially smaller than the original hexagons. We validate the efficacy of our method through several numerical experiments. Furthermore, our algorithm is well-suited for massively parallel execution, facilitating the efficient processing of massive meshes. We have implemented the solution using the Kokkos framework, a portable execution model for GPUs and many-core CPUs, and tested it on both AMD and NVIDIA hardware. Our results demonstrate that parallel execution on GPUs can achieve up to 58 tested hexagons per core/hex, delivering a speedup of up to 20x compared to serial execution. Additionally, we observe that our solution is 1.5 to 2 times faster than the current best parallel algorithm. This enhanced performance is particularly advantageous for applications requiring highly refined meshes, such as those generated by Isogeometric Analysis or fluid-structure interaction simulations. We also highlight the potential for further acceleration by leveraging the latest GPU architectures, specifically those equipped with Tensor Cores. These co-processors can accelerate our algorithm by up to 1.25 times by performing integer operations in integer-arithmetic. This capability is crucial for scenarios involving numerous, very small tested hexagons, where a substantial portion of the work involves checking connectivity between these small elements. We successfully accelerate this specific task using Tensor Cores. Finally, we demonstrate the scalability of our solution on GPU clusters, showing that our approach is 1.5 to 2 times faster than the current best parallel algorithm. This is achieved by reducing the number of tested hexagons from 128 to 64, thereby cutting the communication overhead between nodes in parallel by half. Our results indicate that our solution is 1.5 to 2 times faster than the current best parallel algorithm. Relation extraction (RE) is a critical NLP task focused on identifying semantic connections between entities within natural language text. Although recent studies have demonstrated that pre-trained language models significantly enhance RE performance, they have also revealed that the majority of existing RE datasets are heavily skewed toward zero-shot learning. This limitation stems from the over-reliance on ReVerb2, which provides extensive RE training data but lacks support for few-shot or knowledge graph link prediction learning. To address this, we introduce ReAct, a novel relation extraction framework that enhances RE performance by integrating knowledge graph link prediction learning. ReAct is built upon a straightforward yet effective paradigm that utilizes a single, shared relation classifier for both tasks. Experimental results on the RE and KG link prediction tasks demonstrate that our approach enhances RE performance by leveraging ReVerb2 for knowledge graph link prediction training. Furthermore, we find that the proposed approach surpasses all other methods in RE when evaluated under limited-shot learning scenarios. This study introduces a novel technique for characterizing the analytical inverter lag time of CMOS inverters across various technologies and sizing, utilizing Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox. By applying this approach to inverters fabricated in CMOS processes ranging from 180 nm to 7 nm, the resulting models demonstrate exceptional accuracy, with maximum errors staying below 1.5%. These precise inverter lag time models are particularly valuable for high-speed applications, such as high-frequency SerDes, where they can significantly reduce simulation durations by over 90% when used with SPICE-based simulators. Furthermore, the paper offers guidance on selecting an appropriate inverter load capacitance to ensure measurement accuracy. The technique is also applicable to modeling other delay components, including transmission gates and logic gates. A key advantage of these analytical models is their ability to capture inverter behavior across a wide spectrum of input signal transitions, a capability that standard SPICE simulations often lack. Additionally, the study provides a comprehensive review of inverter lag definitions and examines various methodologies for measuring this parameter. Finally, the paper outlines the fundamental principles of inverter lag and its underlying causes. (Note: The term "inverter lag" is synonymous with "inverter input lag time.") To facilitate adoption, all Matlab scripts required to replicate the technique are included as supplementary material. The authors hope this work will inspire further research into inverter lag modeling. We present a novel framework designed to analyze reinforcement learning (RL) within infinite-state spaces. This design addresses two primary issues: (1) the necessity of a metric to assess practical algorithmic performance, and (2) the challenge of defining value functions in settings lacking a finite state representation. To address these, we propose a metric-based approach grounded in coarse-grained continuity, which enables the application of discrete RL techniques to problems with infinite state spaces. We demonstrate the utility of this framework through two applications: first, it facilitates performance analysis for Q-learning and SARSA by utilizing the continuous coarse-grained model, and second, it enables the derivation of performance guarantees. This achievement is realized through a parametric family of coarse-grained continuity models that incorporate both a metric and a value function. The framework is particularly relevant for RL applications exhibiting approximate or local continuity, such as those involving neural networks or other high-dimensional function approximators. Our analysis covers several state metrics, including those based on Hamming distance, edit distance, and Euclidean distance. Additionally, we illustrate the framework's effectiveness with two concrete examples: an application to a grid-world scenario and an analysis of a graph edit distance metric based on local node edit distance. These cases demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the framework can yield provable performance guarantees. Furthermore, we empirically validate our theoretical findings through experiments conducted on grid-worlds. Our results indicate that our theoretical analysis provides tight bounds on the performance of Q-learning and SARSA. Finally, we show that our framework successfully recovers established results from graph neural networks (GNNs) and graph pooling techniques. Specifically, we prove that GNNs and pooling operators satisfy the coarse-grained continuity condition, thereby offering a theoretical foundation for their application in RL. This insight also suggests a pathway for extending our analysis to other continuous Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our work is the first to provide a general framework for analyzing the performance of Q-learning and SARSA in continuous MDPs. Additionally, it offers a fresh perspective on the conditions required for applying these algorithms in continuous domains. The framework is broadly applicable to any MDP exhibiting local or coarse-grained continuity, including those utilizing neural networks, parametric policies, or other high-dimensional function approximators. We believe this work will significantly advance the theoretical understanding of function approximation and its role in reinforcement learning. The animacy category, which groups objects, people, and animals, is thought to reflect a fundamental organizational principle in the human brain. However, the specific nature of this organization remains unclear. To address this, we examined neural responses in the human ventral temporal cortex using high-resolution fMRI. Our results indicate that the relative positions of cortical regions specialized for distinct visual categories shift systematically across the animacy dimension, suggesting that the essence of animacy organization is a sequential gradient. This gradient is captured by a two-layer model that integrates local category selectivity with a global animacy dimension. We propose that this gradient arises from the brain's capacity to encode visual stimuli at varying levels of abstraction, ranging from highly specific to coarse. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this animacy gradient is more prevalent in the human brain than in the macaque, aligning with the greater complexity of visual experiences in humans compared to macaques. Our findings provide a unified framework for understanding the organization of the ventral temporal cortex and highlight the link between the brain's visual encoding mechanisms and the organization of visual experience. This study represents the first direct evidence of the essence of organization within the human ventral temporal cortex. This study introduces a new, efficient structure-preserving filter for high-order finite element simulations of multiple conservative laws, grounded in convex optimization. The technique effectively smooths finite element results, thereby mitigating the Gibbs phenomenon and enhancing numerical stability. By leveraging the convexity of the underlying physical problems, this approach ensures that filtered solutions strictly adhere to the physical entropy inequality, a capability that distinguishes it from other high-order structure-preserving filters. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through 2D and 3D gas dynamics simulations, which include both smooth and discontinuous initial conditions. These examples illustrate how the proposed filter improves solution accuracy and stability. Furthermore, the paper provides a detailed analysis of the filter's computational cost, showing that it remains comparable to other high-order structure-preserving techniques. Finally, the authors outline potential extensions of this approach to other conservation problems, such as those involving water waves and shallow flows. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/COMP-FE. Type-ax (Type-C) quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients are typically observed during the hard-intermediate state, a phase characterized by a transition from hard to intermediate spectral components and the presence of a prominent type-ax QPO. This transition marks the onset of the hard-intermediate state and signals a shift in the accretion flow structure near the black hole. In MAXI J1535-571, the hard-intermediate state is further marked by a significant rise in hard X-ray flux and the emergence of Type-C QPOs. This study utilizes data from the Insight-HXMT mission to track the evolution of Type-C QPOs throughout the hard-intermediate state of MAXI J1535-571. This study investigates cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) within dynamic environments, where agents must jointly decide actions to achieve shared goals. A primary challenge in MARL is the "non-stationarity problem," which arises because each agent's policy shift alters the environment for its teammates, effectively making the learning target move. To address this, we introduce a new approach called Transfer Empowerment, a novel social intrinsic incentive designed to reliably enable agents to predict and react to one another's actions. This method functions by assigning a higher return to an agent when its action significantly influences a teammate's subsequent behavior. We evaluated Transfer Empowerment across three standard MARL tasks—two board games and a real-time strategy game—demonstrating that it facilitates reliable reaction to partners' actions and enhances joint task performance. Furthermore, we show that Transfer Empowerment is compatible with various existing MARL techniques, including those addressing non-stationarity, local cooperation, and global cooperation. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the method's connection to influence maximization. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/hiroya-koike/Transfer-Incentive}. Identifying materials from visual data is a critical challenge in fields like remote sensing and computer vision, where materials are often heterogeneous and camouflaged within complex backgrounds. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to identify any material from any image with just one representative example. Our approach leverages physics-based rendering to create a synthetic database of material images, which are then paired with real images to train a contrastive learning model. This learned model enables the system to identify a new material anywhere by matching it against the synthetic database. We validate our method using high-resolution satellite imagery, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying representative materials for the International Space Station. Furthermore, we show that our proposed pipeline outperforms existing state-of-the-art single-shot material identification techniques. The source code is available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/one-shot-material-identification. Our findings indicate that physics-based rendering is highly effective for training data-driven models in real-world applications. Additionally, we demonstrate that contrastive learning is a versatile technique that can be applied to various computer vision tasks. Finally, we highlight that our pipeline exhibits strong transferability, successfully adapting to different datasets and scenarios. These results suggest that future research should place greater emphasis on the utility of physics-based rendering and contrastive learning in computer vision. To support this, we have made our synthetic dataset publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/synthetic-material-dataset. We provide an overview of Lie 2-algebras, offering various characterizations through differential equations. Additionally, we present several examples, construct categorical parabolic Lie 2-algebras, and classify the low-dimensional cases. Finally, we demonstrate that every Lie 2-algebra arises as a quotient of a free Lie 2-algebra. This work serves as a foundational guide for Lie 2-algebras, facilitating the categorification of standard Lie algebra concepts. Specifically, it allows for the construction of a cohomology theory for Lie 2-algebras, the classification of extensions, and the categorification of parabolic Lie algebras. The paper concludes with an appendix detailing the equivalence between strict Lie 2-algebras and dg-Lie algebras of degree -1. This research aims to assist in the categorification of Lie algebra notions; related efforts can be found in [1]-[10]. Furthermore, the author's interest in Lie 2-algebras stems from a thesis on categorical parabolic Lie algebras, which will be published as a book by Springer [11]. We introduce a new end-to-end model for keypoint-based image matching that bypasses the traditional two-stage approach relying on local feature descriptors. By utilizing cross-scale patch image codes and fine-tuning a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to map these codes to keypoint locations, our method eliminates the need for keypoint detection. Instead of relying on separate descriptors, we directly compare patch codes across different images to generate keypoint matches. This allows our model to handle generic local features, including complete objects, that standard local detectors often fail to identify. Furthermore, we integrate a transformer-based matching module to establish long-range correlations between keypoints and their corresponding matches. Experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses current state-of-the-art methods on the Pascal 3D+ and NYUv2 datasets. Additionally, it exhibits superior performance on challenging datasets characterized by large viewpoint changes, small scales, and complex backgrounds. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/MAZILab/LoFTR. Video demonstrations can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLC6-6Q65552222222222222222222222222222. This study examines the bias inherent in the Inferred Total Field (ITF) method used for synthesizing line-of-sight (LOS) magnetic field data from vector magnetometer observations. We demonstrate that this algorithm systematically underestimates the absolute magnetic field strength, with the bias intensifying as the angle between the instrument's line of sight and the total field direction increases. Consequently, measurements of weak fields are particularly susceptible to this distortion. We establish that this bias arises from the fundamental design of the ITF method, which relies on a magnetic field direction prior. Furthermore, we identify that magnetic field strength is underestimated when the field vector deviates from the LOS by more than 45 degrees, regardless of the specific prior employed. To mitigate this bias, we propose a straightforward correction algorithm that utilizes magnetic field geometry to calculate and remove the underestimation. This approach is validated using both synthetic and observed data. Our findings indicate that applying this correction restores the accuracy of derived measurements, such as magnetic flux and energy, to the level of the original vector observations. Ultimately, our research confirms that bias in ITF-derived LOS magnetic field data is unavoidable and persists across various magnetic field geometry priors; however, this bias can be effectively corrected through a simple post-processing step. These results are applicable to any data set generated using the ITF method. We conclude that when employing ITF-derived LOS magnetic field data, researchers must account for this bias in their data analysis and subsequent data interpretation. Additionally, we recommend that future studies utilizing derived LOS magnetic field data apply a straightforward correction algorithm to eliminate bias in measurements of weak magnetic fields. Finally, we note that this issue is not unique to the Hinode/SOT data set used in this work, as it is inherent to the ITF method itself. Therefore, any data set utilizing this method, such as SDO/HMI data, may be subject to the same bias. We strongly advise that future research using derived LOS magnetic field data incorporates a correction algorithm to remove this bias. We anticipate that this work will facilitate a more robust understanding of the Sun's magnetic field. Specifically, we suggest that future investigations into the relationship between magnetic field strength and plasma properties, as well as the evolution of magnetic fields over time, should utilize corrected data sets. This is because the current underestimation of magnetic field strength in ITF-derived data may lead to incorrect interpretations of the Sun's magnetic field. This study introduces a novel demand-side management framework that combines consumption scheduling with instantaneous load billing. Within this system, consumers determine their energy usage schedules and pay for electricity based on their actual, instantaneous consumption. To foster efficient resource allocation and equitable cost distribution, we propose a self-governing platform where consumers collaboratively optimize the utility of a concave cost function, which reflects both scheduling efficiency and total billed payment. We further design an incentive-compatible mechanism to ensure the truthful revelation of consumer preferences regarding the concave cost function. Finally, we analyze an aggregative game among consumers to demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of its Nash equilibrium. Simulation results confirm the practical viability of the proposed mechanism and the existence of the Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, these results illustrate that appropriately tuning the concave cost function can encourage consumers to make trade-offs that reduce total payment while enhancing scheduling efficiency. Additionally, the mechanism ensures that consumers with higher peak-to-valley ratios and those with lower energy consumption levels receive greater cost reduction benefits. Finally, numerical results indicate that the proposed mechanism outperforms the time-of-use pricing scheme in terms of scheduling efficiency and cost reduction. Notably, the mechanism achieves a significant increase in scheduling efficiency, rising from 10.2% to 107.5% as the concavity of the cost function intensifies. This improvement is particularly pronounced during peak hours, where scheduling efficiency increases by 11.5% to 12.8%. Furthermore, the mechanism reduces total payment by 10.3% to 11.5%, representing a 1.5% to 1.7% decrease compared to the total payment under the time-of-use pricing scheme. These findings hold true across various scenarios, including different numbers of consumers, varying peak-to-valley ratios, and diverse consumption levels. Consequently, the mechanism is especially effective in improving scheduling efficiency when the population is heterogeneous in their peak-to-valley ratios and consumption levels. Finally, we show that the proposed mechanism is more sensitive to changes in the concavity parameter than the time-of-use pricing scheme. Specifically, increasing the concavity of the cost function leads to a 1.5% to 1.7% reduction in total payment under the time-of-use scheme, whereas the proposed mechanism achieves a more substantial reduction of 10.3% to 11.5%. This study examines charged black strings within Rastall theory, deriving the modified metric and subsequent thermodynamic properties under the Rastall conservation law. By applying the modified conservation equation, we determine the Hawking temperature and analyze the impact of the Rastall parameter on this temperature. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of the Rastall parameter on the event horizon, Hawking temperature, and entropy, noting that these parameters can be tuned to adjust such characteristics. Finally, we demonstrate that the Rastall parameter influences the Hawking temperature, a finding that could be verified through observational data. Additionally, we present the graphical representation of the Hawking temperature for this system. This study examines the application of spectral measures to analyze convergence rates within the classical ergodic average framework of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem. By employing a straightforward analytical method, we first establish a concise inequality that connects the mean square deviation of the ergodic average from its time average with the spectral measure of the underlying dynamical system. Leveraging this inequality, we derive several findings that enable a more precise estimation of the mean square deviation, particularly for systems characterized by a discrete spectrum. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any periodic system, the mean square deviation adheres to a $1/T$ rate, where $T$ signifies the period. Furthermore, we present a counterexample illustrating that no universal convergence rate can be established for the classical ergodic average across all measure-preserving systems. Finally, we explore the connection between this inequality and the uncertainty principle in quantum mechanics. These outcomes are achieved through an investigation into the interplay between the spectral measure and the commutator of two self-adjoint operators, one of which is a rank-one projection. Notably, the proof of this inequality relies on a novel inequality concerning the expectation value of the commutator between two self-adjoint operators, a finding that may hold independent significance. Additionally, we provide a geometric interpretation of this new finding within Hilbert space. Our methodology is notably more direct compared to prior approaches in the literature, which often involved intricate constructions. This simplified approach is anticipated to prove valuable in deriving analogous inequalities and in the broader analysis of uncertainty relations. Our findings may also contribute to the ongoing discussion regarding the complementary relationship between the Heisenberg and Robertson uncertainty relations. Finally, we outline several potential directions for future research. This article is structured as a tutorial on utilizing spectral measures to evaluate convergence rates in classical ergodic theory, with a specific focus on quantum systems possessing a discrete spectrum. We demonstrate that these techniques are not only applicable to periodic systems but also to various other discrete spectrum systems, including those with quasi-periodic behavior. The paper is designed to be accessible to graduate students and researchers in both mathematics and physics. We have made every effort to ensure that all necessary background information is provided, aiming to make this work a valuable resource for those interested in these topics. We introduce a straightforward method for detecting metal-poor stars using the full-sky blue/photometric spectra from the Gaia mission. This approach relies on a single criterion: the ratio of flux at 3800 Å to that at 4000 Å. This ratio serves as a robust indicator of metallicity, as metal-poor stars exhibit a distinct flux peak at 3800 Å caused by the absence of metal absorption features. By applying this condition, we can efficiently identify metal-poor stars within the extensive Gaia BP/RP spectral catalog. Our analysis of the current Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) catalog reveals that this condition successfully identifies stars with [Fe/H] < -2.0. Furthermore, we have developed a selection criterion to isolate stars with [Fe/H] < -3.0, which is particularly valuable for future studies targeting the most metal-deficient population. We estimate that this method can identify approximately 1000 stars with [Fe/H] < -3.0 from the BP/RP spectroscopic catalog. This technique is broadly applicable to any catalog containing blue/UV spectra, offering a valuable tool for the study of extremely metal-poor stars. The code implementing this condition is publicly available at https://github.com/astro-tpa/tpa_code. We anticipate that this method will facilitate the discovery of numerous new metal-poor stars in upcoming Gaia data releases. Additionally, we have identified several new metal-poor stars from Gaia BP/RP spectra that were previously missed by the Gaia Collaboration et al. (2023) study. These newly discovered stars, which were not included in the ESO/Gaia Early Data Analysis Facility (G-EDAF) catalog, are listed in Table 1 of our paper. We have obtained high-resolution spectra for these stars to confirm their metal-poor status and to measure their precise kinematics. We believe that employing this method will aid future researchers in efficiently selecting targets for high-resolution follow-up observations. This study examines the relationship between environmental factors and global Blaze Season Severity (BSS), defined as the total burned area per country during each season. By analyzing BSS data from 1979 to 2018, we investigate correlations with the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and establish country-specific forecasting models. Our findings indicate that El Niño events consistently trigger heightened Blaze Season Severity across all nations. Additionally, we demonstrate that forecasting models utilizing local climate variables achieve superior performance compared to those relying on the Ni\~no 3.4 index. The source code for these models is accessible at \url{https://github.com/DeepLearningTechnologies/BlazeSeasons}. This research holds significant practical value for governments and organizations responsible for fire prevention and response, enabling them to prepare more effectively for seasonal blaze conditions. Furthermore, it aids climate scientists in understanding the specific impacts of El Ni\~no on each country. The global dataset used in this analysis is available at \url{https://github.com/DeepLearningTechnologies/BlazeSeasons/tree/master/data}. We anticipate that this work will inspire similar analyses of El Ni\~no's effects on other countries and additional climate phenomena. The methodology employed is replicable for any country provided that seasonal severity data is available. We have also developed a country-specific Blaze Season Severity forecasting model for Chile, which is documented in our paper on Chilean Blaze Seasons. This paper is structured into three main sections: Section 2 details the data collection process, Section 3 presents the analysis and forecasting models, and Section 4 outlines the conclusions. This study investigates the reliability of various lexical and syntactic metrics for assessing morphological complexity. We gathered and analyzed eight corpus-based measures from literature, applying both linear and non-linear statistical methods to examine their interrelationships. Results indicate that these measures cluster into two distinct groups: one comprising length-based functions (such as L1/Lemma, L1/Lemma+Depth, and MLTI) that strongly correlate with each other, and another consisting of diverse functional and structural indicators (including MLTI_S, MLTI_D, MLTI_S+D, MLTI_N, MLTI_S+N+D, MLTI_N+Depth, and MLTI_S+N+Depth) which are statistically independent of the first group and of each other. Finally, we validated these findings using manual human ratings of morphological complexity, confirming that the corpus-based measures effectively align with human perception. Consequently, we conclude that a comprehensive evaluation of morphological complexity necessitates a multi-faceted approach utilizing both syntactic and lexical measures. Furthermore, we offer practical recommendations for researchers selecting appropriate measures for specific tasks, based on our statistical analysis and validation against human judgment. We investigate gravitational lensing within galaxy clusters, focusing on the substructure generated by satellite galaxies and dark matter halos. Our analysis employs the convergence power spectrum, $C_\kappa^\ell$, to characterize this effect. We demonstrate that the amplitude of $C_\kappa^\ell$ at low multipoles ($\ell \lesssim 10$) is primarily determined by the mean mass of satellite galaxies, whereas high-multipole modes ($\ell \gtrsim 100$) are more sensitive to dark matter halos. Furthermore, we show that self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) can substantially suppress the amplitudes of $C_\kappa^\ell$ at both small and large multipoles. Finally, we apply our framework to the Coma cluster, deriving constraints on halo properties and the self-interaction cross section of dark matter. These constraints indicate that SIDM can be ruled out in the Coma cluster if the halo mass function aligns with the Sheth-Tormen prediction. Additionally, we find that SIDM can lower the upper limit on the dark matter fraction in the central galaxy by a factor of two. This suggests that SIDM may resolve the core-cusp problem in galaxy centers, while preserving the NFW density profile in the surrounding dark matter halo. Consequently, SIDM remains a viable candidate for dark matter. However, further research is required to accurately predict the signal of substructure in cluster light profiles and to identify the most effective clusters for testing the SIDM hypothesis. This study represents a pioneering effort to constrain dark matter properties using gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters. Future efforts should prioritize measuring substructure signals in high-resolution lensing data from clusters such as Coma and Virgo. Moreover, it is essential to investigate the impact of baryonic physics on substructure and the resulting gravitational lensing signals. Finally, future lensing studies of galaxy clusters should aim to constrain the halo mass function and the dark matter self-interaction cross section. We conclude that the most promising approach to test the SIDM hypothesis involves measuring the convergence power spectrum in galaxy clusters. This method offers a direct probe of halo properties and allows for the separation of halo contributions from the smooth gravitational potential. Additionally, it avoids the need for assumptions regarding the spatial distribution of substructure. Model simplification is a critical technique for reducing the computational demands of state estimation. The widely used subsampling algorithm, which reduces a model's state dimension by discarding selected state variables, is generally applied to fully observed nonlinear models. This paper extends the subsampling approach to partially observed nonlinear models by employing a continuous relaxation of the observation model. We demonstrate that the relaxed subsampling filter yields optimal results when utilizing a Gaussian Markov random field continuous relaxation. Furthermore, we show that appropriately approximating the joint distribution of the filtered subsampled state allows for the construction of a recursive filter with virtually identical performance. The proposed method is evaluated on a simple state-space model and a real-world problem involving the localization of a wireless sensor within a room. Simulation results indicate that the suggested algorithm outperforms existing methods. Additionally, the algorithm is observed to be more robust to model mismatches compared to other approaches. Finally, the paper demonstrates that the proposed method can significantly decrease the computational load of state estimation. To our knowledge, this work represents the first extension of model simplification techniques to the domain of partial observations. The software includes implementations of the relaxation and approximation algorithms, as well as a demonstration comparing the performance of various model simplification algorithms on a simple state-space model. This paper introduces M-ar-K-Fast, a novel extension of M-ar-FA, representing a new category of mixed factor analysis models. The term "mixed" signifies the capacity of M-ar-K-Fast to simultaneously identify known mixing factors and discover latent common factors. M-ar-K-Fast builds upon K-Fast, a mixed regression model designed to recover both mixing and latent factors from a known set of observations. By incorporating a specific probabilistic noise model, M-ar-K-Fast enhances the information extracted from these observations. We outline the theoretical foundations of this extended model and present an efficient algorithm for parameter estimation. Furthermore, the study demonstrates M-ar-K-Fast's utility across various applications, including the analysis of Twitter activity, the Common crawl dataset, and the Wikipedia dataset. The results indicate that applying this method to such data yields valuable insights into latent factors and user behavior. Additionally, we show that M-ar-K-Fast can uncover latent factors even when observations are provided by a limited number of sources. Finally, the paper explores potential extensions of M-ar-K-Fast, including its application to M-ar-FA with missing observations and its use as a pre-processing step for downstream factorization tasks. The implementation is available at https://github.com/maurogatti/marfast. The source code for replicating our experiments can be found at https://github.com/maurogatti/marfast/tree/master/data. Supplementary materials for M-ar-FA with missing observations are accessible at https://github.com/maurogatti/marfast/tree/master/data/MarFAMissing. This study introduces a real-time incident detection framework for traffic monitoring by integrating spatio-temporal data mining with social media processing. The system identifies traffic events by analyzing geotagged social media posts and updating traffic demand in near real-time. Temporal analysis pinpoints event occurrences through a time series anomaly detection method based on the autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) model. Subsequently, a geotag-based spatio-temporal analysis technique estimates traffic demand across a time-varying road network, using the distribution of user mentions in geotags to reflect traffic conditions. Finally, a novel incident detection algorithm combines these spatio-temporal insights to identify events. The proposed method was evaluated using geotagged posts from Twitter and Sina Weibo, with performance compared against traditional approaches. Results indicate that the proposed approach significantly enhances detection accuracy and reduces processing time. Furthermore, case studies in Beijing and New York City demonstrate the method's effectiveness in identifying incidents within a dynamic, time-varying road network. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/SocialMedia4Traffic. The findings from this research will be published in the IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems. Keywords: Traffic incident detection, time-varying road network, spatio-temporal analysis, traffic demand estimation, traffic monitoring, social media.

This study establishes existence and uniqueness findings for specific elliptic equations defined on the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^n$ involving surface measures. The analysis demonstrates that solutions are necessarily singular at isolated points, with their singularities fully characterized. These results have significant applications in solving the spherical Sums of Powers problem. The proof methodology relies on a novel technique for decomposing functions on the sphere into orthogonal Legendre polynomials, which yields the existence of a specific type of sign-regular function. This approach is also utilized in related work by the second author regarding the Sums of Powers problem on the sphere. Additionally, the paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions for the equation $\Delta u + \lambda u = \mu$, where $\mu$ is a surface measure, and examines the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the polynomial equation $\sum_{i=0}^{k} a_i x^i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} b_i x^i$. Finally, the authors present an illustrative example to highlight the significance of the polynomial equation findings. The content is structured into ten sections, with the first six focusing on the primary objective and the remaining four addressing applications and examples. The initial four sections are designed to be self-contained for readers. In the current digital landscape, risk-aware bidding has become a critical capability for companies operating in online ecosystems. This research investigates risk-aware bidding within display advertising, specifically addressing the challenge of maximizing expected value under budget constraints. We begin by examining the widely used expected value optimization framework, demonstrating that it suffers from significant flaws when handling large-scale budgets. Subsequently, we introduce ARVB, a novel algorithm designed to overcome these limitations. Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that ARVB surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we explore how risk-aware bidding can be extended to other domains, such as search advertising. Overall, this study aims to provide a comprehensive reference for risk-aware bidding applications in various digital contexts. Wigner negativity is a fundamental characteristic of quantum states that enables non-classical protocols like quantum computing and secure communication. This study investigates how often Wigner negativity is required when quantum systems are controlled. We contrast quantum systems guided by Wigner functions with those guided by quasi-probability distributions derived from alternative state representations. Our findings demonstrate that, in certain scenarios, Wigner negativity is not essential for achieving quantum guidance. Furthermore, we present a protocol that reduces the probability of negativity, thereby enhancing the fidelity of guided trajectories. These insights could prove valuable for designing future applications of quantum systems. Additionally, we highlight that these results extend to scenarios involving multiple quantum systems. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings for quantum control theory and quantum computing. Specifically, within the context of quantum optimal control, we show that the cost function can be formulated to incorporate system guidance, utilizing this approach to generate a new cost function for the universal control problem. This new formulation ensures that the resulting optimal control problem remains convex. These contributions are expected to advance the fields of quantum control theory and optimal control. Additionally, regarding quantum computing, we examine the application of quantum systems guided by Wigner functions to variational quantum algorithms, demonstrating that Wigner negativity can be leveraged to improve the performance of these algorithms. Overall, this work establishes a new framework for the theory of quantum control and optimization, with potential applications in quantum computing. The study also features a rich collection of numerical examples that illustrate the effectiveness of Wigner guidance and its utility in various applications. These examples will deepen the understanding of Wigner negativity and facilitate the design of future quantum systems. Finally, the paper includes an appendix with a review of the Wigner function and its properties, which will benefit readers who are new to the field. In secure quantum key distribution, raw key generation relies on the randomness of measurement outcomes, which are fundamentally rooted in the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. This probabilistic generation is driven by the random selection of measurement bases and the random positioning of qubits within the Hilbert space. However, the randomness inherent in qubit placement is typically derived from a random number generator (RNG) that produces a random seed for privacy amplification. If this seed is not uniformly distributed, the security of the final key is jeopardized. To address this, we introduce a secure limit analysis for quantum key distribution that accounts for non-uniform random seed distribution during privacy amplification. Our proposed security analysis is based on the smooth min-entropy of the raw key. We demonstrate that the secret key rate can be calculated by adjusting the smooth min-entropy to reflect the non-uniformity of the random seed. Furthermore, we establish that the security proof for qubit-based quantum key distribution remains valid even when the random seed distribution is non-uniform. These findings offer a theoretical framework for evaluating the security of quantum key distribution systems that utilize non-uniform random seeds for privacy amplification. Additionally, this study holds significance for systems where the measurement basis is also selected from a non-uniform distribution. We illustrate the practical application of this analysis through the limit evaluation of a six-state quantum key distribution system employing a non-uniform basis distribution. Our results indicate that the achievable secure key rate is reduced due to the non-uniform basis distribution, and we provide the specific quantitative impact of this reduction. This work provides a practical method for assessing the security performance of quantum key distribution systems under non-uniform random seed distribution. Ultimately, this research can guide the development of quantum key distribution systems that utilize non-uniform random seeds for privacy amplification. We conclude that this theoretical analysis serves as a valuable tool for the practical application of quantum key distribution systems. Finally, we suggest that future research should explore the potential of non-uniform random seed distribution in enhancing the performance of quantum key distribution systems. The theoretical analysis of quantum key distribution security presented in this study can be applied to various other quantum key distribution protocols. We anticipate that this theoretical analysis will contribute to the future development of quantum key distribution technology. In summary, the work described in this paper is a significant contribution to the field of quantum information security. It provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for analyzing the security of quantum key distribution systems using non-uniform random seeds for privacy amplification. This study examines the coalescence dynamics of exchangeable Markov processes within a broad class known as Feller processes, which are generated by positive definite kernels on the non-negative real line. These dynamics are characterized by a coalescence measure that can be derived using only elementary calculus. The analysis covers numerous significant special cases, including the standard coalescent, the uniform canonical measure on the infinite rooted binary tree, and various measures on the space of partition-valued paths. Furthermore, the paper investigates a sampling process for Feller processes along the time axis, yielding a corresponding coalescence measure and demonstrating its application in calculating the absolute rank distribution of a Feller process on the unit interval. This result holds for a specific family of processes parameterized by the coalescence measure. The methodology is also applied to the weighted uniform canonical measure on the infinite rooted $k$-ary tree. The paper concludes with several open questions. Notably, the formula for the absolute rank distribution is observed to be closely related to the sampling distribution of uniform random points on the unit interval given their coalescence measure. Dark matter may possess intrinsic spin, which could be exposed through scattering experiments with polarized nuclei. In the standard framework, such interactions are typically analyzed using non-relativistic effective field theories. However, if dark matter is accelerated to high energies, relativistic effects become significant. This study investigates the necessary relativistic extensions for spin-dependent scattering, deriving constraints on the effective operators and examining the resulting cross sections. Furthermore, we explore applications of these findings to specific dark matter candidates, including the fermionic WIMP, the Majoron dark photon, and the majoron itself. Our results indicate that relativistic effects can substantially alter cross sections, a phenomenon that must be accounted for when interpreting data from future high-energy dark matter detection efforts. Additionally, we demonstrate that a non-zero majorana mass can induce a dependence on the scattering angle, offering a means to distinguish between relativistic and non-relativistic regimes. Finally, we show that for relativistic dark matter, spin-dependent scattering can occur even with scalar operators, a possibility absent in the non-relativistic limit. These findings are also applicable to electron-positron annihilation into dark matter, which may be investigated at upcoming colliders. This paper introduces a delay-enhanced variant of conventional non-coherent differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM), which leverages the full energy of every symbol. By utilizing data from earlier time intervals, this approach enhances detection sensitivity, surpassing the performance of standard methods that process only one symbol. Analytical derivations of the equivalent differential scheme and a comparison with existing techniques are provided. The study also examines the computational complexity relative to other schemes and outlines potential applications for the proposed method. Reward learning (RL) represents a promising approach for automatically deriving rewards from demonstrations, thereby eliminating the need for manual annotation. However, current methods often demand substantial computational resources and extended processing times. This paper introduces VACOR, a novel visual cluster-based reward learning framework designed to enhance efficiency. VACOR accelerates reward parameter acquisition by employing visual cluster ranking and limits the required computation through the use of visual graph cuts. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a significant reduction in time complexity. Furthermore, evaluations on both simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks confirm that VACOR learns effective reward parameters and facilitates robust imitation learning. This study employs the diquark clustering model to investigate nucleon structure characteristics within noncommutative space-time. We classify the contributions of vector and scalar channels using 't Hooft's large-Nc limit, demonstrating that nonleading structures in this regime can be observed through precise experimental measurements of proton electromagnetic form factors in scattering processes. Furthermore, we calculate the electromagnetic form factors for protons and neutrons in noncommutative space-time, revealing that deviations from commutative structures are directly proportional to the space-time noncommutativity parameter. Finally, we present potential deviations from conventional protons and neutrons in terms of charge and magnetic moment distributions within the noncommutative framework. These findings aim to provide a theoretical basis for future experimental investigations of nucleon properties in noncommutative space-time. Additionally, we include an appendix detailing the derivation of the Fierz transformation applicable to noncommutative space-time. Our work serves as a foundation for future research into proton and neutron structure characteristics in noncommutative environments. This study investigates the topological characteristics of highly frustrated Toric code models on a square lattice, which serve as two-dimensional quantum spin-lattice systems. By conducting extensive quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we identify a reentrant phase featuring a deconfined Z$_2$ topological order alongside a Z$_2$ geometric line order. This geometric line order arises from the order parameter linked to the string order parameter within the frustrated toric code framework. Furthermore, we observe that the string order parameter exhibits a power-law behavior in the thermodynamic limit, contrasting with its exponential decay in the toric code. These findings demonstrate that topologically ordered phases can coexist with geometric line order, thereby expanding the spectrum of possible states in topologically ordered systems. Additionally, we note that the string order operator functions as a topological marker for these topologically ordered phases. Finally, we propose that this reentrant phase, marked by the interplay between topological and geometric line orders, may be realized in the quantum Ising model subjected to both transverse and bond-random fields. The reentrant phase displays competition between topological and geometric line orders, resulting in a complex phase diagram. This research holds significant implications for the development of topological quantum computing, topological quantum sensors, and topological quantum memory. The statistical distribution of these random matrices is defined by an average over complex Gaussian disorder with a finite bandwidth, where the disorder is weighted by an exponential factor involving auxiliary fields coupled to the disorder's current density. By applying the saddle-point approximation, we derive a simplified model with finite dimensionality. This resulting finite-dimensional model retains the core characteristics of the original system, specifically a phase transition between localized and delocalized regimes. Furthermore, we investigate the model's behavior at low temperatures and in the large-N limit, where N represents the number of bands. Our analysis indicates that when N scales as 1/epsilon^2 (with epsilon being the bandwidth), the model converges to the Hermitian Gross-Witten-Witten matrix model. Additionally, we explore the relationship between our framework and the Hofstadter model, which describes electrons on a two-dimensional lattice subjected to a magnetic field. Finally, we compute the free energy of our model within the large-N limit and compare these findings with the Hofstadter butterfly. This comparison reveals that the Hofstadter butterfly emerges only in the narrow-band limit, where the model approaches a lattice version of the Hofstadter model. In this specific limit, we observe a complete description of the Hofstadter model, including its phase diagram and the Hofstadter butterfly. The latter is characterized by the interplay between the irrationality of the flux per unit cell and the rationality of N. We also discuss the model's behavior in the rational limit, where N is held fixed while the flux varies. In this scenario, the Hofstadter butterfly is only partially captured, and we provide a detailed analysis of the phase diagram. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for Hofstadter fermions in the fractional quantum Hall regime. We investigate a straightforward, meaning-centric strategy for building a dialogue understanding model that bypasses the need for task-specific training data. This approach leverages an existing general-purpose language model by pre-training it to capture the semantic meaning of dialogue utterances. Specifically, we define dialogue meaning as the collection of semantic components present within an utterance and subsequently map these components to specific words within the text. Our method utilizes an existing semantic parsing dataset to establish a semantic parsing layer on top of the pre-trained model, thereby learning to identify semantic components and locate corresponding words. We assess this model across three prevalent dialogue understanding tasks: intent classification, slot filling, and dialogue state tracking. Experimental results demonstrate that this pre-trained model achieves performance comparable to models trained with task-specific data, while offering the added benefit of requiring no such data for training. Furthermore, we find that this model outperforms several state-of-the-art approaches that rely on task-specific data. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical factor in the deployment of machine learning models. However, the prevailing approach to measuring this quality, known as post-hoc explainability, assesses human understanding of already-trained models using techniques like saliency maps and feature importance. This method has significant drawbacks, including the high cost of evaluation and the potential for misleading results. To address these limitations, we propose a novel pre-post-hoc explainability framework that quantifies interpretability during the training process itself. This framework employs a human learner who attempts to replicate an algorithm's decisions using a step-by-step explanation strategy. The learner's success rate serves as a proxy for the algorithm's interpretability. We demonstrate that this framework effectively distingu between the interpretability of various decision trees and post-selected neural networks. Furthermore, we introduce the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS), a new metric that aggregates performance across all possible explanation strategies to provide a comprehensive assessment of an algorithm's interpretability. Our experiments reveal that CCS can clearly differentiate the interpretability of different neural network architectures. Additionally, we show that CCS serves as a strong predictor of generalization performance, outperforming standard metrics such as the number of parameters and tree size. Finally, we explore how both the explainability strategy and the learner's competence influence the proposed framework. These findings offer valuable guidance for designing models with specific interpretability characteristics and for developing appropriate explanation strategies for post-hoc analysis. Outlier detection is a critical challenge in data mining, with Isolation Forest (iF) emerging as a highly effective anomaly isolation technique. However, its practical utility is often hindered by the substantial memory and computational resources required for training and deployment. This paper introduces TiWS-iF, a novel approach designed to enable the rapid training and deployment of iF models within the constraints of Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) and other memory- or compute-limited environments. TiWS-iF achieves this by leveraging the principles of Isolation Surface (iS) and employing a quantization strategy that reduces the model's memory footprint to a few kilobytes. Experimental results demonstrate that TiWS-iF-iF can be trained in under a second on a Raspberry Pi 4B and deployed on an ESP32, all while maintaining competitive detection rates. Furthermore, we illustrate the model's applicability to non-classical iF scenarios, such as detecting anomalies in time series data. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/fernando-ramos/TiWS-iF}. Our findings indicate that TiWS-iF offers superior performance in terms of memory usage and training speed compared to existing iF compression techniques. This paper introduces a reparameterization of the standard log-transformed shape parameter within extreme value analysis, specifically for data modeled as a Poisson process. We demonstrate that this alternative parameterization yields a distribution that is significantly less skewed than the one associated with the conventional log-transformed parameter. Consequently, this improvement facilitates more reliable quantification of parameter uncertainty. A simulation study indicates that the proposed reparameterization enhances the Bayesian estimation of the generalized Pareto model's parameters. Additionally, we apply this method to estimate parameters for Poisson processes derived from the temporal distribution of high-impact Twitter mentions for the companies Amazon, Apple, and Facebook. All findings, including results from the simulation study and the real-world examples, are supported by R code available at https://github.com/alejandro-ortega/PPIEP. This approach is also integrated into the R package `extremepoisson`, which can be accessed at https://github.com/alejandro-ortega/extremepoisson. Furthermore, the package includes a new function, `gevpp_mcmc`, designed for Bayesian estimation of the Poisson GEV density parameters using the proposed reparameterization. This work extends the methodology established in [1] to the broader context of the generalized extreme value density. The author demonstrates that the average cross section remains constant within fixed regions, characterized by a constant second moment of the wave function. Furthermore, an expression for the time-averaged potential is derived, indicating that the average cross section in non-stationary regions is determined by the parameter $\eta$. This parameter is defined as the ratio of the average momentum to the average potential. The analysis covers both bound and scattering states. **Context.** The presence of a metallicity spread within a single stellar population has been suggested as a potential explanation for the existence of multiple populations in globular clusters. However, this interpretation remains controversial, as it requires abundance differences to be detected with sufficient precision to rule out systematic errors.

**Aims.** This study aims to determine the abundances of light elements (C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, K, Ca) in the globular cluster NGC 2808 using high-precision spectroscopy of its most luminous red giant branch stars.

**Methods.** We conducted high-resolution spectroscopic observations of 10 bright stars in NGC 2808. Abundances were derived using the equivalent width method, with errors estimated via Monte Carlo simulations.

**Results.** We report high-precision abundances for the ten observed stars. Our findings indicate a metallicity spread of approximately 0.1 dex among these stars, with a standard deviation in iron abundance of $\sigma_{\rm Fe/H} = 0.09 \pm 0.03$ dex. This spread is consistent with variations in Na, Al, and K.

**Conclusions.** The detection of a metallicity spread in NGC 2808 supports the theory that multiple stellar populations exist within globular clusters. This conclusion is reinforced by our high-precision measurements of the C/N ratio, which show a spread of $\sigma_{\rm C/N} = 0.25 \pm 0.05$ dex. Additionally, we observed a trend between the C/N ratio and the [Fe/H] value, suggesting that the spread in metallicity in NGC 2808 may be linked to the spread in the initial mass of the first generation. These results are also consistent with the presence of a third stellar population in the cluster. Finally, we demonstrate that the equivalent width method is a viable approach for measuring the metallicity spread in globular clusters.

Investigating the duration of first exit times (FETD) is essential for understanding single-file particle diffusion. This study examines a system where $N$ particles, confined within a one-dimensional box of length $L$ and subject to strong entropic repulsion, undergo 1D diffusion. The analysis explores how varying $L$ and $N$ influences the exit duration statistics. Furthermore, the exit duration distribution is modeled using two distinct approaches: first, by calculating the time an exit point remains unvisited, and second, by determining the time required for the exit point to reach its target position for the first time. Finally, the force derived from the exit duration distribution is compared against the entropic force of the 1D system. The findings indicate that the entropic force is repulsive and diminishes as the number of particles increases. Additionally, the entropic force is found to be independent of the box's length. Finally, the paper demonstrates that entropic repulsion within the box results in a non-exponential distribution for the random variable representing exit times. Quantum mechanics presents a unique measurement framework where the order of operations matters, allowing for the definition of conditional probabilities for observables that differ from those in classical probability theory. This discrepancy creates a challenge when interpreting measurement data, as researchers must decide whether to apply Bayes' theorem for data analysis or accept that posterior inferences drawn from such measurements lack consistency. To resolve this dilemma, we propose treating observables as operators within a quantum system and utilizing the quantum analog of Bayes' theorem to determine conditional probabilities. This approach allows for the calculation of both prior and posterior states, ensuring that posterior inferences derived from quantum measurements are consistent. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the consistency of posterior inferences depends on whether the measurement is unambiguous. Finally, we illustrate how to perform posterior inference following a measurement using the quantum weak value formalism. These findings establish a consistent methodology for performing posterior inference based on measurements within quantum mechanics. This Letter reports initial findings from a systematic investigation into the Lattice QCD framework for small volumes, aiming to determine if finite systems exhibit a crossover transition and how this response varies with size. Furthermore, we explore the potential of this approach to investigate finite-volume effects on thermodynamic quantities, correlation functions, and spectral densities. Specifically, we provide preliminary results for the unnormalized trace anomaly and energy density, noting that the latter aligns with prior Monte Carlo calculations. Additionally, we present results for the normalized chiral condensate, observing that while it drops sharply at high temperatures as expected, it remains significantly elevated above its infinite-volume counterpart at the critical temperature. These findings suggest that further analysis of other thermodynamic observables could yield insights into whether finite volumes undergo a phase transition. Finally, we outline preliminary efforts to calculate the pseudoscalar channel correlation function, which is closely linked to chiral symmetry breaking. This work represents a significant advancement over existing studies of the chiral condensate in small volumes. Ultimately, we conclude that this method offers a viable pathway for investigating finite-size effects in QCD. Keywords: Lattice QCD, finite volume, chiral symmetry breaking. The $k$-th Ext group within the Steenrod algebra, where $k$ is an even number, decomposes into a direct sum of "trivial" and "non-trivial" components. The Poincaré series for these "non-trivial" Ext groups have been established up to the 40-th Adams spectral sequence sheet. This note addresses the case of sheet 42, demonstrating that the "non-trivial" part of $\mathrm{Ext}_*^{A} (k, k)$ for $e=42$ consists of a single element. Consequently, the Poincaré series for the "non-trivial" Ext groups is now known up to sheet 44. Additionally, the authors provide a method for calculating the Poincaré series of "non-trivial" Ext groups as a quotient of polynomial rings. Using this approach, the series is determined up to sheet 50. Furthermore, the paper presents a general formula for the Poincaré series of trivial Ext groups and derives a formula for the Poincaré series of Ext groups as a quotient of polynomial rings. These methods are also applied to calculate the Poincaré series for Ext groups at degrees $e=46$ and $e=50$. Finally, the authors identify the Poincaré series for "non-trivial" Ext groups as quotients of polynomial rings in degrees $e=44$ and $e=48$. The results for $e=48$ are derived via a spectral sequence originating from the Poincaré series of the 46-th degree. The paper concludes with a conjecture regarding the Poincaré series for "non-trivial" Ext groups, which posits that it can be expressed as a quotient of polynomial rings. This conjecture has been verified for all degrees $e \leq 50$. The authors express their gratitude to Professor Jie Wu for his insightful discussions. The Lyman-alpha line serves as a critical tool for studying the early universe, yet its observation is hindered by the lack of suitable ground-based telescopes and filters. This study introduces a novel filter design intended to enable the direct, high-contrast imaging of Lyman-alpha emission from distant galaxies. The proposed filter features a 1.5 Å full width at half maximum (FWHM) passband centered at 5107 Å, spanning a 1000 Å range with a 100 mm diameter. To achieve the necessary optical performance, we developed a multi-layer dielectric coating utilizing MgF2, HfO2, and LaF3. This work presents the first experimental characterization of such a filter, detailing its fabrication and testing outcomes. Results indicate that the coated filters meet the design specifications, offering a transmission of 70% at 1.0 FWHM and blocking 99% of light outside the passband. These findings suggest that direct astronomical photometry at the Lyman-alpha line is feasible. Furthermore, the fabricated filters exhibit stability under ultraviolet exposure and maintain their optical properties after multiple thermal cycles. This research serves as a proof of concept for producing filters capable of isolating the Lyman-alpha line from the overwhelming continuum background. The fabricated filters are available for use in astronomical applications. Additionally, we propose a 100 mm diameter filter as an ideal instrument for future space telescopes, such as the proposed NASA Habitable Worlds Observatory. This proposal is supported by the need to observe the high-redshift universe, specifically to study the Epoch of Reionization and the formation of the first stars and galaxies. The paper concludes with a discussion of the scientific potential offered by such a filter. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that high-performance filters are achievable through advanced dielectric coating technology, paving the way for direct Lyman-alpha photometry. Future efforts will focus on scaling up the production of these filters. The current fabrication process is optimized for laboratory-scale research, but expanding production to meet scientific demand requires a more efficient manufacturing method. We will explore alternative coating techniques, such as sputtering, to enhance production rates. Additionally, we plan to investigate the use of more durable substrates, like sapphire, to ensure filter longevity in space environments. These advancements will facilitate the development of instruments capable of high-contrast Lyman-alpha photometry. This paper addresses the graph symmetric problem within distributed optimization frameworks, focusing on systems that exhibit graph symmetries, such as those common in smart grid applications. These symmetries enable the reduction of high-dimensional optimization problems to a series of significantly lower-dimensional subproblems. By utilizing graph filters, we enhance the scalability of distributed algorithms by minimizing the number of agents involved in each distributed step. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under specific filter designs, the entire distributed process can be governed by a single agent, effectively transforming the distributed optimization problem into a non-distributed one. Additionally, we present a method to estimate the order of the graph filter required for each distributed step, showing that this order is independent of the total number of agents. Finally, we illustrate the application of graph symmetric systems in smart grids, specifically concerning distributed optimal power flow and frequency regulation. Simulation results confirm the advantages of our algorithms regarding scalability and computational complexity. Notably, we find that the distributed algorithms proposed in [1] and [2] are special cases of our approach when employing filters of order one. This paper introduces a new method for dynamically maintaining indexed image collections. We propose and evaluate a family of algorithms designed to efficiently manage updates to subset partitions of image feature spaces, which serve as the foundation for indexing and retrieval. Our approach is application-agnostic, requiring no specific knowledge of the image descriptors used. We assess the performance of various indexing strategies on a large-scale web image dataset, comparing both static and dynamic methods. The results demonstrate that dynamic partitions can significantly reduce storage requirements while maintaining or even enhancing retrieval performance. Furthermore, our algorithmic family offers the flexibility to balance trade-offs between storage efficiency and retrieval speed, allowing users to optimize for their specific needs. Finally, we illustrate how this dynamic indexing framework can be extended to support multi-query workloads. Empirical evaluations confirm that our method is scalable, capable of handling image collections with billions of entries. All code and data required to replicate our experiments are publicly available. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of subset partitions to image indexing and the first demonstration of their ability to enable efficient dynamic indexing. Our source code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexschroeder123/dynamic-image-indexing. The paper itself is accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01001. This study investigates keyless verification for the Bernoulli(0.5) erasure channel, where a prover and a verifier jointly utilize a shared secret key to allow a computationally limited verifier to validate computations performed by a more powerful adversary. While previous research has primarily concentrated on the single-probability distribution scenario, this work extends the analysis to cases involving multiple distribution parameters. We introduce a single-probability scheme that is provably optimal and an encryption-based approach for the multi-parameter scenario, demonstrating that these methods represent the best linear and local linear strategies, respectively. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound on the single-probability threshold, prove the optimality of our single-probability scheme within this limit, and propose an infinite family of linear schemes for multi-parameter cases, each achieving optimality. Additionally, we derive an upper bound on the single-probability threshold for the multi-parameter scenario and prove the optimality of our encryption-based scheme under this bound. Finally, we develop an upper bound on secret key requirements for multi-parameter cases and present an upper bound on the single-probability threshold applicable to all schemes. These findings are achieved through a combination of explicit constructions, explicit or implicit lower bounds, and the application of existing literature. Notably, our lower bounds rely on a novel application of the hypercontractive inequality, which may have broader applications in this research domain. This study examines the motion of a charged particle within a washboard potential under the influence of a radio-frequency (rf) field. The particle's dispersionless trajectory is governed by three key parameters: the dc field strength, rf field amplitude, and particle charge. We demonstrate that rf heating can be mitigated by appropriately configuring these parameters. The model predicts that specific combinations of dc field and rf amplitude yield a frequency significantly lower than the natural dc tunneling rate, thereby reducing dc current and preventing heating. These findings are validated by comparing calculated dc current and heating rates against established results from prior literature. Additionally, we identify regimes where dc current vanishes, indicating that the particle becomes trapped in the potential wells. These findings hold significant implications for the design of quantum devices. Specifically, in Josephson junctions, the charged particle corresponds to a phase difference, while in carbon nanotubes, it represents an electron. For carbon nanotubes, the charge is quantized, meaning only discrete values are permissible. Conversely, for Josephson junctions, the Cooper pair charge may vary due to environmental fluctuations. Consequently, we propose that scanning the dc field to locate minima of both dc current and heating rates can identify optimal system parameters, with the resulting positions reflecting the characteristic charge of the specific device type. Furthermore, we outline that appropriate choice of dc field and rf amplitude allows the particle to traverse the periodic potential without exciting quasiparticles, thereby eliminating quasiparticle-induced decoherence. This approach is particularly relevant for investigating the charge of a Josephson junction island, as it enables the analysis of a purely dispersive phase difference. Ultimately, these results suggest that rf fields offer a valuable tool for the precise control of quantum systems. This is evidenced by the ability to manipulate tunneling rates, heating rates, and the localization of wavefunctions. In summary, we demonstrate that applying an rf field to a quantum system situated in a dc field can simultaneously reduce tunneling rates, heating rates, and the localization length of the wavefunction. These findings are particularly pertinent to the design of quantum devices, such as those involved in the development of quantum computers. This study presents a flexible local projection framework designed to estimate dynamic relationships between economic variables, utilizing a state-space model augmented with a countable set of instrumental variables. The projection coefficients are derived via the Kalman filter, while Kalman smoothing is employed to refine estimates of unobserved states and coefficients. We introduce a flexible weighting scheme to combine these refined estimates into a weighted average that minimizes a specific variance criterion. This approach yields a finite-dimensional representation of an infinite-dimensional projection, effectively handling the accumulation of projection coefficients over time. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the proposed method, demonstrating its asymptotic normality and optimal properties. Furthermore, we apply this methodology to various economic scenarios, including the impact of monetary policy, the relationship between inflation and consumption, and the effects of fiscal policy. These applications illustrate the method's ability to enhance estimation precision and mitigate the issues of overfitting and underfitting. Additionally, we demonstrate how the approach can be utilized to construct optimal forecasts for target variables. Finally, we extend the methodology to accommodate structural breaks in regression coefficients, thereby enabling the analysis of structural changes in dynamic economic relationships. The paper concludes with a detailed discussion of the method's performance across different sample sizes and break frequencies. All code required to replicate the results is available on GitHub. Keywords: Dynamic estimation, High-dimensional time series, High-dimensional regression, High-dimensional instrumental variables, Local projections, Structural breaks, Structural change, Structural vector autoregressions.
