Reinforcement learning (RL) addresses challenges involving agents within dynamic settings. However, many real-world scenarios are partially observable, meaning agents must maintain beliefs about their environment to optimize decision-making. This study investigates whether recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can acquire these beliefs in a reduced-dimensional latent space. We begin by demonstrating that RNNs trained on a simple sequential pattern recognition task can encode hidden sequential patterns in a compressed form. Subsequently, we address partial observability in a concave shape learning task, showing that an RNN trained to predict the next agent state can effectively represent the underlying belief of the concave shape's true structure. Our findings indicate that RNNs can learn these concealed states in a manner similar to RL beliefs, despite not being explicitly trained to do so. This suggests that RNNs do not necessarily require direct reward signals to acquire knowledge about their environment. Furthermore, this work contributes to the growing field of neuromorphic computing, which seeks to replicate human-like computational processes. Ultimately, this research supports the hypothesis that humans can utilize their memories in a condensed form to form beliefs about their surroundings. Finally, we outline several promising directions for future research in this area. (Code available at: https://github.com/akshaykumar1997/condensed-memory). Keywords: Reinforcement learning, Reinforcement learning with neural networks, Partially observable Markov decision processes, Latent space learning, Concave shape learning, Memory, Recurrent neural networks.

This paper addresses the challenge of weakly-supervised action detection, where training data consists solely of video-level labels lacking frame-level annotations. While action recognition has been extensively studied, action detection remains underexplored. Existing methods typically rely on temporal or spatial graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to model relationships between adjacent frames or spatial locations within individual frames, respectively. However, these approaches often fail to effectively capture long-range dependencies or integrate multi-frame information. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel GCN-based method that combines multi-frame data and temporal relationships. Our network employs a two-stage architecture: first, it extracts discriminative features from individual frames and then aggregates them using GCNs to learn inter-frame dependencies. Additionally, we incorporate a self-training strategy to leverage high-confidence pseudo-labels from a pre-trained model, thereby enhancing the model's confidence and performance. Experimental results across three large-scale datasets—UCF101, UCFSports, and HMDB51—demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we validate the algorithm's effectiveness on two real-world action detection tasks: human pose action recognition and human-object interaction detection. The project code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenChen1997/Weakly-Supervised-Action-Detection. This work was presented at the 2019 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00020. The presentation details are available at https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2019/html/Chen_Weakly-Supervised_Action_Detection_CVPR_2019_paper.html. The video is hosted on https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (ISC) aimed to identify images depicting the same object or scene to advance research in image retrieval and similarity assessment. This effort builds upon the inaugural ISC held in 2019, which introduced a novel dataset of scene and object images along with a benchmark framework for evaluating performance. Since then, both data and benchmarks have expanded significantly. For the 2021 challenge, we established a test set comprising 1.5 million image pairs, and the community submitted 1,010 solutions from 294 participants. This paper details our methodology for generating the test set and presents an analysis of these submissions. We have also identified several key findings and breakthroughs from the competition, which offer valuable insights for future research in image similarity. Our analysis reveals that deep learning-based methods currently dominate the field, yet we also highlight promising alternative approaches. Furthermore, we note that while deep learning models excel at distinguishing scene images, they struggle with object images. Finally, we emphasize that the most successful methods rely on image patch retrieval, suggesting that this technique holds potential for enhancing image similarity metrics. These insights are expected to guide future research and development in image similarity. The challenge can be accessed at https://image-similarity-challenge.github.io. The dataset is available at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/2575552575/1, and the benchmarking code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepLearningTalent/image_similarity_challenge. This study examines diffusion processes characterized by degradation, degradation-induced boundary problems, metastability within such systems, and the resulting homogenization phenomena. Specifically, we analyze the temporal evolution of a small perturbation $u(x,t)$ governed by the equation $u_t = -\kappa u - \Delta u$ for $x \in (0,1)$ and $t > 0$, subject to boundary conditions of the form $u_x(0,t) = \alpha u(1,t) + \beta u(0,t)$. We explore various scenarios involving distinct parameter values for $\alpha$ and $\beta$, as well as a random variable $\kappa$ representing the degradation rate of individual particles. Furthermore, we address boundary value problems for parabolic equations that emerge from the macroscopic description of these microscopic systems, where the degradation rate $\kappa$ is modeled as a random variable dependent on the particle's initial position $x$. Finally, we investigate the metastability of solutions to this class of parabolic equations, demonstrating how effective descriptions of the slow dynamics can be derived. This analysis covers cases with constant $\kappa$ as well as scenarios where $\kappa$ is modeled as a random variable dependent on the particle's initial position. Additionally, we show that an appropriate choice of the function $\beta$ in the boundary conditions can yield optimal convergence rates for the slow dynamics. These findings are supported by numerical examples. The methodology employed relies on spectral analysis, the construction of effective boundary conditions, and the analysis of perturbed dynamical systems. We also present a numerical approach utilizing finite element methods to compute the first few eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. This approach utilizes off-the-shelf software, requiring only the implementation of a specific form energy functional. The proposed framework is applicable to a broad class of parabolic equations. It is important to note that the analysis of the slow dynamics is contingent upon the fast dynamics reaching an equilibrium state. Consequently, we restrict our focus to scenarios where the fast dynamics converge to a steady state, which is guaranteed when $\alpha < 1$ and $\beta = 0$. However, we also address cases where $\alpha \geq 1$ and $\beta \neq 0$, where the fast dynamics do not settle into a steady state but instead approach a periodic orbit. In these instances, we derive an effective boundary condition for the slow dynamics based on the long-term average of the fast dynamics. To ensure the validity of this approach, we impose a mild condition on the initial data

This study investigates the properties of nuclear matter at zero temperature under strong magnetic fields using the leading-order charge-conjugation invariant (LOCI) framework. By applying the leading-order charge-conjugation invariant (LOCV) method, we determine the energy per particle, momentum, and fractionally filled Landau levels as functions of total density and the external magnetic field. Our results indicate that while the magnetic field does not significantly alter the curve of energy versus density at zero field, it does cause symmetry breaking regarding charge and spin. Furthermore, we observe that the momentum of the symmetric nuclear fluid remains independent of the magnetic field, whereas the momentum of the symmetry-paired fluid increases with the field. Additionally, we demonstrate that the filling factor can be derived from the spin and isospin components of the density matrix. Finally, we present and discuss graphs depicting these findings. These conclusions are supported by the LOCLI method, which yields similar results, and we note that the LOCLI approach is more efficient for practical computations. We also provide the necessary computer code for these calculations. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this work in nuclear physics. Our findings suggest that symmetry-paired matter is favored in environments with strong magnetic fields, such as magnetars. This could explain the existence of matter with non-zero spin and isospin in such regions, as well as the observed octuplet gamma-ray bursts, which may result from the decay of this symmetry-paired matter. We also propose that the magnetic field could be responsible for the observed $T=10^{15}$ K temperature in magnetars. These conclusions are backed by the LOCLI method, which produces the same results, and we emphasize that the LOCLI method is more efficient for these computations. We also discuss the potential applications of this work in nuclear physics. This suggests that the magnetic field could be the cause of the observed temperature $T = 10^{15}$ K in magnetars. This study addresses the challenge of training a global model from distributed data while ensuring privacy and minimizing communication overhead. To achieve this, we introduce a new framework called \emph{Differential Privacy Recommender} (DP-REC), which employs a two-stage training process. Initially, a global model is trained using federated learning with differential privacy (DP) to safeguard data confidentiality. Subsequently, each participant trains a local model on their own data and shares only the quantized weights with the coordinator. The coordinator then integrates these quantized weights into the global model through a weighted averaging process. Experimental results demonstrate that DP-REC significantly reduces communication costs compared to standard federated learning approaches. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of differential privacy on the model's generalization capability. Finally, we validate the robustness of DP-REC against data poisoning attacks, confirming its effectiveness in maintaining security within federated learning environments. Our findings indicate that DP-REC offers a promising solution for enhancing both the efficiency and security of federated learning systems. We conducted far-ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the Taurus-Perseus-Aquila (TAP) complex using the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph on the Hubble Space Telescope. These observations successfully captured FUV emission from the Taurus cloud, including the L1147 star cluster and the L1152 dark cloud, as well as from the nearby supernova remnant G106.3+2.3. By analyzing the FUV emission from the L1147 cluster, we determined that the spectral energy distribution of the L1152 dark cloud is primarily driven by the L1147 cluster. Furthermore, we derived the extinction toward L1152 by comparing its observed FUV emission against a model that accounts for both L1147 and L1152 contributions. This analysis yielded an extinction value of $A_V = 0.55 \pm 0.05$ mag, which is consistent with previous estimates. Additionally, we observed FUV emission from G106.3+2.3, which is likely a blend of emission from the remnant itself and scattered light from the Orion emission region. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the TAP complex. Our results indicate that the remnant's FUV emission is primarily thermal, originating from a hot plasma at approximately $10^6$ K, and that the estimated extinction value for the TAP complex is lower than previously reported. These results suggest that the TAP complex is not as dense as earlier studies had indicated. Furthermore, the FUV emission from the remnant could be influencing the ionization of the TAP complex.

Table extraction from documents, particularly those in the "pay-per-view" format like ScienceDirect and SpringerLink, remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel graph-based retrieval framework designed to locate tables within large collections of scientific articles. Our approach relies on two core components: a graph-based retrieval system and a table representation model. The former utilizes a k-nearest neighbor algorithm to identify candidate articles, while the latter employs various graph neural networks to embed tables. Experimental results across two large-scale datasets, ScienceDirect and SpringerLink, demonstrate that our framework effectively addresses the task, outperforming existing methods. Additionally, we conducted extensive ablation studies to evaluate diverse graph neural network architectures for embedding tables, offering valuable insights into their relative effectiveness. Given the vast size of these scientific document collections, our framework holds great promise for enhancing table retrieval and extraction processes. We anticipate this will contribute to the advancement of scientific literature management and knowledge retrieval. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/GraphNeuralNetworks-and-Representation-Embedding-for-TableRetrieval-in-PDF-Document.

We introduce a new equilibrium concept designed for multi-stage games of incomplete information, tailored to scenarios where players possess only partial knowledge regarding others' payoff functions and strategic capabilities at every decision point. This framework assumes that Bayesian updates of subjective beliefs occur only when a player decides whether to engage in a subgame, while cognitive limitations are addressed through bounded rationality and the use of first-order beliefs. We demonstrate that this approach yields a unique prediction for strict dominance solvable games, remains consistent with standard one-shot models of incomplete information, and offers a plausible forecast for the "Traveler's Dilemma" variant played with an unknown opponent's rationality level. Furthermore, we establish a convergence theorem linking this concept to Nash equilibrium in the limit as rationality approaches infinity. The model is broadly applicable, extending beyond strategic rationality to include bounded willpower in choice theory and asymmetric cognition in the study of irrationality. Specifically, it provides a unified explanation for paradoxical game-theoretic predictions and assists in interpreting experimental findings involving rational agents. Additionally, the proposed framework generates testable hypotheses for games characterized by imperfect monitoring. Finally, we show that the associated best response correspondence exhibits a contraction property under a specific metric, enabling the application of Tarski's fixed point theorem to prove the existence of equilibrium. This contrasts with standard models of incomplete information, where equilibrium existence is typically established via Kuhn's general existence theorem. Finally, we illustrate how this concept can be adapted to multi-stage games of complete information where players possess only partial common knowledge of rationality.

**Keywords:** Bounded Rationality; Cognitive Hierarchy; Traveler's Dilemma; Traveler's Dilemma with Unknown Levels of Rationality; Existence of Equilibrium.

This research investigates the feasibility of employing computer vision and machine learning to achieve sustainable, long-term autonomous population estimates through regular satellite imagery analysis. The study addresses the critical challenge of conducting efficient censuses in remote, hard-to-reach areas without straining local resources. As a proof of concept, we developed a deep learning model to estimate population sizes in northern Mozambique by analyzing both vector and raster data, including features such as night-time illumination, land use, and vegetation. We evaluated various deep learning architectures, achieving an $R^2$ score of 0.82 with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 1,200 inhabitants. Furthermore, we demonstrated that integrating vector data significantly enhances the model's performance. Finally, we outline the potential benefits of leveraging deep learning for future sustainable population estimation efforts. We introduce a new algorithm designed to maintain a collection while supporting precise insertion and iteration, alongside a best-effort filter operation that allows for a configurable failure rate. This approach leverages an existing bounded approximate set data structure. Our method achieves constant-time insertion with linearithmic time complexity for exact filtering, alongside efficient iteration capabilities. This solution is particularly valuable for applications requiring frequent, exact verification of previously filtered elements. Additionally, we have created an optimized variant tailored for scenarios where elements are static post-initialization, reducing the complexity for transient exact filters to the square of the transient filter size. We validated this approach across various contexts, including a distributed exact set for a large-scale online game and a data structure for managing exact and filtered invariants in biological networks. A comprehensive benchmark suite comparing our method against alternatives can be found at https://github.com/InvariantsLab/fsmq. The source code for this implementation is available under the Apache 2.0 license at https://github.com/InvariantsLab/fsmq. Furthermore, we released a C++ header-only data structure for exact membership that utilizes a streamlined version of our algorithm; this is licensed under the same Apache 2.0 terms and accessible at https://github.com/InvariantsLab/fsmq/tree/master/fsmq_exact. This structure supports linear-time construction, constant-time insertion and querying, and linear-time iteration, offering superior performance for large datasets. Its interface is compatible with the C++ Standard Template Library. We also provide a C++ header-only implementation for a transient filter with non-deterministic removal times, available under the Apache 2.0 license at https://github.com/InvariantsLab/fsmq/tree/master/fsmq_exact/tests/fsmq_test_filters. This feature enables linear-time construction, constant-time insertion, and quadratic-time exact filtering, with a worst-case linear-time complexity for transient filters. Its interface is also compatible with the C++ Standard Template Library. We anticipate that this highly performant, simple-to-use data structure will prove beneficial for a broad spectrum of applications. This work was partially funded by the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme (Grant Agreement No. 714032). This is an extended version of our paper accepted for publication in Proceedings of the 2021 International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE'21). The extended version includes significant enhancements to the algorithm, benchmarking, and code, alongside minor updates to the introduction

We introduce a theoretical framework for achieving coherent transitions between spinor atoms and molecules within an ultracold three-atom system. This is accomplished through a resonant, Raman-type coupling of the three-atom states to a two-body molecule plus a photon state, achieved using a single coupling laser. We demonstrate that this process, representing the three-body analogue of Raman adiabatic passage (RAP), enables near-perfect atom-molecule conversion even in the presence of significant two-atom losses. Furthermore, we show that these near-optimal operating conditions are robust against variations in the coupling Rabi frequency, collisional shifts, and dephasing rates. Finally, we outline potential applications of this novel Raman-type protocol in quantum information processing and spectroscopy. Additionally, we discuss how this approach extends to molecular dimerization via three-molecule recombination. Our findings are validated by experimental data from a recent study [J. Ye et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 073201 (2019)]. We anticipate that this versatile and robust method will be widely adopted in upcoming quantum information and spectroscopy experiments. To facilitate this, we have provided a user-friendly numerical simulation tool that models the dynamics of coherent atom-molecule recombination, including the specific experimental parameters reported by Ye et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 073201 (2019)]. This tool is available at https://github.com/QuantumOpticsLabUoT/RAP3. The source code is also included in the supplementary materials. Users can explore the dynamics of coherent atom-molecule recombination, as well as trimerization and dimerization via three- and four-molecule recombination, respectively, by adjusting various experimental parameters. The tool is designed to be easily adaptable for simulating diverse quantum optical processes involving multi-atom recombination. We have also included a theoretical analysis of the atom-molecule recombination mechanism, which is expected to be valuable for researchers in quantum optics. We believe this will facilitate the development of new quantum optical processes utilizing multi-atom recombination. This theoretical framework is expected to be beneficial to the broader quantum optics community. The code is also being considered for publication in an open-access journal. We have also prepared a tutorial to guide users in employing the tool for their own research. This theoretical framework is anticipated to be useful for a wide range of researchers. This paper introduces a SPH-ARL framework designed for fluid-structure interaction problems involving multiple fluids with distinct physical properties. The ARL method is a newly developed numerical approach that offers the benefits of adaptive meshless techniques while maintaining lower computational costs. It is applied to high-Reynolds number fluids and implemented within a multi-resolution strategy. This approach enables the use of highly resolved fluid meshes near solid boundaries to accurately capture complex flow phenomena, while coarser meshes are utilized in regions where physical quantities exhibit minimal variation. The study demonstrates the framework's capabilities through several applications, including multi-component fluid-structure interactions, with a specific focus on a blood flow simulation inside an aneurysm. The results indicate that the proposed method is both efficient and effective for solving complex fluid-structure interaction challenges. Furthermore, the proposed multi-resolution strategy is particularly advantageous for problems characterized by highly non-uniform physical fields. Finally, the paper concludes that this numerical approach is well-suited for application in medical engineering. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abdelhamid-benali/SPH-ARL. This study explores quantum machine learning applied to the unsupervised analysis of quantum data, utilizing a variational approach to construct a generative model for data exploration. We demonstrate that this model can be effectively trained on processors featuring both high and low gate fidelity. The research examines the characteristics of trained models and the nature of generated data, revealing that low fidelity results in models that fail to accurately represent the data distribution. Furthermore, we show that guiding model training with conjugate gradient-based quantum natural gradient descent significantly enhances performance, enabling the model to more closely approximate the data distribution even under high noise conditions. These findings underscore the critical role of variational optimization techniques and convergence methods in the domain of quantum machine learning. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for future quantum hardware and the development of quantum algorithms. This paper introduces a timbre-preserving pitch augmentation technique designed to enhance pitch control robustness and generalization within the FastSpeech2-based pitch augmentation branch of FastPitch. By utilizing local spectrogram warping, the method maintains the speaker-specific vocal characteristics essential for pitch prediction during pitch shifting. The study demonstrates that spectrogram warping effectively retains the quality of synthesized speech. Experimental results indicate that this approach boosts robust pitch control by 1.5% and improves pitch control generalization by 2.0%. Additionally, the research confirms that pitch augmentation branch training is crucial for achieving these experimental outcomes. The source code will be made available to the public. Keywords: Pitch Control, Pitch Shifting, Synthesis, Neural TTS, Timbre Preservation.

Long-term spatiotemporal prediction is essential for numerous real-world applications, including weather forecasting, traffic flow prediction, and wind speed estimation. Traditional approaches typically rely on multi-step models that sequentially forecast one time step ahead and repeat this process to estimate future values. However, these methods often fail to capture the inherent correlation between distant time steps. To address this limitation, we introduce Hopper, a novel multi-hop Transformer designed for multi-hop inference in spatiotemporal forecasting. Unlike conventional single-hop architectures, Hopper effectively captures both spatial and temporal dependencies by implementing a multi-hop attention mechanism. Furthermore, the model incorporates various position-wise encodings to encode position information and enhance generalization. Extensive experiments across three public datasets demonstrate that Hopper outperforms leading single-hop models, achieving a 2.2% to 10.4% reduction in RMSE. Additionally, comparisons with state-of-the-art multi-hop models show that Hopper improves accuracy by 1.2% to 4.6%. The project's source code is accessible at https://github.com/leehyomin/Hopper. We present a concise overview of a next-generation collider initiative aimed at precisely measuring the Standard Model (SM) Higgs boson couplings and conducting thorough investigations into new physics. This proposal entails constructing a high-energy $e^+e^-$ collider with a center-of-mass energy of approximately 250–300 GeV to conduct an exceptionally precise Higgs factory experiment involving a few hundred $bb\ell^+\ell^-$ events. Furthermore, we examine a complementary collider option that would operate alongside the Higgs factory to determine the Higgs self-coupling and explore new physics. This secondary option involves a multi-TeV $e^+e^-$ collider capable of producing approximately 100 $bb\ell^+\ell^-$ events, which would complement the Higgs factory by studying Higgs boson couplings through off-shell production. This approach would also enable the study of other Higgs processes, such as $H\to WW^*$, $H\to ZZ^*$, and $H\to\tau^+\tau^-$, in association with heavy quark pairs. We demonstrate that combining data from both colliders could determine the Higgs boson self-coupling with a precision of roughly 5% (statistical) and 7% (total). Additionally, we show that a similar combination of data from the two proposed colliders could determine the $W$ boson mass with a precision of approximately 2 MeV (statistical) and 3 MeV (total). This level of precision is essential for interpreting potential deviations from SM predictions that may arise from measurements at the LHC and future hadron colliders. We also discuss other observables that could be measured with comparable precision using these facilities. Finally, we address the necessity of performing theoretical calculations at higher orders in perturbation theory to achieve the required precision. We conclude by discussing the scientific and societal benefits of these proposed colliders. Mafia, also known as Criminal, is a social deduction game where two factions compete: the Mafia aims to eliminate all civilians, while the civilians seek to identify and remove every Mafia member. This paper offers a comprehensive mathematical analysis of these mechanics, enabling a deeper exploration of optimal strategies for both sides. We examine how various game parameters—such as the number of players, the initial count of Mafia members, and the presence of a Doctor who can negate one civilian kill per night—influence the mafia-to-civilian ratio required for a balanced game. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of a "Sheriff," a civilian who can verify one Mafia member's identity each day. Our findings indicate that both the Mafia and the civilians possess winning strategies when the starting force is sufficiently strong. Additionally, we analyze a variant where the Doctor belongs to the Mafia and can eliminate one civilian each night; we demonstrate that this adjustment shifts the optimal balance, making the game easier for the Mafia. Finally, we outline a winning strategy for the Mafia in a specific scenario and discuss how both factions can adapt their approaches based on evolving in-game information. This study establishes a foundation for future research into Mafia game dynamics.

This study demonstrates phonon-assisted electronic conduction in a macroscopic film of armchair carbon nanotubes (CNTs), observed through a distinct 60 \mu eV phonon resonance within temperature-dependent conductivity measurements. This finding indicates that electron-phonon coupling is substantial in this system. Additionally, we document a 200 \mu eV electronic conduction bandgap and a pronounced electron-phonon coupling-induced bandgap modulation. These results are accurately modeled using a conformation-dependent tight-binding approach. Our findings suggest that engineering electron-phonon interactions in CNT films could enable the tunable control of electronic transport properties. Furthermore, the tunable dielectric constant arising from this coupling may facilitate the design of novel phonon-engineered devices and tunable electronic systems. Finally, our work establishes a foundation for investigating phonon-assisted transport in other two-dimensional materials exhibiting strong electron-phonon coupling. To achieve this, we introduce a straightforward model for analyzing phonon-assisted conduction in CNT films. This method relies on the product of two factors: the phonon density of states and the phonon-assisted transmission probability, the latter of which depends on the variation of the conduction bandgap induced by specific phonon modes. We demonstrate that this approach can explain experimental data and predict the resonant phonon energy. Our methodology is easily adaptable to other materials, such as transition metal dichalcogenides, and can be readily extended to other phonon modes. This tool will be valuable for guiding future research into phonon-assisted conduction in CNT films and other two-dimensional materials. Our findings also offer insights into the design of phonon-assisted optoelectronic devices utilizing strong electron-phonon coupling in CNT films. Specifically, we show that these resonances can be controlled by adjusting the CNT diameter. Additionally, we identify that doping the CNTs can further modulate these resonances, providing a pathway for controlling phonon-assisted conduction in CNT-based optoelectronic devices. To achieve this, we have developed a method to calculate the shift in resonant phonon energy caused by phonon-assisted transitions between the valence and conduction bands. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, which combine linear experts guided by a gating network, are widely used across various machine learning applications. These findings establish a foundation for future research into efficient and consistent learning methods for general MoE structures. Our experiments confirm that these proposed algorithms outperform existing approaches in terms of both efficiency and consistency. Quantum gravity is anticipated to induce new physics in light propagation, specifically through the modification of the kinetic term for the gauge field associated with global symmetries within effective field theory. This mechanism could result in novel phenomena, such as the deflection of light by Earth's atmosphere or variations in the speed of different colors. Furthermore, if a global symmetry is broken by quantum gravity effects at the Planck scale, matter fields will acquire effective charges relative to it. Consequently, cosmic vortices linked to this symmetry would exert forces on matter, and the atmosphere would function as an optical prism, deflecting different colors at distinct angles. Utilizing measurements of cosmic double refraction, we establish constraints on global symmetry breaking in quantum gravity, limiting the effective charges of fermions and bosons. These limits reach approximately $\mathcal{O}(10^{-13})$ to $\mathcal{O}(10^{-15})$ for fermions and $\mathcal{O}(10^{-11})$ to $\mathcal{O}(10^{-13})$ for bosons. Additionally, we outline potential experimental methods to further constrain or detect global symmetry dynamics. Our findings underscore the significance of conducting or conducting precise experiments involving light passing through the atmosphere. They also highlight the necessity of investigating or searching for cosmic double refraction and vortex interactions, as these would provide a definitive signature of global symmetry breaking. We conducted a UVIT observation of the globular cluster NGC 4147 to investigate the ultraviolet (UV) bright stars within it. The study identified 13 such stars, with 10 being previously known and 3 discovered for the first time. We determined their physical parameters, including effective temperature, surface gravity, and radius, by comparing their UVIT UVW1 and WFC2 images with synthetic images generated from theoretical models. Additionally, we analyzed the photometric variability of these stars using the UVW1 filter data from UVIT. The derived parameters and variability findings are presented alongside existing literature data for comparison. We propose that the newly discovered UV bright stars are likely Be-type stars, which are rare in globular clusters. This discovery suggests that Be-type stars can form in these clusters, either through the collapse of a single star or via binary star interactions. Furthermore, we observed that some of these UV bright stars exhibit photometric variability, a characteristic also noted in similar stars in other globular clusters. Finally, we determined the age of NGC 4147 to be 11.9 billion years. The paper concludes with a summary of the study's results. (Abridged)

This book offers a modern exposition of the Mumford conjecture, now termed the stable Whitney conjecture. This conjecture asserts that the Euler class provides an isomorphism between the second homology of the stabilisation of a closed orientable surface and the stable cobordism group of degree-two maps to a $K(G,2)$ space for a given group $G$. While this conjecture is equivalent to the Mumford conjecture in specific instances, it represents a significantly more challenging and broadly applicable problem. The text elucidates the conjecture's background and statement, demonstrates how topological techniques can yield a $443$-dimensional proof, and contrasts these with the intricate algebraic approach developed by Galatius and Randal-Williams. Additionally, we present an alternative formulation of the stable Whitney conjecture involving the non-linear stable homotopy groups of spheres, a perspective that offers deep insight into the conjecture's nature and highlights the fragility of the $b$-principle. Finally, we explore several generalisations and their associated conjectures. This work is based on the author's thesis, which was supervised by Peter Kronheimer. Our approach diverges substantially from standard treatments found in literature such as Hatcher's or the papers by Galatius and Randal-Williams. We hope that our unique perspective will inspire new research into this fascinating area of mathematics. A key motivation for this project was the desire to demonstrate that topological methods, which can be more accessible, provide valuable insights. Furthermore, we aim to encourage mathematicians from physics backgrounds to engage with this field, as the topological proof reveals structures that may facilitate a quantum understanding of the conjecture. We anticipate that our exposition will inspire novel approaches to the problem and new research directions. Our hope is that this book will inspire a new generation of mathematicians to tackle this intriguing and challenging problem. Transferability is a critical capability for deep learning, yet recent studies have established two transferability agreements that restrict a model's ability to adapt to new tasks. The first agreement posits that models trained on difficult tasks exhibit superior transferability to new domains compared to those trained on easy ones. The second states that a model's transferability performance remains consistent across various target tasks once it achieves convergence on the source task. These limitations are particularly problematic for continual learning scenarios, where each newly acquired task is potentially more challenging than previous ones. Consequently, these agreements hinder the continued improvement of deep learning models as their knowledge base expands. This paper challenges both assumptions and offers a counter-example based on cross-entropy minimization to demonstrate that these two agreements are not universally valid. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the transferability dynamics during gradient descent for linear regression, revealing that these two types of transferability can be decoupled. Finally, we validate these findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results confirm that an encoder trained on an easy task can outperform those trained on difficult tasks, and that model transferability can fluctuate throughout the training process even after achieving convergence on the source task. These observations align with our theoretical predictions. Overall, this work offers new insights into transferability and lays the groundwork for designing learning algorithms with more stable transferability characteristics. Additionally, it addresses the critical challenge of continual learning, facilitating the continual enhancement of deep learning systems as their knowledge base grows. Networks are inherently modular, and this structural characteristic significantly influences the dynamics of information spread. While prior research has primarily examined how a network's overall density alters the relationship between module density and diffusion speed, it has overlooked the critical role of the network's total density. This study demonstrates that average inter-module link density is a pivotal factor: the mean of these inter-module connections dictates the connection between network density and the velocity of information diffusion. Furthermore, we validate these findings across both synthetic and real-world networks. Consequently, our results indicate that the average density of inter-module connections is essential for comprehending how network topology governs information diffusion processes. This insight holds particular relevance for engineering networks designed to either accelerate or decelerate the spread of information. Our findings are applicable to a wide range of network systems, including those governing the propagation of diseases, rumors, and misinformation. Additionally, we offer a Python-based tool to facilitate the investigation of network modularity and its impact on information diffusion. Finally, our approach can be extended to other network properties, such as community size, to explore their effects on diffusion dynamics. The accompanying Python code is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi1997/NetworkModularityDiffusion.

The Android operating system, built on a Linux kernel, is widely used for mobile applications. Its open-source nature has facilitated various security vulnerabilities that have been addressed through multiple patches. This paper provides a comprehensive review of past Android security flaws, categorizing them into seven primary issues: memory corruption, privilege escalation, application permissions, third-party libraries, third-party components, third-party frameworks, and third-party applications. We analyze the root causes of these flaws, their associated risks, and the specific patches that resolved them. Additionally, we examine the limitations of our survey and outline several promising directions for future research. Our findings suggest that while significant progress has been made in mitigating historical Android issues, emerging threats continue to arise. Furthermore, we note that many past vulnerabilities were resolved through third-party libraries, components, and frameworks rather than direct patches from the OS developers. This underscores the critical need for thorough code reviews and rigorous testing of the extensive third-party code integrated into the Android platform. Finally, we recommend that future research prioritize the development of automated testing frameworks and the adoption of advanced machine learning techniques to enhance Android security. This survey offers valuable insights for researchers aiming to strengthen the Android ecosystem. To our knowledge, this remains the first study to explore the evolution of Android security flaws and their corresponding resolutions. Our work can assist researchers and practitioners in identifying emerging threats and implementing more effective security measures. The survey is accessible at https://github.com/ashraf1999/Issue-Space-Evasion-Attacks-in-the-Android-OS-a-Survey. Our contributions are as follows: (1) We offer a thorough analysis of security flaws in Android applications, including their root causes, consequences, and mitigation strategies; (2) We examine the flaws within the Android ecosystem, which is expanding rapidly with the inclusion of third-party libraries, components, and frameworks; (3) We provide an overview of the patches that have resolved past Android security issues. Our survey can help researchers and practitioners detect emerging threats and adopt more robust security solutions. (4) We offer insights into the patches used to fix historical Android security flaws. This work can assist researchers and practitioners in identifying emerging threats and implementing more effective security measures. (5) We propose future research directions for Android security, such as automated testing frameworks and machine learning techniques. Container orchestration platforms are widely adopted for managing large container clusters, yet they are typically complex and resource-intensive. We introduce a unified theoretical framework capable of modeling both fractional quantum Hall phases and reentrant integer quantum Hall phases. This model incorporates moderate strength interaction, represented by a generalized pseudopotential, and finite Zeeman splitting. By analyzing the single-particle spectrum, we identify multiple reentrant integer quantum Hall phases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that established reentrant integer phases, which are typically linked to quantum phase transitions involving composite fermion Fermi liquid states, are intrinsic outcomes of strong correlation effects within our model. Utilizing density matrix renormalization group techniques, we investigate the phase diagram and determine critical exponents for quantum phase transitions between various fractional quantum Hall states. Our findings indicate that the Zeeman field influences the relative stability of different fractional quantum Hall phases, leading to reentrant transitions of the fractional quantum Hall liquid as it varies. Specifically, we identify a reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall phase under moderate Landau level mixing and an applied Zeeman field. This result is corroborated by precise finite-size scaling analysis. Consequently, our study reveals a rich phase structure in two-dimensional electron systems subjected to moderate interaction strength and finite Zeeman splitting. We propose that this reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall phase may be experimentally observable. Additionally, we elucidate the relationship between the reentrant integer quantum Hall phase and the reentrant fractional quantum Hall phase. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting this reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall phase through magnetotransport measurements. This work expands upon our earlier research, which was published in Phys. We demonstrate that the metric proposed by Thakurta for a stationary black hole, which is claimed to represent the most general solution to the Einstein equations under the assumption of homogeneity, is fundamentally flawed. Specifically, the solution fails to satisfy the field equations, and the claimed generality is incorrect because the homogeneity condition actually restricts the solution to the well-known Schwarzschild metric. Furthermore, we note that recent constraints derived from the non-detection of gravitational waves by LIGO and Virgo provide significant limits on the abundance of primordial black holes with masses near the detector's lower threshold of approximately $30M_{\odot}$. These constraints are independent of any theoretical errors within the Thakurta paper. Additionally, we observe that the theoretical issues affecting the derivation of the generalized Schwarzschild metric also impact the derivation of the spherically symmetric, stationary metric solution. Consequently, the errors in the relevant section of the original paper prevent a proper description of massive black holes, including cosmological ones. Therefore, the lower mass limit for non-radiating primordial black holes in the current era, as established by LIGO and Virgo, remains robust. This implies that primordial black holes cannot account for a substantial portion of dark matter, nor can they explain the recently identified intermediate-mass black holes observed by LIGO and Virgo. We also examine other potential candidates for dark matter and intermediate-mass black holes, such as stellar-mass black holes and supermassive black holes. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the future of the LIGO and Virgo observatories. Our conclusions are also relevant to the upcoming KAGRA and the future Einstein Telescope. We conclude that the KAGRA observatory will be able to probe lower masses than currently possible, thereby extending the search for non-radiating PBHs to even lower values. Moreover, the future Einstein Telescope will enable the study of even lower-mass non-radiating PBHs, potentially reaching masses as low as $10^{3}kg$. This represents a lower limit for non-evaporating PBHs, assuming they do not emit gravitational waves detectable by the Einstein Telescope. We also address the issue of PBHs as a potential source of dark matter. We show that the upper limit on the fraction of dark matter that can be attributed to PBHs is approximately $10^{-9}$, which is significantly lower than the upper limit for radiation. Accretion of pebbles by planetary embryos is a critical mechanism for forming super-Earths and the cores of gas giants. This study investigates how local density fluctuations in a pebble disk influence embryo accretion rates and their subsequent growth. We developed a new model that accounts for stochastic density variations in pebble disks, calculating both the mean growth rate and its variance as functions of embryo mass and orbital distance. Results indicate that the standard accretion model fails to capture these fluctuations. Our proposed stochastic model successfully reproduces the growth of Kepler-357d, a super-Earth, and predicts the mass distribution of multiple embryos in that system. Furthermore, the model successfully accounts for the formation of the hot Jupiter Kepler-1138b. These findings suggest that incorporating stochasticity into accretion models is essential for a realistic understanding of planet formation. The study concludes by outlining the implications of this stochastic growth for the broader field of planetary science. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of the stochastic accretion model to facilitate future research. This work was conducted using the ALMA, VLT, and Hubble Space Telescope. The Python code is available at https://github.com/SeijiMiyoshi/pebbleAccretion. Data utilized in this research were gathered by the ALMA, VLT, and Hubble Space Telescope. Overparameterized models are common in machine learning, where the number of parameters exceeds the sample size. While prior research attributes this trend to statistical goals like minimizing test error under distributional assumptions, this paper offers a computational perspective. We demonstrate that limiting optimization to computationally feasible algorithms, such as gradient descent, can account for overparameterization. Specifically, we examine a linear regression framework with a design matrix featuring random entries, a constant number of features, and a target function with sparsity $s$. We prove that although the minimum norm solution is infeasible for gradient-based methods, an equivalent solution reachable by gradient descent contains only $O(s \log n)$ non-zero entries. This significantly narrower support enhances robustness against distributional shifts, a benefit that the inaccessibility of the solution rather than explicit statistical constraints. Furthermore, this phenomenon extends to other overparameterized models, including matrix completion and clustering. Finally, we outline a framework for analyzing such statistical properties arising from computational constraints. Our work highlights that the standard focus on minimizing test error may overlook the critical role of distributional shifts in real-world applications. We conclude by suggesting that future research should prioritize the analysis of the "computational gap"—the difference between the behavior of the minimum norm solution and that of a gradient-descent-equivalent solution. A key open question remains: can we establish a general relationship between the computational gap and the test error of optimally optimized models? Addressing this would require developing new algorithms for finding equivalent solutions and novel statistical tools to assess their generalization performance. We believe this computational viewpoint will drive future advancements in understanding the interplay between computation and statistics. Our code is available at https://github.com/ashwinbalsubramani/OCOLINER. Supplementary materials can be found at https://ashwinbalsubramani.github.io/overparam/. Let $G$ be an infinite abelian group with torsion subgroups that are finitely generated, and let $A \subseteq G$ be a subset whose difference set $A-A$ contains a Bohr set $B$ of rank at most $d$ with size at least $\gamma > 0$. We demonstrate that $A$ can be expressed as the sum of a Bohr set $B_0$ of rank at most $d+2\gamma$ and a finite set. Furthermore, if $A$ possesses non-empty interior, it is the sum of a Bohr set of rank at most $d+2\gamma$ and a finite set contained within that Bohr set. These findings extend the work of the second author and J. P. C. Shao, who established analogous results for $\mathbb{Z}^n$. The proofs rely on an abstract version of the Steinhaus theorem and an application of the second author's work. Additionally, we present an example showing that the rank bound is sharp when the group is not locally finite. Finally, we briefly discuss an extension of this work to non-abelian groups. This study addresses dial-a-ride problems featuring flexible pickup and delivery time windows, numerous customers, and constrained driver routes. We introduce a Branch-and-Cut framework that utilizes a novel formulation and a diverse array of valid inequalities to tackle these challenges. Specifically, we develop pickup and delivery cut families, which are a specialized form of generalized pickup delivery cut applicable to problems with time windows, alongside preflow-based inequalities for the VRP with time windows. Additionally, we implement various pricing algorithms to address a rich prize collection problem that incorporates time-dependent costs, soft time windows, and customer preferences for early or late arrivals. Finally, we introduce a new preprocessing technique to enhance the efficiency of the branch-and-price procedure. Computational results demonstrate that this approach can solve instances with up to 100 customers in under 10 seconds, yielding high-quality lower bounds and operational solutions. Furthermore, we present a method to evaluate the performance of heuristic solutions on real-world data. A case study on mobility in the city of Turin illustrates the practical applicability of our approach. The proposed method successfully solves all small instances and 10 out of 11 large instances, achieving a significant reduction in the number of vehicles used. The only instance that remains unsolved requires 1.6 times more vehicles than the optimal benchmark, yet still necessitates only a minor increase in total distance. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/riccardocaprioli/Dial-a-Ride. This study explores a multi-modal pretraining approach for e-commerce that leverages knowledge graphs. We pretrain an multi-modal BERT by jointly utilizing visual and textual e-commerce data, ensuring that visual features align with understanding-based features within the same knowledge graph. This shared space enables the model to mitigate discrepancies between visual and understanding-based representations found in pixel-based color or texture features. To achieve this, we introduce a new triplet contrastive loss function. Experimental results indicate that models leveraging these shared knowledge spaces outperform those lacking them, and that multi-modal color or texture features can directly enhance product similarity search performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our shared space in generating interpretable explanations for the multi-modal e-commerce platform. Finally, we validate the approach's effectiveness on the public FashionIQ benchmark. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ruixuanwang1997/UE-KG-MMP. This study introduces a new deep learning approach designed to forecast the progression to Alzheimer's disease (AD) in individuals carrying the APOE $\epsilon$4 allele. The method integrates both clinical data and data-driven phenotypes derived from neuroimaging. We evaluated a novel architecture known as the "prediction autoencoder," which employs a bidirectional autoencoder to model the joint distribution of input features at two time points, thereby capturing their dependency structure. This technique enables the imputation of data from one time point given the data from the other. To assess its efficacy, we compared AD conversion rates predicted by the prediction autoencoder against those predicted by the dependency matrix derived from canonical correlation analysis (CCA). Results indicated that the prediction autoencoder outperformed CCA in modeling the dependency between clinical and imaging features within this cohort. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the prediction autoencoder can forecast the progression to AD in APOE $\epsilon$4 carriers. These findings suggest that the prediction autoencoder holds promise for characterizing the dependency between clinical and imaging features and for predicting AD progression in individuals with a family history of the disease. This approach is particularly relevant for studying the preclinical stages of AD, where the transition to the disease is gradual and influenced by multiple factors. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/PredictionAutoEncoder. The dataset used in this research is available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-020-0894-x. Additionally, we have released a Python package implementing the prediction autoencoder, which can be installed via pip using the command: pip install https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/PredictionAutoEncoder/archive/refs/heads/master.zip. The package is also accessible at https://pypi.org/project/PredictionAutoEncoder/ and https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/PredictionAutoEncoder. This tool is especially valuable for researchers studying the progression to AD. The package includes a function to predict the conditional distribution of one time point's data given the data at another time point, facilitating the investigation of how one time point influences another. This capability is essential for understanding the progression to AD. This paper introduces a recurrent neural network architecture designed for state-of-the-art performance in Natural Inference Tasks (NITs), including Natural Deduction (ND), Coreference Resolution (CR), and Comprehension Question (CQ). The model employs a memory-based approach to effectively capture long-term dependencies within sentences, which is essential for NITs. Furthermore, it utilizes a gating mechanism to regulate information flow between layers during modeling. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves competitive performance in CQ and CR tasks while surpassing existing models across all three NITs. Additionally, the model exhibits strong robustness against adversarial attacks. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/SEM-Comprehension.

In the absence of crystal-field anisotropy, spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can be expressed as a two-body interaction between spin and orbital degrees of freedom. This equivalence implies that the impact of SOC on electronic properties is governed by the interplay between its intrinsic strength and the orbital-valence space mixing induced by band folding and correlation effects. Consequently, SOC is not merely a material constant but can be significantly enhanced in correlated systems. We demonstrate this through a detailed examination of the iron pnictide BaFe$_2$As$_2$, a prototypical system where this mechanism is expected to operate. Our analysis reveals that SOC is amplified by a factor of approximately 100 in BaFe$_2$As$_2$ due to hybridization between Fe $3d$ valence states and $3s/3p$ core states. Furthermore, this enhancement is exacerbated by strong correlations, which reduce the orbital-valence gap and further promote mixing. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating a realistic band structure into SOC-based models for pnictides and other correlated materials. Additionally, we explore the implications of this strengthened SOC for spin fluctuations and magnetism. We examine the framework's implications for cosmology, including dark radiation, the matter power spectrum, and the formation of dark matter halos. Additionally, we analyze its potential role in explaining the baryon asymmetry of the universe. Finally, we outline the necessary experimental evidence required to validate this theory. Our proposed approach offers a fresh perspective on dark matter, dark energy, and the physical origin of the electroweak scale. It also provides a viable resolution to the coincidence problem, which remains a significant challenge in standard $\lambda$CDM cosmology. Specifically, it addresses why the energy densities of dark energy and matter remain comparable at the current cosmic epoch. We anticipate that this framework will serve as a valuable tool for investigating the nature of dark energy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this theory can account for the observed $5\sigma$ anomaly in the Hubble parameter, which has been detected in both the Supernova Cosmology Project and the SH0ES collaboration. Regulatory bodies are increasingly scrutinizing the generalizability of AI software intended for medical device certification. However, validating these algorithms remains difficult due to the vast volume of training data required and the high costs associated with obtaining human expert labels. Consequently, researchers are investigating alternative testing methods that maintain robustness against distribution shifts without requiring extensive labeled datasets. This study introduces a novel approach that integrates conformal prediction with hypothesis testing to establish prediction sets for new instances, ensuring coverage guarantees under distribution shifts. We evaluate this method using a classification model trained to predict myocardial infarction from chest X-rays. Our results demonstrate that the proposed technique can achieve a coverage probability of 90% or higher, even when the test data is sourced from different hospitals than the training set. Furthermore, we find that this technique outperforms standard methods in terms of both precision and recall across multiple scenarios. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's performance under varying conditions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/CPHT.

Enhancing the sampling of rare events is a critical challenge in molecular modeling. While numerous methods have been developed to address this, their application to large, flexible biological systems remains limited. This study demonstrates that applying a rigid substrate biasing potential to DNA sequences, which are known to adopt non-B-form conformations, significantly improves the sampling of these states. This technique was validated on the cytosine-rich DNA sequence CACCCCGGCGCGCC, which is documented to transition into a bulged conformation. By combining this approach with Metadynamics simulations, we successfully captured the complete conformational pathway of this transition. Furthermore, we employed a Markov State Model to characterize the system's dynamics, revealing that the CACCCCGGCGCGCC sequence exhibits a higher propensity for non-B-form conformations compared to other DNA sequences. These findings indicate that rigid substrate biasing serves as a valuable tool for molecular modeling, facilitating the study of both the structure and dynamics of DNA conformations. The associated Python code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez/rigid-substrate-biasing. The Ansitz entropy encoding (ANS) is a widely used method for entropy coding in modern compression algorithms. This paper investigates the behavior of ANS entropy, specifically addressing the question of whether a first-order coding algorithm can achieve performance comparable to optimal coding. We demonstrate that ANS entropy increases proportionally to the codeword length and provide experimental evidence indicating that ANS coding yields performance similar to optimal coding. Furthermore, we have developed a new entropy coding algorithm based on ANS that outperforms existing methods in terms of compression ratio while maintaining the same decoding speed. Finally, we apply this new coding technique to entropy coding for neural networks, showing that it successfully reduces the storage space required for model parameters. These findings suggest that ANS entropy encoding is a promising approach for compressing neural network models. Additionally, we have released our implementation under the MIT license to facilitate further research and experimentation. The dielectric properties of cement-based construction materials are closely tied to the electrical behavior of their constituent pore solutions. This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the dielectric response of calcium chloride solutions across various concentrations and temperatures. By analyzing dipole moments and dipolar relaxation mechanisms of water and chloride ions, we establish a concentration-temperature-dependent dielectric constant for the pore solution. Furthermore, we examine the frequency dependence of dielectric loss, noting that at low frequencies, the dissipation caused by the dipolar orientation of water is overshadowed by the migration of ions. These findings are corroborated through statistical analysis of relevant microscopic variables. Additionally, we compare our simulation results with experimental data for concentrated salt solutions and discuss the implications of these results for cement-based systems. Ultimately, this research offers a quantitative assessment of the dielectric response in concrete structures, which is essential for evaluating their condition and durability. Such information can enhance the accuracy of non-destructive testing methods, including dielectric spectroscopy, ground-penetrating radar, and electrochemical techniques. The accompanying Python code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2019/MD_simulation}. The deployment of swarms of small, inexpensive unmanned aircraft offers significant potential for military applications, including search and rescue operations, disaster relief, and intelligence gathering. However, the dynamic nature of battlefields and the need for real-time data necessitate advanced communication methods to coordinate these swarms effectively. This study investigates the driving factors behind the adoption of LoRa and UAV swarms by analyzing 15 scientific papers that discuss the benefits and drawbacks of LoRa communication within this context. Through a combination of manual and automated text mining, the research identified 151 text segments that were subsequently categorized into four main driving factors: (1) reliability, (2) security, (3) cost, and (4) energy efficiency. The findings reveal that UAV swarms utilizing LoRa communication are particularly well-suited for missions that are not time-critical. Furthermore, the study underscores the critical role of UAV swarm communication in military operations. Finally, the research demonstrates the efficacy of employing natural language processing techniques to extract relevant information from scientific literature. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/Analyze-of-Enabler-of-UAS-UAV-Swarm-Communication. Future work will expand this approach to additional datasets to further validate the methodology. Additionally, the authors intend to investigate the influence of various hyperparameters on the outcomes of such text mining studies. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable tool for investigating the cosmological properties of dark matter and baryons. This study introduces a novel statistical framework for analyzing the three-dimensional correlations of Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers, which allows for the direct derivation of cosmological parameters without relying on simulations. By modeling the relationship between the three-dimensional auto-correlation function of Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers and the underlying dark matter distribution, we demonstrate that the mean redshift separation between them can be predicted using only a minimal set of cosmological parameters. We then utilize this prediction to extract the mean linear bias of Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers from the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Furthermore, we show that the mean bias of baryonic matter can be directly inferred from the ratio of the mean redshift separations between Lyman-$\alpha$ absorbers and dark matter halos. These findings indicate that the mean linear bias of baryonic halos with a virial mass of $10^{10}M_{\odot}$ is approximately 0.9, with a potential uncertainty of less than 10%. Additionally, we demonstrate that the mean linear bias of dark matter halos with a virial mass of $10^{12}M_{\odot}$ can be deduced by comparing the mean redshift separation between halos of $10^{10}M_{\odot}$ and those of $10^{12}M_{\odot}$. Consequently, the mean linear bias of halos with a virial mass of $10^{12}M_{\odot}$ is approximately 1.2, with an uncertainty of roughly 10%. These results suggest that the three-dimensional correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest could provide a new method for determining the mean bias of halos. This approach is particularly advantageous because it avoids the systematic errors inherent in simulations and does not require assumptions regarding the internal structure of halos. The mean bias of halos can be determined using only the three-dimensional correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, which can be measured from a single redshift survey. We conclude that this method will be highly effective for extracting the mean bias of halos from future large-scale redshift surveys. We demonstrate a successful experimental transfer of both longitudinal and longitudinal emittances from an oscillator beam to a flat beam. By utilizing a magnetic bottle combined with a DC electric field, we achieved the capture of transversely emitted particles and controlled their longitudinal emission. The manipulation of emittance transfer was governed by the phase-space volume, adhering to Liouville's theorem. This research holds significant potential for beam cleaning, beam shaping, and waste particle disposal. Furthermore, the beam cleaning technique developed here could be applied to mitigate beam-halo issues in future high-energy colliders. The beam-shaping method offers a pathway to create flat beams for high-intensity physics applications. Additionally, the disposal of waste particles offers a solution to the problem of lost particles in high-intensity accelerators. These findings were presented at the 12th International Particle Accelerator Conference (IPAC'2021) in Lyon, France. The corresponding authors are Dr. Shengyuan Wang and Dr. Shengqiang Zhang. This paper introduces a new multi-ego-vehicle trajectory prediction framework that incorporates time-variant social awareness. The proposed Social VAE model addresses the challenge of capturing time-varying social awareness by employing two sequential VAEs that slide through the trajectory trajectory data. The initial VAE learns the average social awareness, while the second VAE updates the social awareness information provided by the first. Additionally, the model generates multiple future trajectories for each input, accounting for the uncertainty inherent in social awareness. The predicted results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves higher accuracy than existing state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, the Brier score improved by 10.5%, and the MD score increased by 11.5% compared to previous models. These findings indicate that the model's performance is enhanced by its ability to learn social awareness through a sequential process and to predict trajectories that reflect this uncertainty. This paper introduces a novel Information-Theoretic Metric of Complexity (ITMOC) designed for Boltzmann Machines. Drawing inspiration from the Fisher-Rao metric, this new approach is demonstrated to satisfy established properties of Riemannian metrics and offers distinct advantages over conventional statistical complexity measures found in existing literature. Specifically, unlike the Free Energy, Fisher-Rao metric, and Fisher information, the proposed ITMOC remains valid even when a probability distribution is undefined. Furthermore, it exhibits Riemannian characteristics that allow it to capture the intrinsic geometric structures of Boltzmann Machines. Finally, the study applies this metric to analyze how temperature influences complexity within Ising models. The results indicate that low temperatures generate more complex structures, whereas high temperatures reduce complexity, causing the system to approach uniformity. Additionally, the ITMOC successfully identifies two critical phase transitions: the paramagnetic-ferromagnetic transition and the paramagnetic-glass transition. These findings underscore the ITMOC's utility as a valuable tool for investigating the geometric properties of Boltzmann Machines. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar2002/ITMOC. Future research will explore extending this metric to broader probabilistic models, including Deep Boltzmann Machines and Restricted Boltzmann Machines. This paper introduces a novel, vision-based Human-Swarm Interaction (HSI) framework designed for outdoor environments. The system relies on a deep neural network trained to identify five distinct hand gestures. By integrating this recognition technology with a decentralized swarm control architecture, the study successfully demonstrates real-time communication between a human operator and a swarm of quadcopters flying within an open area. This capability enables the system to execute various maneuvers and formations based on the operator's instructions. Furthermore, the research establishes a foundation for future studies aimed at enhancing both the HSI framework and the associated neural network model. To achieve this, the authors propose implementing real-time, online training of the neural network using the extensive dataset of hand gestures captured during operation. Additionally, efforts will be made to reduce the computational load on the onboard computer by optimizing both the neural network and the recognition algorithm. Finally, the study intends to expand the recognized gesture set to facilitate more complex commands, such as generating specific trajectories or executing maneuvers. The validity of these proposals is supported by preliminary experiments indicating that the suggested improvements can significantly boost the performance of the HSI framework. These outcomes are expected to advance the field of HSI by providing a robust baseline for further investigation. Additionally, the work contributes to the realization of autonomous applications, including environmental monitoring and surveillance, by demonstrating the feasibility of controlling large quadcopter swarms using human input. This approach holds promise for reducing the operational costs associated with deploying and managing extensive drone fleets. The paper concludes by outlining these and other potential applications of the proposed HSI framework. Source code and experimental data will be made available to the community to foster continued research and development in this area. The experimental setup, neural network architecture, and performance results are detailed in the corresponding video. Additionally, the authors have published a related article in a peer-reviewed journal. This study addresses the challenge of classifying various blood cell types, a task with significant potential for enhancing diagnostic efficiency in medical fields. We introduce a neural network architecture designed for periodic image patches, utilizing a combination of Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks. The architecture is trained via contrastive loss to generate cell-specific embeddings. We evaluate several models for feature extraction, with periodic image patches serving as input. Furthermore, we explore multiple strategies for integrating these models to create an ensemble system. Our approach achieves an accuracy of 96.5% on a test dataset, outperforming the most accurate individual model by 1.5%. Additionally, we demonstrate that our ensemble outperforms the state-of-the-art method described in the paper. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/MBH2019.

Counterdiabatic (CD) protocols have been widely investigated to control quantum systems, including applications in ground-state initialization via adiabatic evolution of a parameter-dependent Hamiltonian. However, for generic quantum systems, an exact CD driving term is typically not available, necessitating approximate terms that are often difficult to implement experimentally. This study introduces a variational approach to determine an optimal approximate CD term. We apply this method to the one-dimensional Hubbard model, employing both a su(2) Lie algebraic CD term and a perturbation CD term. The optimal CD term is derived by minimizing the CD action, which quantifies the rate of change of the ground state. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed method is general and can be extended to various other quantum systems. Furthermore, we confirm that the proposed CD term is experimentally feasible, as it can be realized using local two-qubit gates. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed CD term is effective in preparing a pure ground state. These results indicate that the variational CD approach is highly promising for achieving pure ground-state initialization. Additionally, the simplicity and feasibility of the CD term suggest that this method can be extended to other quantum systems, such as the Heisenberg model. This work provides a foundation for future research into ground-state initialization. This paper introduces a novel, high-speed discoloration metric grounded in color temperature, designed for tone-mapping applications. Unlike traditional methods that rely on expensive spectral measurements or complex mathematical models, our approach offers a simple yet effective solution. We provide a practical empirical formula for calculating this metric and validate its utility for both local and global tone-mapping tasks. Specifically, we demonstrate its application in local tone-mapping, global tone-mapping, and tone-mapping parameter estimation. Additionally, we present a real-time implementation built on the OpenCV library, highlighting its computational efficiency. Experimental results confirm that our method produces visually competitive outputs compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques while maintaining significantly higher computational efficiency. Additionally, it acts as a precursor to upcoming research on "sin and cos Taylor expansion" and "cosine integral expansion." All supporting code and data are publicly accessible. Additionally, we explore the connections between our findings and the study of harmonic maps into general manifolds possessing curvature pinching conditions. Finally, we generalize the concept of harmonic branched coverings to apply to harmonic maps that are immersions outside of a set of measure zero. These results are supported by the development of a novel theory of harmonic homotopy, which is presented as it may hold independent significance. We illustrate this with examples involving harmonic immersions, maps with curvature pinching conditions, and maps defined on minimal surfaces. The paper concludes with an examination of the relationship between harmonic homotopy classes and classical topological homotopy classes. This investigation yields a new topological characterization of harmonic homotopy classes and offers a novel approach to the study of harmonic maps based on this characterization. This approach is grounded in the combined application of quantum electrodynamics and kinetic theory.
