We introduce a novel centrality metric grounded in triangle inequality excess, termed Gromov centrality. This measure evaluates how closely a node's distance relationships to the rest of the network conform to an Euclidean metric, thereby revealing the node's level of adaptation to the network's intrinsic metric. Gromov centrality demonstrates robustness across various synthetic network models and effectively identifies key nodes in real-world datasets, including the human interactome and a world airline network. Furthermore, we link this centrality measure to the concept of intrinsic dimensionality, demonstrating that it can serve as a metric for the intrinsic dimensionality of both random networks and real-world networks. These findings suggest that Gromov centrality offers a multi-scale perspective on node importance, enhancing our ability to prioritize nodes for analysis in network science. The Gromov centrality method is accessible via an open-source Python package. Additionally, we have released a collection of real-world networks, along with pre-calculated Gromov centralities and low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, to facilitate the development of new methods. This data can be accessed at https://github.com/alextrembisky/Network-Dimensionality. Our method is detailed in the paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01001. We also provide a video tutorial for method implementation at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. We welcome any feedback or questions. Thank you. Aleksey Trembisky, Daniel Cremers, and Alexander Alemani. 2021.

We introduce a novel gravitation model grounded in an extension of Special Relativity, termed "Azimuthally Symmetric Relativity," which incorporates spatial and temporal azimuthal dimensions. This framework generates an additional azimuthal component within the relative velocity, which we demonstrate can be utilized to explain various gravitational phenomena. The corresponding action functional, along with its general equations of motion, is derived. Furthermore, the azimutal velocity component gives rise to a corresponding force that closely resembles Newtonian gravitation. In the weak-field regime, this model aligns with both the Equivalence Principle and the predictions of the weak-field limit of General Relativity. Additionally, the derived weak-field solution for the Schwarzschild metric offers a straightforward explanation for the bending of light. The corresponding paper is designated as (I). A subsequent contribution, (II), will detail the model's application to the perihelion shift of Mercury. These findings will ultimately facilitate the formulation of a set of weak-field solutions applicable to all cases in General Relativity. **Keywords:** Azimuthal symmetry, Azimuthal velocity, Schwarzschild metric, Equivalence Principle, Weak-field limit, Weak-field solution, Weak-field bending of light, Perihelion shift of Mercury. **PACS:** 04.20.-q, 04.25.N-, 95.30.Sf. **MSC:** 83C05, 83C10, 83C15, 83C57, 83C57, 83C80. **DOI:** 10.26507/1555-1397-10.1.1. **URL:** http://arxiv.org/abs/1001.0101v1. **Date:** 2010.01.01. **Language:** English. **Type:** Research. **Section:** 1. We examine matrix operators and their collections under strict equivalence, a form of equivalence that is more granular than standard equivalence. This framework encompasses concepts such as module equivalence, index equivalence, and rank equivalence. Our primary focus is on operator bundles, which consist of matrix operators sharing an identical bundle of range spaces. We present a classification based on the invariants of these operators, specifically utilizing the right nondegenerate characteristic sequences and their transposes. In the process, we derive the "first Fitting ideals," which correspond to the ideals generated by these sequences. Additionally, we establish the transposes of these sequences for both matrix operators and scalar polynomials. We demonstrate that these sequences fully characterize bundle equivalence and derive several significant corollaries. Finally, we apply these findings to the issue of reducing matrix operators within a bundle to a canonical form. To achieve this, we introduce a new canonical form termed the quasi-rectangular form, alongside an equally novel reduction procedure known as quasi-rectangular reduction. We prove that this quasi-rectangular form is the unique canonical form under quasi-rectangular reduction, and we outline the steps to obtain it. Furthermore, we examine matrix operators within a bundle under the looser concept of quasi-bundle equivalence, revealing that the invariants for this case are simply the collection of all right nondegenerate characteristic sequences. We also provide a practical method for identifying a bundle's invariants. The paper concludes with an illustrative example demonstrating the reduction of matrix operators in a bundle to quasi-rectangular form, including the calculation of the bundle's invariants. This example was generated using a computer program, for which we provide the source code. We note that the quasi-rectangular form lacks uniqueness with respect to left nondegenerate characteristic sequences; however, we propose that a form unique under quasi-bundle equivalence would be valuable. We address this by introducing another canonical form called the quasi-diagonal form and a corresponding reduction process, quasi-diagonal reduction. We establish that this form is unique under quasi-bundle equivalence and prove that the quasi-diangular form of matrix operators in a bundle is unique under the same equivalence relation. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm for computing the quasi-diagonal form with a specific example. This form is constructed via the quasi-diagonal form of matrix operators within a bundle, which is derived from the quasi-rectangular form. We demonstrate that applying T-folding to the topological CFT on a twisted cylinder yields a non-geometric background that remains geometric only after deformation. By performing T-folding on all four sectors of the topological string on a cylinder with a $\mathbb{Z}_N$ twist, we explicitly construct the resulting non-germetric sigma model. We explicitly calculate the background fields and demonstrate that they satisfy the equations of motion. Furthermore, we show that incorporating a background deformation restores geometric interpretability, with the deformation parameter relating to the B-field of the topological cylinder via a specific factor. We also provide the spectrum of the open string sector for all cases. Finally, we offer a brief discussion on how T-folding on a topological cylinder with $\mathbb{Z}_N$ twists corresponds to a generalized quotient by a discrete subgroup of $O(2,2,\mathbb{Z})$. Additionally, we examine the relationship between our findings and existing literature, particularly in the context of orbifolds. Specifically, we show that our results align with the case of an orbifold formed by quotienting a torus by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ twist, which is dual to a twisted cylinder. We also demonstrate that our findings are consistent with the case of quotienting a torus by a $\mathbb{Z}_3$ twist, which corresponds to a twisted torus. However, for a $\mathbb{Z}_3$ twist orbifold, we observe that the open string spectrum is not fully captured by the open string on the twisted torus. This discrepancy may stem from the fact that we have not fully explored all possible $\mathbb{Z}_3$ twists of the topological cylinder. We leave this investigation for future work. Additionally, we note that for a twisted torus, the background is non-geometric only when $N=3$, whereas it is geometric for $N=2$. This distinction may also contribute to the discrepancy in open string spectra. We also note that for $N=3$, the open string spectrum is not fully captured by the open string on the twisted torus. This discrepancy may also be due to the fact that we have not fully explored all possible $\mathbb{Z}_3$ twists of the topological cylinder. We leave this investigation for future work. Additionally, we show that for a twisted torus, the background is non-geometric only for $N=3$, whereas it is geometric for $N=2$.

Graphs with bounded treewidth are highly tractable for numerous algorithmic challenges. However, determining whether a specific graph belongs to this category or constructing a linear-time tree-decomposition for minor-free metrics remains an open problem. This paper introduces a novel graph class known as graphs of bounded treewidth and bounded clique-size, which encompasses all sparse graphs, including planar and minor-free metrics. We demonstrate that these classes are closed under edge contraction and even under edge deletion. Leveraging these properties, we propose a straightforward algorithm capable of identifying and constructing a linear-tree-decomposition for any such graph. Consequently, this yields efficient methods for solving various hard problems on planar and minor-free metrics, including shortest paths, longest paths, Hamiltonicity, and minimum vertex covers. Furthermore, our findings suggest that minor-free metrics may possess inherent treewidth bounds. Finally, our work offers a unified framework for addressing questions about the boundedness of treewidth and maximum clique size in metrics. Notably, we establish that no universal treewidth bound exists for isometric subgraphs of treewidth-$k$ metrics, nor for metrics derived from isometric subgraphs of treewidth-$k$ metrics. The latter result is particularly significant as it refutes a conjecture by Bousquet et al. (2018). Additionally, we construct an infinite family of metrics with bounded treewidth and clique-size that remain bounded only when edge weights are relaxed. We examine smooth strongly monotonic discrete-time dynamical systems operating within the real vector space $\mathbb{R}^d$. We demonstrate that, absent any additional constraints, the prevalent long-term behavior of these systems involves convergence toward fixed points or periodic orbits, where the associated Jacobian matrices possess all real eigenvalues. This result is derived from the observation that linear time-invariant systems exhibiting complex eigenvalues occupy only a null set within the space of all possible initial conditions. Furthermore, we establish that analogous conclusions hold for algebraic varieties of codimension at least one in the space of all possible initial conditions, with the corresponding null sets or varieties arising from the absence of complex eigenvalues in specific subspaces of the parameter space. Finally, we extend this finding to the scenario where a non-empty open subset of the parameter space lacks complex eigenvalues. These findings are applicable to various problems in economics and operations research. Additionally, we present a counterexample illustrating that convergence to fixed points or periodic orbits is not necessarily the prevalent outcome for smooth strongly monotonic systems that are either time-varying or possess a parameter space containing complex eigenvalues. Finally, we address an open question by providing a counterexample to the claim that the set of initial conditions leading to convergence to fixed points or periodic orbits is dense in the state space. This counterexample relies on the construction of a smooth strongly monotonic system that converges to a chaotic attractor with a non-empty interior. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first instance of a chaotic attractor with a non-empty interior for a smooth strongly monotonic system. Moreover, this example is the first instance of a chaotic attractor with a non-empty interior arising from a smooth, strongly monotonic system that is both simple and explicit. Specifically, the example is a time-varying system where the Jacobian matrices are all diagonal and the transition function is piecewise linear. We also provide an example of a smooth strongly monotonic system that converges to a chaotic attractor with a non-empty interior, where the Jacobian matrices are all diagonal and the transition function is piecewise linear, and the parameter space includes real eigenvalues. However, we note that the parameter space in this example is not open. Additionally, we observe that the prevalent behavior of this example is convergence to the chaotic attractor, despite the existence of initial conditions that converge to fixed points. Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) represent a promising approach for utilizing near-term quantum hardware to tackle complex problems, such as simulating quantum many-body systems. However, a primary challenge in VQAs is determining the optimal parameters for preparing the target state. Current methods often rely on adiabatic state preparation, which demands extensive circuit resources, or ad-hoc strategies that yield suboptimal results. This study introduces a novel adaptive VQA that employs qubit-excitation-based mixing operators to automatically identify optimal parameters. The efficacy of this adaptive algorithm is validated through its application to finding the ground state of the transverse-field Ising model. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of the method's convergence is provided, demonstrating that it can efficiently ground the transverse-field Ising model even in regimes characterized by complex quantum phase transitions. Additionally, the algorithm is evaluated for scalability, showing that it can ground larger instances of the model with increasing system size. Finally, the study extends this approach to prepare the Bell diagonal phase of a generalised transverse-field Ising model, confirming that the adaptive algorithm successfully reaches the diagonal phase. These findings indicate that qubit-excitation-based adaptive VQAs are highly effective for ground state preparation tasks. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/quantum-machine-learning/adaptive-vqa. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are deep generative models that approximate the posterior distribution of latent variables using a variational method. This study investigates whether replacing the mean-field variational approach with a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate for latent representation estimation can enhance VAE performance. We introduce a new class of models termed deep generative encoders, which employ iterative optimization techniques to derive these MAP estimates. Our findings demonstrate that this architecture can achieve exact recovery of synthetic data representations. Furthermore, when applied to single-cell RNA sequencing data, the model surpasses standard VAEs in accurately inferring cell types and gene programs. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexmaher/dge.

Recent findings from the NANOGrav pulsar timing array and the Advanced LIGO-Virgo interferometer network indicate a stochastic gravitational-wave (GW) background with a strain amplitude of $A_0 \sim 10^{-9}$ at a frequency of $f_0 \sim 25$ nHz and $A_0 \sim 10^{-2}$ at $f_0 \sim 25$ Hz, respectively. We demonstrate that a primordial GW spectrum amplified by dark energy quintessence in the early universe can account for these observations. This model predicts a blue-tilted spectrum ($n \gtrsim 0$) that remains consistent with current constraints from Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN), and standard pulsar timing analyses. Furthermore, we show that this background can resolve the tension between the Hubble constant ($H_0$) values derived from Planck CMB measurements and those from the SH0ES distance ladder. Specifically, the presence of such a GW background reduces the inferred value of $H_0$ from SH0ES by approximately 1.5$\sigma$, bringing it into alignment with Planck results. Within a regular differential category, such as a regular differential topos, we construct Lie groupoids along with exponential objects representing smooth groupoid morphisms. We demonstrate that every groupoid, including classical Lie groupoids, possesses a canonical integration to Lie algebras in this setting. By extending the definition of internal completeness to groupoids, we establish the following key results: 1) In any regular differential topos, a connected Lie groupoid exhibits internal linkedness between its Lie algebra and the Lie groupoid itself; 2) In any differential category, a finitely generated internal Lie algebra is integral complete with respect to a groupoid $G$ if the canonical map from its complete subalgebra to $G$ is an internal isomorphism; 3) In a well-adapted differential category, the Lie algebra of a connected Lie groupoid is complete with respect to the groupoid; 4) In a finitely complete differential category, a groupoid is connected precisely when the integration map from its Lie algebra to the space of paths is an internal isomorphism. These findings generalize and extend prior work on Lie algebras and groups in differential categories to the context of groupoids. Furthermore, we provide an alternative characterization of internal linkedness for groupoids using internal universal coverings and demonstrate that internal completeness for groupoids can be characterized via internal universal coverings and connected Lie groupoids. Finally, in the specific case of finite groupoids, we characterize internal linkedness and internal completeness using monoids and algebras, respectively. These results hold in any well-adapted differential category, with the stack of paths serving as the universal covering groupoid. Additionally, we present a characterization of groupoid connected components via internal connected components and connected Lie groupoids. All results are developed in finite dimensions. The growing demand for high-quality, large-scale data in biomedical research is driving an increasing number of scientists to adopt the FAIR data principles, which ensure data is Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. While adhering to these principles enhances the utility of data for diverse applications, it also introduces security challenges, particularly when handling sensitive information. This paper introduces the concept of a "scientific data gateway" to facilitate secure data sharing. By combining data gateway technology with the Federated Identity Management (FIM) paradigm, we can securely grant data owners access control while allowing researchers to collaborate without needing direct data access. This approach preserves data privacy and confidentiality, ensuring that data owners can monitor access and usage. Additionally, we outline a research agenda aimed at developing gateway technology to support secure data sharing within the biomedical and health care domains. Given the domain's specific requirements, this proposed gateway technology is expected to evolve into a distinct cyberinfrastructure component. Furthermore, we demonstrate the viability of gateway technology by detailing its implementation as a gateway service within the Open Science Grid (OSG) and Federated Data Gateway (FDG) platforms. These systems provide a foundational layer for data sharing, enabling researchers to collaborate on secure and effective data exchange. Finally, we discuss the associated security challenges and potential solutions. Our primary contribution lies in introducing the scientific data gateway as a secure data sharing mechanism and our second contribution is the demonstration of gateway technology as a foundational layer for data sharing, supported by existing cyberinfrastructure. This work is part of a broader initiative to provide secure data sharing for the biomedical and health care domains, which is currently being funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) under grant numbers 1629600, 1629610, 1629619, 1629620, 1629621, and 1629622. This initiative is a key component of the Cyberinfrastructure for Biomedical Data Sharing (CyBiDS) project. The CyBiDS project aims to provide a cyberinfrastructure solution that enables secure, privacy-preserving, and effective data sharing for biomedical research. This solution is designed to be domain-agnostic, allowing it to be easily adapted for use in other areas such as biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, and agriculture. The project's vision is to provide a secure and privacy-preserving infrastructure for data sharing, with the expectation that this will foster a data-sharing culture among scientists

This study addresses the identification and estimation of mediation parameters within a survey design that collects longitudinal data through case-control sampling. We establish that, under a specific identification assumption, case-control sampling does not hinder the estimation of natural direct and indirect effects. Furthermore, we present a parametric mediation analysis framework that utilizes sampling weights to accurately estimate these effects. We derive an identification region for the natural direct effect, demonstrating that point identification of the natural indirect effect relies on additional constraints. Additionally, a simulation study is conducted to evaluate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimator. The application section utilizes data from the Canadian National Population Health Survey to analyze the impact of a binary lifestyle intervention on cardiovascular disease risk, operating through a binary diet mediator. Our findings indicate that the point identification region for the natural indirect effect is not the entire parameter space, yet it is sufficiently broad to conclude that the intervention reduces cardiovascular disease risk by improving diet quality. Finally, we discuss extensions of this work, which include handling sampling weights, addressing missing data, and analyzing designs involving multiple time points. The primary contribution of this paper lies in its identification results and the development of a general mediation analysis approach capable of accommodating survey weights. This methodology is applicable to designs where longitudinal data collection is interrupted by a survey design, such as case-control sampling. Additionally, the proposed approach can be adapted to handle missing data via multiple imputation and to analyze multi-level designs, including nested case-control studies. The methods are implemented in an R package named `medcheck`, which is available on CRAN. The package includes a simulation example and an application to a cardiovascular study. The code for mediation estimation, along with the R scripts for simulations and analysis, can be accessed via a link in the supplementary materials. While the `medcheck` package is designed for users with a basic understanding of R, it is not intended for statisticians, as it omits several features found in other R packages. The package's scope is limited to scenarios involving a binary outcome, a binary exposure, and a binary mediator. Furthermore, `medcheck` does not offer sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding, nor does it provide tools for estimating an identification region for the natural indirect effect. The authors acknowledge that the `medcheck` package is a work in progress. Future research will focus on expanding the package to support multivariate mediators and longitudinal mediators. Additionally, we plan to refine the sensitivity analysis to account for missing data and unmeasured confounding. Our work also aims to extend the approach to more complex sampling designs

This study examines a secure, multi-user radio over Gaussian wiretap channel enhanced by a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS). The primary objective is to maximize the secure sum rate (SSR). To address this, the authors propose a robust RIS transmission strategy utilizing a semidefinite relaxation (SDR) method. This approach generates a quasi-diagonal diagonal precoder for the source and an optimal reflecting configuration for the RIS. Simulation results are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. Furthermore, the impact of various factors, including the number of RIS elements, the count of legitimate users, and the number of eavesdroppers, is evaluated. Finally, the performance of the robust strategy is compared against an information-theoretic lower bound and a non-robust strategy to demonstrate its superiority. Additionally, the influence of different types of HIs on the SSR is investigated. Finally, the proposed strategy is benchmarked against conventional designs that ignore hardware impairments and eavesdropper position uncertainty. These comparisons illustrate that the robust strategy outperforms its non-robust counterpart and that the potential performance gains from incorporating hardware imperfections and eavesdropper position uncertainty can be substantial. This study investigates the application of contrastive value functions (CVF) within executive function (EF) through a single task demonstrating their potential to reframe an agent's perception of an environment by sampling and relabeling historical states and actions. We illustrate how this approach, combined with hindsight summarization, can resolve issues in sparse reward settings, such as a simple grid world. Furthermore, we show that the proposed CVF-based method enables an agent to learn a more robust policy in a more complex, non-Markovian environment, which serves as a stepping stone toward full-world learning. Finally, we present a basic discussion on how CVF can be applied to goal-conditioned navigation tasks in simulated 3D worlds. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/aleksandar-milanovic/contrastive-value.

The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the contrastive value function. Section 3 outlines the motivation for using CVF-based methods in EF, with Section 3.1 detailing the approach for learning from scratch in non-Markovian environments, and Section 3.2 exploring its application to goal-conditioned navigation. Section 4 presents experimental results, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

**Keywords:** Executive function, value-based methods, non-Markovian environments, contrastive value functions, hindsight summarization, goal-conditioned navigation.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved significant success in decision-making tasks across various domains, including games, robotics, and autonomous vehicles. However, RL often struggles with reward shaping, particularly in scenarios where rewards are sparse and difficult to define. This challenge is prevalent in many real-world scenarios, such as autonomous driving, where agents must navigate complex scenarios without explicit guidance on what constitutes successful behavior.

The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) has recently provided the first in-situ measurements of solar breeze energy flux within the inner heliosphere. Utilizing data from the SWEAP (Solar Wind Experiment on Parker Solar Probe) aboard the Parker Solar Probe and the ACE (Advanced Composition Explorer) spacecraft, this study compares energy fluxes across different reference frames. Results indicate that energy flux is not invariant relative to the spacecraft's frame of reference, with the PSP frame yielding the highest values. This discrepancy is primarily attributed to the definition of energy flux itself; when analyzed, the kinetic energy component dominates the energy budget, whereas the Poynting flux (electromagnetic energy flux) remains negligible. Consequently, the PSP measurements confirm that solar breeze energy flux is predominantly kinetic, a finding consistent with earlier PSP observations of solar coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Furthermore, the paper explores the implications of these measurements for understanding solar wind energy transport and the broader energy budget of the inner heliosphere. Finally, the study proposes a method to distinguish between kinetic and Poynting flux contributions using in-situ spacecraft data, which could facilitate future heliospheric energy budget studies. This work represents the initial effort to quantify energy flux in the inner heliosphere, with future investigations expected to provide more comprehensive insights into solar energy transport. Additionally, the analysis reveals that, on average, the kinetic specific energy of the solar breeze increases with heliocentric distance, a trend that may be influenced by the interaction between the solar breeze and slow solar wind streams. These findings are supported by a dataset of 100 days of PSP observations and 100 days of ACE observations. The associated data repository can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7205000. This paper examines the optical response of a $q$-deformed optomechanical system coupled with a two-level atom operating near a $q$-deformed mechanical resonance. We analyze how $q$-deformation affects the optical response, transparency, and the magnitude of anomalous dispersion associated with both gain and loss scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that nonlinearity can be leveraged to achieve clarity in both fast and slow light regimes, as well as in situations involving gain and loss. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Our results indicate that these effects are highly tunable through various control parameters, offering significant potential for applications in quantum information processing and communication. Additionally, we note that our framework remains valid for standard (non-$q$-deformed) deformation as a specific limiting case. Our study thus establishes a foundation for investigating the interplay between $q$-deformation and atomic interactions within optomechanical systems. Finally, we suggest that these conclusions can be extended to other quantum systems, such as cavity QED, circuit QED, and spin systems. This study investigates the properties of R-parity even and odd states within the "two-rotors model," which features a potential designed to mimic the spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry. We demonstrate that both the potential and the Hamiltonian remain invariant under a Z2 symmetry, which corresponds to the parity of the collective field. Furthermore, we identify R-parity even and odd scissors modes situated near chiral partner doublets, with the odd scissors mode exhibiting adverse characteristics. We also examine the overlap between ground states and excited states composed of particle-hole pairs, discovering that the ground state exhibits significant deformation. Additionally, we explore the influence of the potential's tail on the system's spectrum and analyze the behavior of the chiral order parameter as a function of coupling constants. Finally, we establish that the Hamiltonian's spectrum remains invariant under chiral rotations, regardless of the specific potential selected. These findings suggest that the model effectively simulates the spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry in the presence of Z2 parity symmetry. Consequently, it serves as a valuable tool for investigating the interplay between parity and chiral symmetry breaking, as well as the formation of parity doublets. The model can be extended to include additional degrees of freedom, such as orbital angular momentum, to study symmetry breaking in systems with orbital angular momentum. Finally, we outline the necessary modifications to the model to account for the spontaneous breaking of parity symmetry. These results are supported by numerical computations of the spectrum and the chiral order parameter. The methodology employed is analogous to that used in the nuclear sector for describing parity and chiral partner states. Furthermore, this work offers a framework for incorporating parity violation in two-body systems, a topic of interest in the context of the recent discovery of a permanent electric dipole moment in a neutron. The model is also applicable to the study of parity violation in nuclei. To facilitate further research, we provide a Fortran code that calculates the spectrum and chiral order parameter for the model. This code is available at: https://github.com/fernando-ramos-perez/Two-Rotors-Model. Additionally, a Python version of the code can be found at: https://github.com/fernando-ramos-perez/Two-Rotors-Model/tree/Python. Both versions are also accessible via the following link: https://github.com/fernando-ramos-perez/Two-Rotors-Model/tree/Nuclear-physics. The code was developed by F.R.P. and is shared with the community to facilitate further research

This study introduces a cell-mean based neural network (CMNN) designed to address various hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. Unlike traditional neural network approaches that rely on automatic differentiation for calculating gradients, the proposed CMNN method utilizes analytical gradient computations. The technique is initially applied to solve multi-dimensional multi-source multi-dimensional Burgers' equations, yielding accurate results. Furthermore, an inverse problem involving the reconstruction of multi-dimensional multi-source initial conditions from observed data is formulated and resolved using the same CMNN framework. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the CMNN approach in solving multi-dimensional Burgers' equations. We introduce a joint syntactic and meaning parsing framework that leverages the shared structure of a parse tree to enhance syntactic accuracy and generate diverse semantic representations. By training jointly on the Parallel English Treebank and the semantic dataset Universal Dependencies + SemEval-2013 Task 2, our approach demonstrates that joint training yields superior performance across all semantic metrics compared to standard sequential methods. Furthermore, this method outperforms sequential strategies in producing less biased outputs, a conclusion supported by experiments using intrinsic validation and human evaluation. Finally, we show that a stochastic decoder utilizing beam search can effectively generate multiple syntactic and semantic trees, facilitating joint inference. This study investigates how the postmerger evolution of a dynamically and thermally cold, magnetized neutron star disk influences the characteristics of jets generated by newborn black holes. We perform binary black hole mergers using the moving-puncture method within the Einstein Toolkit, creating accretion disks with temperatures below the neutrino decoupling temperature ($T\lesssim 10$ MeV) and strong magnetic fields ($B\gtrsim 10^{14}$ G). Our results indicate that the neutrino-cooled disk's magnetic field amplifies the mass loss rate of jets via the Blandford-Znajek mechanism, reaching $\dot{M}\sim 10^{-2}$ M$_{\odot}$/s. Consequently, the energy and momentum deposited into the surrounding environment are significantly higher than in neutrino-cooled disk-free scenarios, which can suppress or completely halt jet formation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these postmerger outflows can eject a substantial portion of the accretion disk's mass within seconds, potentially hindering the accretion of material needed to fuel jets onto the newly formed black hole. These findings suggest that outflows from binary neutron star mergers can substantially impact the ejecta and gravitational wave signals from subsequent black hole-matter interactions. Finally, we outline the implications of these results for understanding kilonovae and short gamma-ray bursts. This study examines the tidal features of 1.2 million early-type galaxies (ETGs) with a stellar mass exceeding $10^{10} M_{\odot}$, identified within a 1.4 square degree field in the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). We analyze how the flux of these features varies with stellar mass, redshift, and luminosity. We determine that ETG features are most prevalent in galaxies situated near the bright end of the luminosity function, where the median flux is $10^{-3}$, and that the flux-luminosity relation is primarily driven by the distribution of feature presence. Furthermore, we establish a robust correlation between feature flux and the merger rate ($\Gamma_{\rm merger}$), finding that $\Gamma_{\rm merger}$ increases with luminosity and peaks at redshifts of $z \sim 0.5-1.0$. Finally, we establish a relation between the flux of tidal features and the dynamical age of the most recent merger, revealing that higher flux corresponds to a younger dynamical age. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the flux of tidal features scales with the dynamical age of the most recent merger. Additionally, we present the first evidence that the flux of tidal features in ETGs is influenced by the morphological type of their progenitors. Specifically, we find that the flux in features resulting from the merger of two elliptical galaxies is approximately 1.5 times greater than that of an elliptical galaxy merging with a disc galaxy. This result aligns with the expectation that the greater mass of elliptical galaxies, compared to discs, leads to more extended tidal features. Overall, our results indicate that the flux of tidal features in ETGs is governed by the properties of the merging galaxies. These conclusions are supported by N-body simulations of elliptical-elliptical and elliptical-disc galaxy mergers. We also demonstrate that the flux of tidal features can be utilized to constrain the dynamical age of the most recent merger and to estimate merger rates. Finally, we show that the flux of these features can distinguish between mergers of similar and dissimilar galaxies. These findings suggest that tidal features in ETGs serve as a valuable tool for investigating galaxy interactions. Fast radio bursts (FRBs) represent a class of enigmatic, millisecond-duration radio transients of extragalactic origin. While their origins remain uncertain, numerous FRBs are believed to be associated with compact objects, such as neutron stars. This study reports the results of an optical follow-up campaign targeting 10 well-observed FRBs, utilizing the Large Binocular Telescope and the Liverpool Telescope. Our findings reveal no optical emission within 10 seconds before or simultaneously with the radio bursts, establishing an upper limit of $10^{-14}$ solar luminosities at 5000 Å for a 1 ms burst at a distance of 1 Gpc. Furthermore, we conducted an optical search for delayed emission occurring between 10 seconds and 100 days post-burst. For the three FRBs with the most comprehensive monitoring, we found no evidence of delayed optical signals. These null detections are consistent with the absence of a persistent compact object or a supernova explosion at the FRB source locations. However, the non-detection of simultaneous optical emission suggests that the sources may be intrinsically radio-dominated. Additionally, we provide a detailed investigation of the optical light curve for FRB 121102, which exhibits a significant flux excess approximately 100 seconds prior to the burst. We propose that this excess may stem from a variable radio burst that is preferentially refracted toward the optical band by the interstellar medium. Text generation is typically guided by textual instructions, where prompts like "translate to German" or "summarize" signal large language models (LLMs) to produce specific outputs. However, in many scenarios, richer or more natural controls are necessary. For instance, providing input text for summarization or an example sentence for style transfer offers more precise guidance than generic commands. This work introduces a novel framework that integrates various modalities—including text, images, and video—into LLM generation processes. By employing a multi-modal, multi-task learning approach, the model can handle diverse tasks and controls simultaneously. Experiments on visual sentence pairing and image captioning demonstrate that this framework effectively learns to adapt language generation based on different visual inputs. Furthermore, the framework exhibits emergent capabilities in visual question answering and image captioning when leveraging paired data. The approach is highly scalable, supporting the joint training of multiple models on multi-modal, multi-task datasets. The framework is implemented in PyTorch and made available on GitHub. This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a novel ring signature and ringCT payment protocol designed to enhance anonymity in blockchain transactions. Our approach leverages Bulletproofs to construct the set membership proof, offering a more concise proof size compared to the Pedersen-based method used in our predecessor, Delegated MultiSigCT. This improvement stems from utilizing the power of elliptic curve cryptography within ring signatures. Furthermore, we propose a new technique for verifying the number of signatures, which significantly boosts verification speed. Experimental results demonstrate that the average verification time for a ringCT payment using 16 addresses is 1.5 milliseconds, representing a 20-fold acceleration over the original RingCT protocol. Additionally, we outline methods to further minimize both the size and number of signatures required for ringCT payments. Ultimately, Delegated RingCT enables ringCT payments to achieve transaction sizes comparable to standard coin transactions, thereby facilitating faster and more efficient anonymous transactions. The source code is available at https://github.com/BitBashers/delegated_ringCT. Future work will explore enhancing transparency and decentralization, specifically by developing a mechanism to identify double-spending. We also aim to investigate the feasibility of using Schnorr signatures to further reduce signature counts and overall transaction size. Finally, we plan to extend Delegated RingCT to support multi-recipient payments, building upon our prior Delegated MultiSigCT protocol which already offers more efficient n-recipient ringCT payments than current solutions. To achieve this, we will implement the proposed signature number verification technique and apply the Bulletproof-based membership proof method to the Delegated MultiSigCT protocol. The resulting Delegated MultiRingCT protocol will enable ring-of-set ringCT payments, where each recipient selects a subset of signers from the original ring-of-sets, resulting in smaller transaction sizes. The brightness of particle beams is a critical parameter for assessing their suitability in diverse beam-driven applications. This parameter is defined as the count of particles within a phase space volume element, specifically representing the product of transverse area and longitudinal charge. While direct measurement is impossible due to the beam's inherent disturbance, brightness can be determined by measuring the longitudinal charge transferred to a target during a brief scan across a beam segment. The paper outlines various target options and demonstrates how to calculate brightness from brightness scans. It also addresses potential pitfalls, such as beam self-distortion caused by space charge forces, and methods to mitigate these effects. Additionally, the discussion covers how to measure alternative scan quantities, such as differential flux density, and how to derive other beam parameters from scan data. This paper revisits the "Genuine Jacobi group," a concept originally developed by B. L. van der Waall and later extended by R. S. Phillips and R. P. Schiffler. We demonstrate that a version of the two variable model Jacobi-Eisenstein series proposed by van der Waall admits a series expansion featuring a finite field of view. Furthermore, we establish that this series converges uniformly on compact subsets of the upper half plane and provide an explicit formula for it. Additionally, we offer a concise re-examination of model Jacobi-Eisenstein series within the context of the genuine Jacobi group. Our findings include the derivation of a transformation law under the theta-series of a symplectic matrix, which can be interpreted as a generalization of the reciprocity law for symplectic Kloosterman sums. We also present the Fourier expansion of these series and explore their behavior under the action of the genuine Jacobi group. Finally, we extend the theory to multivariable model Jacobi-Eisenstein series associated with the $n$-variable Heisenberg group. In this generalized setting, the transformation law involves a symplectic sum, and the Fourier expansion incorporates Kloosterman sums. We anticipate that these series will hold significant value for the study of the generalized genuine Jacobi group. Throughout this work, the symplectic group is defined over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. However, we note that all arguments remain valid when working over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, with the finite field replaced by $\mathbb{Z}$. Consequently, our results apply to the genuine covering group of the symplectic group over $\mathbb{Q}$. To facilitate this broader application, we have incorporated several technical lemmas that are of independent interest. These lemmas are essential for analyzing the transformation law of the symplectic covering group and for elucidating the relationship between covering symplectic matrices and covering Heisenberg matrices. We anticipate that these lemmas will prove useful in future research concerning covering symplectic and Heisenberg matrices. Additionally, we have included lemmas regarding covering symplectic and Heisenberg sums, which are required to determine the Fourier expansion of the covering symplectic group. Table-based fact verification is a task where a model determines if a natural language query aligns with a specific table. To address this, we introduce DISA, a disassembly-based approach that first breaks down both the question and table into elementary semantic units before verifying facts. These units are identified using pre-trained language models and a novel table encoding framework. Experiments on the TabFact benchmark show that DISA surpasses previous methods, achieving 70.0% accuracy on non-trivial tables and 69.0% on mixed tables. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are powerful tools for synthesizing realistic images, yet their generated samples often suffer from lack of controllability. While techniques like Inversion Mapping (I-Map) allow image-like inputs to be fed into trained GANs for controlled generation, they are limited to this specific format and struggle with diverse user inputs. This paper introduces a flexible I-Map variant that accepts varied hidden space conditions rather than relying solely on image-like inputs. By employing a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to project arbitrary user inputs into the trained GAN's latent space, we enable realistic image synthesis under these variable conditions. Our results demonstrate that images generated via this VAE-based approach are visually superior to those produced by standard I-Map methods when given hidden conditions. Furthermore, we validate our hypothesis by successfully generating images of people engaged in various activities based on image embeddings extracted from Google's Image Search. Bayesian model comparison typically relies on computing the marginal likelihood, a task that is generally computationally prohibitive. Nested sampling addresses this by transforming the multidimensional model parameter space into one dimension characterized by a decreasing posterior mass. This work compares three methods for selecting points at each algorithmic step: nested importance sampling, nested random sampling, and the nested slice drawing method. We introduce a proven approximation that enables the calculation of exact posterior masses, facilitating model comparison. Model parameters are explored using nested random sampling, with step selections guided by nested importance sampling, slice drawing, or hybrid approaches. Applying this method to a normal linear regression model, we demonstrate that the nested importance sampling approach yields superior performance compared to nested random sampling. Furthermore, we find that nested slice drawing outperforms nested importance sampling when utilizing the proposed mass calculation technique. Finally, we illustrate the method's effectiveness through its application to a gamma generalized linear model and a spatially structured disease model. These examples show that the dimensionality of the parameter space can be extremely high, yet the algorithm remains efficient and effective in such scenarios. Additionally, the approach demonstrates robustness in the presence of multimodal posteriors. Overall, this method is applicable to any model where nested importance sampling is feasible. A key advantage is that it avoids the need for repeated Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, a requirement in techniques like thermodynamic integration. Consequently, this work expands the range of models for which nested sampling can be effectively employed. This study investigates two-particle correlations within a driven, dissipative Bose-Hubbard model, examining how these correlations evolve over time and vary with frequency. The analysis covers both normal and Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) phases. In the BEC phase, the system exhibits two distinct sets of peaks in the two-particle correlation function: one set arises from collective excitations of the condensate, while the other results from the scattering of two particles. In the frequency domain, the former corresponds to single-particle excitations, and the latter represents two-particle scattering. When the system resides in the normal phase, these correlation features are significantly suppressed. Furthermore, we analyze how noise influences two-particle correlations and the associated spectral density. Finally, the experimental implications of these findings are discussed. These results offer valuable insights for future experiments and suggest that two-particle correlations can serve as an effective tool for characterizing the phase of a driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard system. Additionally, the methodology employed can be extended to explore other nonlinear optical phenomena in dissipative quantum systems. The simulations were conducted using the Qutip-5.0.0 package. We extend the theory of elliptic equations in divergence form by allowing the lower-order terms to be represented as $L^2$-valued currents. The coefficients are assumed to be symmetric and bounded, while the main result establishes the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a specific subset of these $L^2$-valued currents, strong solutions exist within a weighted Sobolev space. This work serves as a continuation of our previous study (arXiv:2005.07300), where we addressed elliptic equations involving $L^2$-valued differential forms. The material presented here expands upon the first author's thesis, which was supervised by the second author. Additionally, this research builds upon the work of Fabes, Jodeit, and Serrin (1982) regarding elliptic operators with lower-order terms in Lebesgue spaces. Our primary tool involves the parametrix transformation method, which was introduced in this context by the first author in 2018. This method relies on the fact that a suitable change of variables can convert any elliptic operator into a form featuring a flat connection, thereby reducing the problem to analyzing a flat connection. This approach is an adaptation of the technique originally developed by Kodaira (1957) in the context of complex analysis. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the necessary background on $L^2$-valued currents and their properties; Section 3 presents the extension of elliptic theory to equations with lower-order terms in the form of $L^2$-valued currents; and Section 4 provides an example of such an equation. Finally, Section 5 offers a brief discussion on the application of our findings to mathematical physics. In this section, we examine the stationary Schrödinger equation and the Yang-Mills-Higgs equations, both of which can be expressed in the form of elliptic equations with lower-order terms as $L^2$-valued currents. We also provide a brief overview of the current research landscape regarding the solvability of the stationary Schrödinger equation with a magnetic field and a complex-valued potential belonging to $L^p$ for $p>2$. This research was conducted within the framework of the first author's thesis, which was supervised by the second author. This paper introduces Distributional Gaussian Processes (DGP), a new Bayesian nonparametric approach designed to model functions as collections of random variables. While standard Gaussian Process (GP) regression treats functions as random variables, DGP extends this by treating the domain itself as a random variable, thereby representing functions as collections of random variables linked to specific domain values. This additional stochasticity enables DGP to more effectively capture the uncertainty inherent in learning functions from data. We demonstrate that this enhanced uncertainty modeling improves out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in machine learning. Furthermore, we show that a specific instance of DGP is equivalent to learning a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) for the function values. We evaluate DGP using a simple regression task and a real-world UCI credit scoring dataset. Additionally, we apply our GMM-based DGP to a real-world inductive machine learning problem for OOD detection, comparing it against state-of-the-art GPs and recent GMM methods. Our results indicate that DGPs offer superior performance compared to both GP and GMM baselines. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez/DGP.

We present a statistical time-domain analysis of nonlinear phase noise in optical clocks, deriving a general expression for the Allan variance that is independent of the specific clock model. This derivation relies on three key assumptions: (i) the conversion of optical phase noise to frequency noise during readout, (ii) the whitening of this noise after readout, and (iii) the stability of the free-running laser. The resulting formula is broadly applicable to any optical clock, regardless of its physical design. We validate the derived expression using a distributed feedback laser as the primary oscillator and an electro-optic modulator to represent the conversion and whitening processes. The simulation results align closely with our theoretical predictions, with minor discrepancies attributed to finite data length. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Allan variance of such a clock is highly sensitive to the statistical distribution of the white phase noise. Specifically, we find that heavy-tailed distributions, such as the Cauchy distribution, can cause the variance to diverge, rendering the Allan variance undefined. This insight is broadly relevant to any oscillator exhibiting non-periodic behavior. Finally, we outline a method to quantify non-periodicity by analyzing the statistics of the clock's phase noise. This approach indicates that optical resonators in current optical clocks, such as those based on Yb$^+$, Sr, and Al$^+$, display a degree of non-periodicity that is significantly lower than that observed in the Yb$^+$ electro-optic modulator. Consequently, the impact of this sensitivity on these atomic clock systems is negligible. Our findings underscore the critical role of the readout mechanism in optical clock performance and suggest that future research should prioritize the development of superior readout schemes. Additionally, we provide a Python package to facilitate the implementation of this theoretical framework. The choice of loss function significantly influences neural network training. While prior research has primarily examined the impacts of L2 and KL divergence losses, this study investigates the effects of other losses, such as L1, by applying gradient surgery techniques. Our methodology involves either (a) retaining the original gradients from specific literature while substituting the loss function, or (optionally) (b) adjusting gradient scaling to ensure a fair comparison. We evaluated these approaches across various classification and regression tasks. We demonstrate that this modification can be implemented efficiently via a holographic algorithm, resulting in a new class of codes known as Hyper-INVERTIBLE topological codes (HINVCODES). These codes maintain both volume-law entanglement and power-law mutual information while supporting an holographic complexity-time duality. Furthermore, we prove that for any constant $k$, a family of HINVCODES exists where the distribution of long-range boundary qubits follows a $1/n^k$ power law. Our analysis reveals that the distribution of these inter-filament distances is highly non-Gaussian, indicating that the population does not arise from a uniform medium. Furthermore, we find that the mean separation between the most obvious filaments is approximately 0.1 pc. These findings suggest that the filaments are components of a hierarchical structure, where they group together to form larger, more extended entities. Additionally, the observed mean separation aligns closely with the typical width of a single filament, implying that the transition from filament to extended structure occurs at a scale roughly equal to the filament's width. Finally, we demonstrate that the internal structure of the most visible filaments is not uniform; rather, it consists of smaller clumps that are more readily identified in high-resolution observations. This study investigates an optimal Conservation Voltage Reduction (CVR) strategy designed for simultaneous network-wide implementation within integrated primary-secondary distribution systems. Addressing the challenge that increased load flow nonlinearity and secondary transformer saturation render conventional CVR methods ineffective, the proposed approach utilizes a nonconvex optimization framework. This framework incorporates distribution system constraints, specifically nonlinear load flow equations and CVR saturation limits, alongside power quality constraints such as voltage limits and CVR efficiency. To enable simultaneous execution, the problem is decomposed into two stages: a central utility first solves a master problem to determine optimal CVR levels at secondary transformer terminals, and then solves an auxiliary problem to evaluate the resulting CVR efficiency. Subsequently, individual distribution substations independently resolve their respective subproblems by exchanging only low-dimensional information with the utility. Simulation results using a real-world 12-bus integrated system demonstrate that this proposed scheme achieves performance comparable to centralized optimization while significantly reducing communication overhead. Furthermore, an online implementation was tested on a modified 33-bus integrated system to assess its performance under varying conditions. The study concludes that the proposed distributed optimal CVR strategy offers a viable solution for real-world deployment. Additionally, the methodology is adaptable to other distributed optimal power flow problems characterized by nonlinear constraints and saturation effects. To further enhance scalability, the paper introduces a new distributed Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) variant that supports distributed Optimal Power Flow (OPF) solutions. This algorithm is proven to converge to the KKT point of the optimal OPF problem and remains applicable to general network structures. Finally, an extensive simulation on a 39-bus system validates the proposed ADMM algorithm's performance. This work serves as a foundation for future research into distributed optimal power flow solutions. Ultimately, the developed distributed ADMM algorithm can be extended to address other distributed OPF problems involving nonlinear constraints and saturation issues. Additionally, the algorithm demonstrates robustness against communication failures and malicious attacks, a property verified through extensive simulations. These findings pave the way for future investigations into resilient OPF solutions. Keywords: Conservation Voltage Reduction, Nonlinear Constraints, Saturation, Distributed ADMM, Cyber Security.

This work investigates a delay-agnostic advisor, capable suggesting arms to a learner within a multi-armed bandit framework even before the learner receives feedback from its own selections. We introduce a general delay model applicable to both online and offline contexts, where a specific arm $i$ incurs a delay of $d(i)$ periods, with $d(i)$ varying by arm. We present an advisor algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\sum_{i} \mathrm{regret}_{\text{uniform}}(i) + \log K)$, where $\mathrm{regret}_{\text{uniform}}(i)$ represents the uniform regret for arm $i$ and $\mathrm{regret}_{\text{weighted}}(i)$ denotes the weighted regret when $\mathrm{w}_{i} = 1/K$. This result holds for both offline and online delay models and surpasses the best previously known uniform regret bound for the general delay-setting, which was $\tilde{O}(\sum_{i} \mathrm{regret}_{\text{weighted}}(i) + \log K)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the uniform regret of the advisor is optimal in the offline scenario and nearly optimal in the online scenario, differing only by a $\log K$ factor. Our findings apply to both stochastic and non-stochastic environments. Additionally, we extend our analysis to the setting where the advisor possesses partial knowledge of the mean rewards. In this extension, we show that the advisor's regret is optimal up to a $\log K$ factor in both stochastic and non-stochastic cases. Finally, we explore a scenario with time-varying arm delays and present an algorithm for the offline setting that attains a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(\sum_{i} \mathrm{regret}_{\text{weighted}}(i) + \log K)$ in the stochastic setting. In this final setting, we also establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\log K)$ for the advisor's regret. Our proofs rely on a novel analysis technique that may have broader applications. This study introduces a system capable of generating high-quality, human-like text in multi-turn conversations. We present LEATHER (Learning to Engage in Adaptive and Human-like Text Responses), a new evaluation framework that assesses response quality across four dimensions: coherence, fluency, relevance, and creativity. Using this framework, we developed an end-to-end text-generation model that outperforms current state-of-the-art models on the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) and matches top-performing models on the MultiNLI dataset. Our model achieves human-level scores on all four evaluation metrics. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhi-agarwal/LEATHER. This work is based on our first-author publication, "LEATHER: Learning to Engage in Human-like Conversations," by Abhishek Agarwal, Shourya Dasgupta, and Abhishek Das, which appeared in the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), Madrid, Spain, July 2020. The paper can be found at https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.105. Our submission includes two components: (1) responses to the Directly Evaluated Tasks (COT) for the NLP4Creativity Challenge, and (2) our LEATHER model applied to the COT tasks on the NLP4Creativity challenge. The model was trained on the CMU-MOS-creativity dataset, which consists of 1,000 creative text samples annotated with a creativity score by a human panel. We evaluated our model using the LEATHER framework, which offers a more nuanced assessment of text quality than traditional coherence and fluency metrics. The results demonstrate that our model produces highly creative and human-like responses. Accurately modeling the stochastic load responses of offshore wind turbines is vital for their structural design. This study introduces a novel probabilistic surrogate model for wind-turbine stresses, utilizing a sequence of chained Gaussian processes. This approach is demonstrated using an 11.44 MW semi-submerged floating wind turbine subjected to various wind and wave conditions. The methodology is validated against Monte Carlo simulations, showing strong agreement with the surrogate model. Furthermore, the framework is highly adaptable to diverse wind-turbine configurations and can be easily extended to other stochastic responses, such as turbine power output. The model demonstrates exceptional efficiency, requiring only seconds to generate predictions for any specific environmental scenario. These findings can facilitate the development of stochastic control strategies and robustness assessments for wind-turbine loads. Social media platforms have become integral to daily social interactions, with Twitter being particularly prominent for news dissemination and crisis management. This study analyzes Twitter data from the May 2011 Izmir Earthquake in Turkey to determine the platform's efficacy during emergencies. By examining tweets from May 12, 2011, the research categorizes the content into seven groups: news, jokes, songs, prayers, emotions, information, and others. The findings reveal that users primarily shared news, jokes, and emotions, while prayers and songs were also common. The analysis indicates that Twitter served as a valuable source of news during the earthquake. Furthermore, employing topic modeling proved effective for classifying tweet subjects, and the investigation highlighted specific linguistic characteristics of Twitter usage in crisis situations. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. (Note: This study was conducted in 2011.) Keywords: Twitter, Social Media, Topic Modeling, NLP, Text Classification, Natural Language Processing, Crisis Management, Turkey, Izmir, Earthquake.

We demonstrate that specific generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups, which are not themselves group trivial, possess the $R_\infty$ property within their nilpotent quotients. This finding stands in contrast to the established result that all generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups are residually torsion-free nilpotent and possess finite $\infty$-genus. Additionally, we provide a criterion to determine whether a given nilpotent group is group trivial. Finally, we outline an approach for calculating the Betti numbers of these nilpotent quotients by utilizing presentations of the groups. This method builds upon the work of Chen, Danchev, and Lin, who developed a technique to derive nilpotent presentations from group presentations. Our work extends this by adapting the method to handle presentations that include relations of degree greater than 2, thereby enabling the calculation of Betti numbers for a broader class of nilpotent groups. As an illustration, we apply this procedure to generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups to explicitly compute their Betti numbers. These computations not only validate existing results but also identify a previously unresolved case. Furthermore, we provide a criterion for identifying group trivial nilpotent groups that relies on the vanishing of their odd-rank Betti numbers. This criterion successfully confirms the group triviality of the nilpotent quotients of various groups in the literature that previously lacked this property. However, we also note a limitation: the criterion does not apply to a specific group mentioned in the literature, which is not group trivial, and we demonstrate this by explicitly calculating its Betti numbers. To address this gap, we introduce an alternative criterion that does not depend on Betti number calculations. This second criterion requires the use of abelianizations and demonstrates that the direct product of two group trivial groups remains group trivial. We also calculate the Betti numbers for the direct product of two groups to show that it is generally impractical to determine group triviality via Betti numbers in this manner. Leveraging this observation, we construct an infinite family of group trivial nilpotent groups that cannot be identified as group trivial through Betti number calculations alone. This family encompasses the nilpotent quotients of all instances in the literature that were previously considered to have the group trivial property. Our work thus establishes the first instance of an infinite family of group trivial nilpotent groups and provides the first explicit construction of such a family. We introduce a new framework for reconstructing time-resolved data, such as spatially dependent material properties or dynamic structures, from experimental measurements. The method involves optimizing a test trajectory alongside forward simulations to match simulated data against experimental observations. This framework is demonstrated using material tomography performed with a pump-probe x-ray micro-diffraction setup, where a test trajectory represents the unknown time-evolution of the material's internal structure. We show that the resulting inversion is superior to a standard inverse-optimization approach, which simultaneously updates both the initial structure and its parameters to align simulated data with experimental observations. Furthermore, we establish that the proposed method yields a unique reconstruction, whereas the standard approach produces an ill-posed inverse problem. Finally, we explore how this reconstruction can be utilized to determine the internal stresses within the material. These findings are illustrated using data from a tomography experiment conducted at the Diamond Light Source. The core concept of optimizing a test trajectory is also applicable to other reconstruction challenges, including dynamic electron tomography and electron diffraction tomography. In these applications, the test trajectory can represent the time-evolution of a material's internal structure or a series of intermediate states during a multi-step process. The proposed framework is implemented in Python and is available as open-source code. Additionally, we have developed a user-friendly graphical user interface to facilitate its application. Both the code and GUI can be downloaded from https://github.com/alexanderhagen/PyPPOPT. This work was supported by the EPSRC grant EP/R003025/1. This paper introduces SceNDD, a situation-based naturalistic driving dataset designed to facilitate research into automated driving and intelligent vehicle systems. Derived from the Italian NDD4AD project, this public resource comprises 1,000 carefully selected driving episodes. Each episode includes 360-degree visual imagery, vehicle sensor data, and manually annotated information regarding the driving context, traffic participants, and events. The dataset is organized into four distinct scenarios: urban driving, roundabouts, merging, and driving near parked vehicles. We offer a detailed description of the data and demonstrate the utility of SceNDD for common driving-related tasks by training and evaluating several machine learning models. Our findings indicate that the dataset supports the development of robust models capable of accurately classifying driving situations and identifying the characteristics of driving participants. The data can be accessed at https://scendd-dataset.github.io. The source code for the experiments is available at https://github.com/AndreaBertacchini/SceNDD-Paper. Additionally, the paper is accessible in English at https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2109.03008 and in Italian at https://doi.org/10.32872/ditalianascienzeingegneria.articolo.1142.

This paper introduces a channel matrix estimation technique for OFDM systems utilizing reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), operating under conditions of imperfect hardware and reduced cyclic prefix (CP) length. The proposed enhanced extreme learning machine (EELM) model integrates a radial basis function kernel with least squares learning. By employing a sigmoid activation function, the method minimizes the mean squared error between actual and predicted values, thereby achieving high estimation accuracy. Furthermore, the study analyzes the EELM's performance in scenarios involving insufficient training samples and discusses the computational complexity associated with calculating the radial basis function kernel. Simulation results confirm that the proposed method outperforms both the least squares and standard extremal learning machine approaches. Additionally, the study examines the impact of noise variance and sampling count on estimation performance, while also evaluating the computational cost of the radial basis function kernel. Finally, the influence of noise variance and training sample numbers on the enhanced ELM is investigated. The effects of imperfect hardware, specifically quantization errors in the EELM weights, are also addressed. The findings demonstrate that this approach effectively mitigates the adverse impacts of imperfect hardware and a reduced CP. Ultimately, the proposed method offers a cost-effective solution for estimating channel matrices in RIS-assisted OFDM systems. Keywords: RIS-assisted OFDM, EELM, Channel Matrix Estimation, Radial Basis Function Kernel, Least Squares Learning, Imperfect Hardware, Insufficient CP.

This work examines the existence of a one-parameter family of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds, demonstrating that instanton existence is not guaranteed by this condition. The article concludes with a discussion of how positive1-curvature facilitates the existence of a specific type of instanton family. Additionally, we present two distinct constructions of instanton families: the first arises on manifolds possessing a circle action, and the second is derived through twisted connected sums. Furthermore, we investigate the moduli space of instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifolds, showing that under favorable circumstances, it can be represented as a quotient of an open subset of a representation space by the Lie group $\mathrm{SU}(3)$. Finally, we explore applications of this quotient structure to identify low-dimensional instanton spaces. Specifically, we identify the instanton space on the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton twisted connected sum XZ in instances where $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ is replaced by a holomorphic torus, and we determine the instanton space on the $G_2$-instanton Hopf fibration. Additionally, we demonstrate that the moduli space of instantons on a family of nearly $G_2$ manifolds is one-dimensional whenever a circle action exists. Finally, we provide an alternative derivation of the result that the moduli space of instantons on Bryant's $\mathrm{G}_2$-manifold is empty. This paper introduces a code-creator tool written in ACL2 that is based on a paper Shallow Embedding of C into ACL2. Unlike other tools in this category, which utilize an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)-based approach, our embedding is proof generator-based. This method enables the system to verify embedded C code within ACL2, allowing it to verify not only individual programs but also complete code bases. The tool is implemented using the LISP-based computer algebra system ACL2 and serves as a proof generator for C programs embedded in ACL2. While the tool can verify standard C code, it cannot verify code containing dynamic memory allocation or pointers. Future work aims to extend this paper's methods to generate proofs for C code involving pointers and dynamic memory allocation. All code used in this paper is available in the repository https://github.com/akshaykumar2002/c2acl2. Additionally, the authors are currently developing a tool to verify standard C code with pointers and dynamic memory allocation, which will be released soon. Users can access this tool by cloning the repository at https://github.com/akshaykumar2002/c2acl2 and running the command `c2acl2` in their terminal. The authors are also preparing a book on this topic, which will be published in the near future. Interested readers are encouraged to reach out to the authors for further details. This study presents a dynamical analysis of the asteroid resonance region surrounding (39991) Iochroma, utilizing a model that accounts for both the J2 term of asteroidal oblateness and Yarkovsky forces. The asteroid resides near the 3/1 mean motion resonance (MMR) with Jupiter, and our investigation explores the dynamics of bodies in its vicinity. We identified two chaotic layers linked to the 3/1 MMR, with Iochroma located between them. Our findings indicate that both the Yarkovsky effect and J2 significantly influence the dynamics of asteroids within the 3/1 MMR. Specifically, the combined impact of these forces on Iochroma results in a substantial reduction in the size of the stable islands associated with the 3/1 MMR. Furthermore, the trajectories of asteroids in this region exhibit complex dynamics, characterized by alternating transitions between chaotic and regular states. Finally, we demonstrate that the Yarkovsky effect can facilitate the escape of asteroids from the 3/1 MMR. These results offer valuable insights for understanding the dynamical evolution of the Iochroma family. Additionally, our findings may assist in refining the dynamical models of other bodies situated in similar resonance zones. The research is accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07001. The authors extend Ramanujan's series for odd zeta values by incorporating Hurwitz zeta functions. This approach yields a more streamlined version of the Stoyanov-Kaczorowski method, which utilizes Euler's reflection formula to relate the Hurwitz zeta function to the Riemann zeta function. Through this formula, the study generates several novel identities for Bernoulli numbers. Additionally, the text provides a specific instance of the Burchnall-Catalan identity, offering new proofs for both its general and restricted formulations. Finally, comparisons are drawn between the resulting identities for Bernoulli numbers and those of similar nature found in the literature. The paper concludes with a series of conjectures and open questions for future research. This work serves as a contribution to the field of analytic number theory.
