We establish the circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory, specifically under a logical action, for the space of complex projective lines $CP(V)$, where $V$ is a finite-dimensional complex vector space equipped with a circle action. This theory is defined within topos-theoretic terms relative to a universe of sets and a topos of circle actions. Furthermore, the circle action on $CP(V)$ arises from a representation of the group $SU(V)$. Consequently, we compute the circle-equivariant cohomology of $CP(V)$ for an $SU(V)$ acting on $CP(V)$ via vector addition. This computation is performed in topos-theoretic terms with respect to a universe of $G$-sets, where $G$ denotes the automorphism group of the representation of $SU(V)$. Finally, these objects are demonstrated to be equivalent to those computed in the universe of ordinary sets. The resulting cohomology is expressed as a circle-equivariant version of the Weyl group alternating character ring. Additionally, the circle action on this ring corresponds to the circle action on the equivariant elliptic modular function, which aligns with the circle action on the Weyl circle-almost-periodic representation of the affine Kac-Moody Lie algebra associated with type $A_{n-1}$. This affine representation was originally identified by Reshetikhin and Wakimoto in their construction of the Weyl module for the affine Schur algebra. Furthermore, this circle action is linked to the action of the Hecke algebra on the circle-equivariant elliptic Hecke-Chevalley correspondence. The equivalence between these two perspectives on the cohomology of $CP(V)$ is realized through the equivariant Atiyah-Segal index map. This map is derived from the equivariant Grothendieck-Riemann-Weil formula applied to a specific family of circle-equivariant correspondences. These correspondences are equivariant extensions of the geometric Satake correspondence, which relates the cohomology of $CP(V)$ to the Hecke algebra. The circle-equivariant extensions of these correspondences involve the equivariant K-theory of the affine Grassmannian and the equivariant elliptic Hecke-Chevalley correspondence, respectively. The circle action on the equivariant elliptic Weyl alternating character ring is identified as the equivariant form of the equivariant elliptic modular function, which serves as a deformation of the equivariant Hecke algebra center. This paper introduces a new quadrature rule designed to precisely handle the numerical integration of solar irradiance. Given that solar radiation is primarily determined by the solar elevation angle $\theta$, which evolves over the course of a day, we formulate a solar-dependent Gaussian quadrature rule. By aligning the nodes and weights with the probability density function of $\theta$, the method achieves high precision. We derive a closed-form expression for this probability density function, applicable to any day and location on Earth, and validate the quadrature rule through multiple examples. Results demonstrate exceptional accuracy, achieving an error below $10^{-14}$ for both direct and diffuse irradiance. Furthermore, the rule is shown to remain effective across a wide range of latitudes and solar elevations. Finally, we provide a free MATLAB code implementation of the solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature rule for practical use. This approach offers a precise and efficient means of calculating the time-averaged power received by a surface, a critical factor in solar energy applications. Consequently, the solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature rule is poised to become a valuable tool for modeling solar power systems. Our findings are detailed in the accompanying paper: "Solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature for the precise numerical evaluation of solar irradiance," published in *Journal of Computational Physics* (2021). The curvature information provided by the generalized Gauss-Newton (GN) matrix is essential for comprehending the geometry of deep learning. This paper introduces a low-rank approximation of the generalized GN matrix based on the parameter differences between two training trajectories, yielding a more robust estimator than standard GN. We demonstrate that this approximation corresponds to the squared Frobenius norm of the difference between two rank-one matrices, which depend on the first and second derivatives of the loss with respect to a specific parameter. This approach, termed the generalized GN-rank, is also applicable to Newton's method. By comparing various parameter update strategies, we identify that the generalized GN-rank is low-rank when utilizing a layer-wise learning rate, allowing for efficient curvature estimation via a ViViT architecture. Furthermore, we prove that the curvature of the deep learning landscape can be characterized by the eigenvalues of this low-rank approximation. Finally, we apply this method to evaluate the curvature of the image classification landscape. Experimental results indicate that the generalized GN-rank is highly effective for models with limited depth and width, providing valuable insights for future research. Accurate forecasting of spatio-temporal traffic flow is essential for traffic management and control. However, traffic data is inherently sparse, as data collectors are scarce and the number of traffic cells is vast, complicating prediction. This paper introduces a new attribute-based deep learning model designed to enhance forecasting accuracy for large-scale, high-dimensional, and highly dynamic traffic data. The approach leverages the similarity between traffic cells to extract predictive attributes, which are then utilized to construct a dynamic graph for the forecasting cell. By integrating these attributes and graphs, the proposed model, called SparseNet, achieves state-of-the-art results on two major traffic datasets, significantly outperforming existing methods. Additionally, we explore the application of this framework in short-term traffic flow control. Experimental results demonstrate that SparseNet can reduce congestion in large-scale networks by 10% to 20% compared to other control strategies. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1990/SparseNet.

This paper introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for learning from interventionally augmented datasets to address both top-level and local contrafactual queries. VACA achieves this by modeling the conditional mean and mean-magnitude of a Gaussian latent variable using a mean parameterized by a graph convolutional network and a magnitude parameterized by a graph auto-encoder. We establish the conditions under which VACA can exactly answer exact-linear, quadratic, and quadratic-plus-constant contrafactual queries, and we propose a constrained optimization framework to simultaneously train the model parameters and the graph structure for various approximate-linear queries. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that VACA surpasses existing methods in answering general contrafactual questions. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis of the VACA model and its associated optimization problem offers a novel perspective on the graph learning problem. Finally, we illustrate the utility of VACA by addressing local contrafactual queries in a real-world application focused on predicting the impact of COVID-19 interventions on US states. The Irish LOFAR station, situated in the west of Ireland, offers a compact array optimized for rapid monitoring of the dynamic radio universe. Since its deployment, a new backend has been developed to facilitate real-time data access and visualization, enabling the immediate identification of transient sources. This system supports an on-demand data retrieval feature, allowing users to access data from specific time intervals. We present initial results from both data and image visualization, highlighting notable radio transients captured by the Irish LOFAR station. These findings demonstrate the station's ability to detect a diverse array of phenomena, including Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), pulsars, solar bursts, and radio galaxies. The capabilities of the REALTA backend are expected to significantly enhance the array's scientific output. Future work will focus on implementing data storage and image archiving, as well as exploring data mining techniques to identify new sources. Additionally, we will address the challenge of distinguishing between real and spurious sources caused by radio frequency interference (RFI). Ultimately, these advancements will improve the array's sensitivity to rare and elusive events, such as FRBs and Fast Ignition Gamma-ray Bursts (FIGBs). The REALTA backend is currently accessible via a web interface at http://www.los.lmo/realta. This study examines the interaction between frequency and voltage dynamics within electrical systems characterized by constant power loads. It demonstrates that nontrivial coupling with voltage dynamics can stabilize an operating point that remains unstable under conventional frequency-only control. The analysis focuses on nonlinear differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) representing realistic system dynamics, utilizing Lyapunov exponents to evaluate stability. Additionally, the paper explores the impact of algebraic voltage coupling on the local stability of these operating points. This study introduces MAPPIES, a novel Monte-Carlo code designed to simulate the production of electromagnetic radiation by relativistic electrons in the presence of external radiation fields and spin-1/2 particles. The framework incorporates a comprehensive set of physical processes, including linear and circular Compton scattering, linear and circular inverse Compton scattering, linear and circular Breit-Wheeler processes, linear and circular Bhabha scattering, linear and circular M\"{u}ller scattering, and Klein-Nishina scattering. These mechanisms are essential for explaining the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess observed in the spectra of blazars. By comparing calculated spectra with observational data, we demonstrate that a superposition of relativistic electrons and positrons, moving at various velocities and distributed according to a power law, can effectively account for this excess. Furthermore, we show that the polarization of both the seed photon field and the background electron-positron population can be utilized to constrain the relative contributions of electrons and positrons to this radiation source. Finally, we apply this methodology to analyze the UV/X-ray excess in the spectrum of the blazar Mrk 401.

We examine the extension of real-variable function theory to complex domains, a consideration crucial for techniques like parameter localization and understanding degeneracies. By introducing a metric derived from the Hessian, we can quantify the distance between points and assess function variation. This approach generates a metric landscape, where the geometry reflects both the function's behavior and the access pathways between points. We demonstrate that for the Minima First (MF) algorithm, this variation determines the cost of the landscape, thereby influencing the time required for the algorithm to transition between points. Furthermore, we present a method to estimate the access time between points using this variation, which aligns with observed transitions in the f6 function. This insight offers a pathway to analyze transition times in other benchmark functions, such as the f7 and f8 cases, where the Hessian is non-degenerate. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the domain of analyticity and the Hessian metric, showing that while related, they are distinct concepts. We propose a function class that exhibits this property, which could be valuable for studying parameter identification and other inverse problems. Finally, we illustrate how the Hessian metric can be applied to visualize landscapes, providing a complementary perspective to traditional 2D plots. This capability is particularly useful for investigating parameter landscapes, such as those arising in quantum field theory effective actions. In this context, we note that the variation in complex landscapes can be linked to the Borel resummation of perturbative series. These findings may have broader implications for numerical methods, including genetic algorithms and Markov chain Monte Carlo techniques. Our results are supported by various numerical examples. This work addresses the quantum detection and discrimination problem for symmetric states using online measurements. Within the online framework, the goal is to identify the underlying state from a known set by performing sequential measurements and analyzing the resulting outcomes. We introduce a general method that leverages online measurements to detect any family of two-qubit unentangled pure states, thereby extending prior restricted findings [Phys. Rev. Lett. 121, 190501 (2018)]. Furthermore, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for successfully discriminating arbitrary three-qubit unentangled pure states. Finally, our proposals are validated through both theoretical analysis and experimental data obtained from photonic quantum systems. Our research expands the scope of quantum online detection and discrimination, offering potential applications in quantum key distribution and sensing. Additionally, the online detection of unentangled pure states serves as a foundational element for discriminating more complex entangled and mixed states. Our methodology is also applicable in broader contexts where online decision-making is required. We anticipate that these findings will inspire further investigation into quantum online detection and discrimination.

Baryon production is investigated through the quantized fragmentation of a QCD string, incorporating a drag force that simulates the influence of a quark-gluon plasma. The analysis focuses on a string with helical momentum distribution, where dimerization drives meson formation. In this framework, baryons emerge via trimerization. The resulting spectra for both mesons and baryons are compared against experimental data. Additionally, the study examines the impact of drag force on the production of multibaryon states, such as the tetrbaryon, within the context of a four-trimer fragmentation process. The findings indicate that trimerization remains the primary mechanism for baryon formation even in the case of tetrbaryons. Finally, the article explores the possibility of detecting the QCD string's thickness via the production of these exotic hadrons. To achieve this, a specific ratio of tetrbaryon to proton yields is proposed, which may offer a viable method for determining the QCD string's geometric properties. This ratio is calculated for both the string-drag and no-drag scenarios. Furthermore, the string-drag model predicts that the tetrbaryon signal could be observable at the LHC. Consequently, measurements of the tetrbaryon-to-proton ratio could serve as a valuable tool for extracting string parameters, including its thickness. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential experimental strategies for measuring this ratio. Keywords: QCD string, baryon production, tetrbaryon, string drag, QCD string thickness. We investigate the detection of stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) signals generated by stochastic primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) within the Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) frequency band. Our analysis reveals that a two-point correlation function of the PMF produces a distinct SGWB spectrum, while the three-point correlation function yields a signal that is significantly weaker and potentially unobservable. We demonstrate that PTA experiments can constrain the amplitude of PMFs at scales corresponding to the age of the universe at recombination, provided the field adheres to a power-law power spectrum. Specifically, we establish that PTA data can limit the magnetic field strength to below approximately $10^{-9}$ G under these conditions. This finding indicates that PTA observations can significantly tighten existing constraints on the amplitude of cosmological PMFs. Additionally, we examine the impact of a dynamical PMF on the SGWB spectrum and find that it generates a signal roughly two orders of magnitude weaker than that of a static field, rendering it beyond the current sensitivity of PTAs. We also explore the possibility of enhancing PTA sensitivity to PMFs through future observations. Finally, we outline the potential for future radio astronomy facilities, such as the Square Kilometre Array, to further tighten constraints on cosmological PMFs. These results suggest that future PTA observations could probe the existence of a PMF in the early universe. Furthermore, we show that PTA observations can constrain the amplitude of a PMF with a power-law power spectrum to less than $10^{-10}$ G, a value two orders of magnitude lower than current constraints. This represents the first time such a tight constraint on a PMF has been established. Consequently, PTA observations can significantly improve our understanding of the universe during the recombination era. We also discuss the implications of these results for the formation of primordial black holes. Finally, we address the potential for future PTA observations to further constrain the amplitude of a PMF, thereby enhancing our comprehension of the universe during the recombination era. These findings underscore the critical role of future PTA observations in constraining cosmological PMFs. In conclusion, we emphasize that future PTA observations could probe the existence of a PMF in the early universe. Additionally, we show that PTA observations can constrain the amplitude of a PMF with a power-law power spectrum to less than $10^{-11}$ G, which is one order of magnitude lower than current constraints. This highlights the significant potential of future PTA observations to constrain cosmological PMFs

Light field imaging has become a popular method for capturing rich 3D scene details by recording both spatial position and ray direction at each pixel. However, this technology often suffers from significant artifacts in scene geometry and texture, which degrade the quality of light field based augmented reality applications. To address this, we introduce a novel learning-based compression framework designed to minimize these distortions. Our approach utilizes a deep neural network to optimize traditional compression standards without discarding raw data. Specifically, we develop a new loss function that prioritizes the geometric coherence of synthetic images across multiple views, thereby enhancing their realism. Additionally, our model predicts high-fidelity reference views from neighboring frames to accelerate the compression process. Experimental results demonstrate that our system significantly reduces geometric distortions while maintaining the same bitrate as prior methods. Furthermore, comparative tests show that our model outperforms other compression techniques. Finally, we release the entire codebase to support future research. Interactive and non-interactive search frameworks represent the two primary modalities in information retrieval. While recent interactive frameworks have demonstrated superior performance in cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR), they suffer from latency due to the necessity of multiple online queries per retrieval task. Conversely, non-interactive frameworks offer a swift and efficient solution for CLIR. This study investigates methods to enhance the efficacy of non-interactive approaches by leveraging the benefits found in interactive models. We introduce an explicit latent relevance signal derived from reasoning within online interactive frameworks, which is integrated into the non-interactive query representation. Experimental results indicate that incorporating this relevance signal into non-interactive frameworks yields a significant performance boost, achieving a 10.5% mAP improvement on CLIR benchmarks. Furthermore, our approach attains performance levels comparable to the state-of-the-art interactive framework while delivering a 2.5x speedup. Small area estimation (SAE) is essential for generating reliable estimates in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where critical data such as health and demographic indicators are frequently collected via surveys that lack sufficient sample sizes to produce reliable estimates for every parameter of interest. This study evaluates the performance of four SAE methods—R2SUE, PYM, FLEX, and BLU—against a design-based estimator (DUE) using census microdata from Malawi. We analyzed two surveys: the 2008/09 Malawi Household Survey and the 2015/16 Malawi Integrated Household Survey, focusing on estimates for 2-digit regions regarding fertility, mortality, and education. Our findings indicate that the DUE estimator performs comparably to SAE methods for regions with a population exceeding 10,000. However, for the 2-digit regions in the 2008/09 survey, which average only 4,000 people, SAE methods yield significantly higher correlations with the "true" population parameters. Furthermore, SAE approaches demonstrate greater robustness to model misspecification, particularly in scenarios involving highly correlated covariates. We also compared model-based estimators utilizing fixed covariates versus those integrating both fixed and population-level random effect covariates, observing that the latter enhances performance. Finally, we examined the impact of varying spatial scales on SAE accuracy and explored the potential of incorporating random effect covariates to further improve results. Overall, this work provides guidance on selecting the most appropriate SAE method and spatial scale to optimize estimator performance in LMIC settings. Additionally, we introduce a novel algorithm for identifying an optimal set of random effect covariates, which can be applied to any dataset. The accompanying R package, `R2SUELMIC`, is designed to facilitate the use of the R2SUE estimator in LMIC contexts. All data, code, and packages required to replicate these findings are available at: https://github.com/JuliaKorbel/R2SUELMIC. The package includes a tutorial on the methodology discussed in this paper. Keywords: Small area estimation, low and middle income countries, design-based estimators, model-based estimators, robustness. Corresponding author: Julia Korbel (j.korbel@liverpool.ac.uk). We investigate a model where an investor distributes their capital across multiple quantum systems, each representing a qubit prepared in an arbitrary state. The investor's returns are determined by measuring these qubits in the computational basis. Within this framework, we examine the investor's optimal betting strategy by calculating their expected payoff and comparing it to classical scenarios. Our findings indicate that, relative to a classical investor, one can either enhance expected profits or decrease the probability of total capital loss. Furthermore, regarding partial capital allocation, we demonstrate the possibility of achieving a higher probability of not losing any capital. These results are derived using continuous variable techniques, specifically employing the Wigner function and quasi-probability distributions. Transition metal and group 14 dichalcogenides and difluorides have garnered significant interest for their diverse electronic structures, including metal, semimetal, and semiconductor phases. This study investigates the electronic and optical characteristics of MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds, where M represents Mo, W, or Ti, and Z represents N, P, As, Si, or Ge. Utilizing density functional theory, we examine various stacking configurations and compare their optical responses. Our findings indicate that the inversion symmetry of the MA$_2$Z$_4$ lattice is essential for in-plane polarization, while out-of-plane polarization arises from spin-orbit coupling. We demonstrate that the band structure of MA$_2$Z$_4$ can be categorized into three groups based on the arrangement of quasiparticle bands. Furthermore, we identify a unique excitonic state that remains stable across different stacking configurations and exhibits minimal sensitivity to strain. These results offer valuable insights for designing optical devices utilizing MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials. Additionally, our analysis of the quasiparticle band structure in these compounds provides a foundation for future research into valleytronics. Finally, our work establishes a systematic framework for classifying the quasiparticle band arrangement in such materials. This classification scheme can be readily extended to other materials, thereby advancing the understanding of quasiparticle band arrangement in a broader range of systems. The LHCb experiment analyzed 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV to search for the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. No prior world measurements existed for this specific decay. An upper limit of $B(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) < 1.1 \times 10^{-10}$ was established at 90% confidence level, which is approximately 100 times more sensitive than the previous best limit. Furthermore, an observation of this rare decay has been confirmed with a statistical significance of 5.2 standard deviations. The observed event count aligns with Standard Model predictions within the allowed theoretical uncertainties. Additionally, the study provides the first measurements of the differential branching fraction and forward-backward asymmetry, both of which are consistent with Standard Model expectations. The observed branching fractions across various kinematic regions also align with the results from the LHCb experiment's earlier study of the similar decay $\Sigma^+ \to p e^+ e^-$. These findings are crucial for investigating flavor and CP violation within the Standard Model and for exploring physics beyond it. The measured branching fractions for $\Sigma^+ \to p \ell^+ \ell^-$ (where $\ell = e, \mu$) are roughly two orders of magnitude larger than those for $\Lambda \to p \ell^+ \ell^-$, a discrepancy that may indicate a violation of SU(3) flavor symmetry or the presence of new physics. This analysis represents the first time that the differential forward-backward asymmetry in such rare hyperon decays has been measured. Additionally, the forward-backward asymmetry in the radiative decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \gamma$ was measured for the first time. These results are essential for comprehensively understanding strangeness-changing electromagnetic transitions. We present a three-dimensional simulation of prestellar core collapse that incorporates both gravitational and radiative transfer, designed to trace the formation of a protostellar disk. Utilizing the AMReX code, we model the physical evolution of the core and apply a simplified radiative cooling function to represent thermal processes. Our results indicate that the disk forms within approximately 10,000 years, with its structure shaped by the interplay between the collapsing core and the magnetic field. The AMReX simulation reveals that the disk is primarily established by the removal of angular momentum via magnetic braking. Additionally, radiative transfer calculations demonstrate that the disk remains cold throughout its formation. We observe that the disk's inner region is created by the development of a quasi-stationary accretion flow, which is driven by the core's collapse and the generation of a dead zone. Furthermore, the outer disk is fed by a low-density gas stream that originates from the equatorial plane of the collapsing core. Finally, our simulation successfully reproduces the mass and angular momentum distributions found in observed disks. These findings suggest that the disk formation process is closely linked to the star formation process, implying that disk formation is a natural consequence of the core collapse. Consequently, our results support the hypothesis that disks are not formed separately from stars but emerge simultaneously during the collapse of prestellar cores. This represents a significant advancement in theoretical understanding, as it provides a viable mechanism for disk formation that aligns with the observational data. Our findings also offer a new perspective on the initial conditions of the solar system, suggesting that the gas and dust in the solar nebula were inherited from the prestellar core collapse. This implies that the solar nebula was not formed separately from the Sun but emerged simultaneously with its formation. Our results therefore support the hypothesis that disks form concurrently with stars during the prestellar core collapse. Overall, this study demonstrates that the three-dimensional simulation of prestellar core collapse is a promising approach for investigating disk formation. In the future, we aim to conduct more detailed simulations of star and disk formation by including additional physical processes, such as the effects of turbulence and self-gravity. This will enable us to better understand the physical mechanisms underlying star and disk formation. Additionally, we plan to compare our simulation results with observational data to further validate our hypotheses. Ultimately, this will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the physical processes governing star and disk formation. Atmospheric dispersion correctors (ADCs) are instruments designed to eliminate atmospheric dispersion, a phenomenon where the atmosphere acts like a prism and disperses light into colors. This paper presents a methodology for quantifying the performance of an ADC across all wavelengths. It details the characteristics of the air through which light travels, defining the specific parameters required to model dispersion for every possible combination of wavelength, temperature, and pressure. Additionally, the study outlines a procedure for generating synthetic observations using these parameters. This work serves as a foundation for an analysis method that can be applied to any ADC design. These methods will be utilized to evaluate the performance of various proposed ADC designs and to analyze on-sky data from the recently installed HARPS3 ADC on the ESO's HARPS spectrograph. The results will be published in a subsequent paper. The code used for these calculations is available at https://github.com/tperez/ADC_dispersion. This paper corresponds to the second installment in a series of three; the first can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.03009. The third paper, which presents the analysis results, is forthcoming at https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.03010. We introduce a Bayesian approach that integrates sparse modeling with deep neural networks for multi-period time series. This method employs a variational inference framework to approximate the intractable posterior of parameters within a linear-in-parameters model. The resulting sparse models are computationally efficient, enabling rapid predictions on new data. This finding relies on adapting Bezem's example concerning the nonexpressibility of continuity in constant logic. Furthermore, our proof provides an independent demonstration that constant first-order logic with a unary function symbol and the successor is inadequate for expressing the continuity of morphisms between finite-dimensional vector spaces over non-trivial locally countable topological fields. Finally, we briefly examine the challenges associated with extending constant expressibility to languages enriched with expressions from Taylor's sequence of expressive power. These difficulties stem partly from the inability of such languages to define the order on their underlying fields and from specific characteristics of the morphisms between them. The latter issue is particularly significant when employing the spectral method to analyze the expressibility of continuity. This method relies on a characteristic property of continuous morphisms, which is derived from the Taylor spectrum of their graphs. We illustrate this property through an example involving a continuous morphism between finite-dimensional vector spaces over $\mathbb{Q}_p$. This explanation is based on an example by Bezem demonstrating that the constant successor cannot express the finiteness of its universe. Federated learning (FL) represents a distributed approach to machine learning that prioritizes data privacy by ensuring data remains on user devices rather than in a central repository. This focus on privacy also enhances data utility, as training on local device data yields superior performance compared to data that has been differentially privatized. Consequently, this paper investigates the simultaneous application of differential privacy (DP) and federated learning, with the specific goal of addressing fairness bias. We examine two distinct scenarios: vertical FL, where data columns are missing, and horizontal FL, where data is noisy. For both scenarios, we introduce a novel algorithm that leverages both FL and DP to mitigate bias within utility models. We validate the effectiveness of this algorithm through experiments on real-world datasets, and the code will be made available on GitHub. Our findings demonstrate that our proposed FL-DP algorithm achieves a balanced trade-off between privacy and bias, outperforming existing methods. Specifically, in the vertical FL setting, our approach reduces bias by 10% while maintaining a comparable level of privacy. Similarly, for noisy horizontal FL, the algorithm decreases bias by 10% without compromising the model's accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze the computational complexity of our method and establish a theoretical link between FL and DP. We find that the communication cost of our algorithm is $O(\log(n))$, where $n$ denotes the number of users. Additionally, we prove that the privacy cost of this algorithm is $O(\log(n))$. These results indicate that our algorithm offers a favorable balance among privacy, bias, and computational efficiency. Finally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the algorithm's limitations and outline potential directions for future research. We conclude that FL-DP methods hold significant promise for enhancing the privacy and fairness of machine learning models, and that further research is needed to optimize their performance and scalability. Our work is expected to inspire future advancements in the fields of privacy and fairness for FL. We anticipate that FL-DP research will continue to drive innovation in the areas of privacy and fairness for ML models. Ultimately, our contributions highlight the potential for FL-DP to improve the privacy and fairness of ML models, inspiring future research in these domains. We introduce a supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_X$ model at the TeV scale featuring right-handed neutrinos that account for dark energy. This framework naturally explains the observed dark energy density through the decay of a heavy right-handed neutrino, while simultaneously addressing the neutrino oscillation data. The proposed $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, which extends the Standard Model, is well-motivated by string theory and the see-saw mechanism. Furthermore, the $Z'$ boson associated with this symmetry can resolve the current tension in the $W$ boson mass measurements. We provide the most stringent constraints on the $Z'$ mass derived from LEP data and discuss the model's testability at the High-Luminosity LHC. Additionally, we examine the model's implications for neutrinoless double beta decay and the detection of dark radiation. Finally, we demonstrate that the model's parameter space can be significantly restricted by comparing experimental limits on $W$ boson mass with theoretical mass predictions. This analysis reveals a narrow window of parameter space where the $Z'$ boson mass is approximately 1.5 TeV, with a $W$ boson mass near 80 GeV. The $Z'$ mass in this region is determined by the see-saw mechanism, while the $W$ boson mass is influenced by the decay of the right-handed neutrino. Consequently, this narrow parameter space offers a promising target for future $Z'$ searches at the High-Luminosity LHC. Furthermore, within this region, the lifetime of the heavy neutrino aligns with the timescale of dark energy density, providing a natural explanation for dark energy. This leads to a testable prediction: the mass of the $W$ boson should be approximately 1.5 GeV. A future measurement of the $W$ boson mass with 1% precision could confirm or rule out this viable parameter space. Finally, we explore the stability of this parameter space against $Z$-pole data from LEP. Although the $Z$-pole constraint is weaker than the $W$ mass limit, it still excludes a portion of the parameter space, leaving a residual viable region. This remaining space predicts a $Z'$ mass of roughly 1.5 TeV and a $W$ mass near 80 GeV, with a heavy neutrino lifetime consistent with dark energy timescales. This parameter space remains a promising target for future neutrino experiments, including neutrino factories and dark radiation searches

High-purity $^{186}$Hg sources were generated from a $^{185}$Pt(n,$\gamma$) reaction involving highly enriched $^{185}$Pt targets. This approach enabled the first direct measurement of the beta-decay half-life for $^{186}$Hg, determined to be $T_{1/2} = 1.22 \pm 0.04$ s. Additionally, beta feeding intensities to excited states in $^{186}$Pt were measured via the $(E_{\beta}, E_{\gamma})$ coincidence technique. These experimental results were compared with predictions from various beta-decay models, and the derived ft values were analyzed in the context of the weak-interaction mixing amplitude $\lambda$ and the log ft values associated with second-forbidden non-unique transitions. Furthermore, the experimental data were compared with shell-model calculations utilizing the KB3L effective interaction. The study concludes that the low-energy spectrum of $^{186}$Hg is well described by the KB3L Hamiltonian, while the calculated ft values align with the experimental findings. Additionally, the experimental results are compared with the predictions of the interacting boson model. This comparison demonstrates that the low-lying level structure of $^{186}$Hg can be effectively modeled using an $N=10$ boson system. We introduce a unified framework that simultaneously accounts for dark matter and neutrino mass generation. This model incorporates a complex scalar field, which includes a dark matter candidate within its real component and a neutrino mass term derived from the imaginary component. The self-interaction of this scalar field is constrained by leptogenesis requirements, which rely on a yotta-electronvolt (YottaeV) mass superpartner. This superpartner annihilates with its antiparticle into two Higgsinos, yielding a dark matter relic density of approximately 0.12. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the parameter space aligning with relic density predictions and YottaeV neutrino masses is also consistent with the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe. Finally, we examine the potential for detecting this dark matter candidate through both direct and indirect detection experiments. In the context of direct detection, we note that while the cross-section is below the current experimental limit, future facilities may achieve the necessary sensitivity. Regarding indirect detection, we find that the annihilation cross-section into YottaeV states is insufficient to explain the gamma-ray excess observed by the Fermi-LAT in the Galactic Center. However, we show that the parameter space capable of reproducing these gamma-ray fluxes remains viable for dark matter production during the leptogenesis era. Additionally, we discuss the potential for detecting YottaeV neutrinos through their decay into gamma rays. Finally, we conclude that this model offers a novel approach to establishing a lower mass limit for dark matter. Specifically, we derive a lower mass bound of $m_{\chi} \geq 10^{15}$ eV, which is independent of the annihilation cross-section. This limit arises from the requirement that the decay width of the dark matter particle must not exceed the inverse of the age of the universe. We also note that this lower mass bound is contingent upon the dark matter density not surpassing the observed relic density. Consequently, this work represents the first instance of a dark matter lower mass limit being established through the analysis of relic density. We anticipate that this result will stimulate further research into dark matter detection. Finally, we emphasize that the YottaeV neutrino mass scale predicted by our model is consistent with recent findings from the OPERA experiment. Overall, our framework provides a promising explanation for both dark matter and neutrino mass phenomena. This paper introduces a learning-based control framework designed for systems with unknown dynamics, limited data availability, and access to side information. The proposed method relies on two core components: a data-driven controller and a cost-to-go function approximator. The controller utilizes the cost-to-go approximation to determine the optimal control input for the current state, while the approximator is refined through data generated by the controller. States and trajectories are evaluated using the current cost-to-go estimate; those yielding lower costs are preferred for updating the function approximation. This selection mechanism enables the system to adapt to unknown dynamics and converge to an optimal controller. To demonstrate the approach's versatility, it was applied to both linear and nonlinear systems, achieving successful generalization across various reachability tasks, walking and swimming simulations, and a flight scenario. The results indicate that the proposed method can learn to reach, swim, walk, and fly in a single attempt. Furthermore, the approach exhibits robust generalization capabilities when initial conditions or wind disturbances change. The method's generality is highlighted by its application to a x-plane, which features a more complex structure than the simplified models used in prior examples. Additionally, numerical results confirm that the proposed approach outperforms established methods in terms of performance and data efficiency. Finally, the paper outlines the method's limitations and suggests several directions for future research. This work is particularly relevant for control applications involving unknown dynamics, such as autonomous vehicles, humanoid robots, and soft robots. Additionally, we derive several consistency conditions that the conformal blocks must satisfy. Our findings align with those obtained through an independent bootstrap analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these results are equivalent to continuous extensions of the Ward identities for conformal blocks in rational conformal field theories associated with sl(3). Finally, we discuss the relationship between these continuous and discrete Ward identities. The technical computations are supported by computer algebra. Relation networks have recently gained significant attention for their ability to model interactions between objects within an image, achieving state-of-the-art results in few-shot learning and other tasks. However, current relation network approaches rely on fixed, pre-labeled support sets, a limitation that restricts their effectiveness in complex environments like natural images. To address this, we introduce a triplet loss that enables the relation networks to autonomously learn optimal configurations for classification. Building on this loss function, we also develop a novel generative adversarial network framework called RelationGAN. This approach leverages adversarial training to facilitate joint learning of class-specific concepts and discriminators, thereby enhancing few-shot learning performance. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our methods surpass existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, visual comparisons highlight the model's capacity to generate diverse and realistic images. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2019/RelationGAN}.

Twin-field quantum key exchange (TF-QKE) has recently emerged as a promising technique for long-distance secure key distribution, offering the potential to scale transmission distances beyond the standard quantum limit by employing an interference phase between transmitted signals at a repeater node. However, maintaining this phase requires precise phase locking, which complicates experimental implementation. This study demonstrates that twin-field quantum key exchange can be achieved without phase locking by utilizing two distinct twin-field protocols: the original TF-QKE protocol and a newly developed variant called TF-QKE with twin-field phase reference (TF-QKE-TPR). The latter protocol achieves comparable key rates and maximum transmission distances as the original method. Numerical simulations indicate that both approaches outperform the standard quantum key exchange protocol in terms of secret key capacity across long distances. These findings suggest that TF-QKE without phase locking is a practical solution for long-distance secure key transmission. Furthermore, the introduction of the TF-QKE-TPR protocol establishes a new benchmark for evaluating the performance of long-distance quantum key exchange systems. Finally, we outline potential avenues for future experimental verification. Our results are supported by an open-source Python package named PQKE. (Supplementary material includes detailed derivations, a comparison of key rates between TF-QKE-TPR and standard quantum key exchange, and the PQKE package.) Current object identification methods are restricted to a fixed set of classes, preventing open-vocabulary inference on unseen categories. This paper introduces a new approach to achieve open-vocabulary object identification at scale by utilizing pseudo bounding-box annotations. Our strategy involves training a vision transformer on image-level labels for various classes and subsequently applying a bounding box detector to this model to generate pseudo-bounding box data for training on image-bounding box pairs. We demonstrate that this method enables identification across tens of thousands of object classes, surpassing the capacity of existing systems. Furthermore, we show that our approach can identify novel object classes using only a few examples, effectively combining open-vocabulary identification with few-shot learning. Experimental results indicate that identification accuracy exceeds 50% for classes observable within the image, even when limited to just 4 labeled images per class. We present a new study on the gas distribution surrounding the Rho Oph S1 star, utilizing data from the IRAM 30m telescope at 1.3 and 2.3 mm, along with the VLT and Hubble Space Telescope in optical and UV bands. Our analysis of optical and UV images reveals a complex network of ionized gas filaments that appear to trace the edges of molecular outflow cavities. By examining 1.3 mm CO isotopologue data, we identified a series of elongated low-density regions that align with the boundaries of these ionized filaments. This spatial correspondence suggests that the ionized gas is sculpting the surrounding low-density molecular material. Additionally, we detected a new 2.3 mm PDR bubble that is spatially linked to the CO structures and ionized filaments, indicating that PDRs are likely triggered by the low-energy UV radiation emitted by the low-mass companion of the S1 star. The distribution of ionized, atomic, and PDR gas around S1 demonstrates a causal chain driven by the star's high-mass and low-mass companions, respectively. This chain begins with high-mass stars creating ionized gas via photoevaporation, which subsequently generates atomic gas through photoionization, and finally produces PDRs via low-energy UV photons from the low-mass companion. Our findings support the hypothesis that PDRs are integral components of the complex nebular structures observed around high-mass stars. Furthermore, the presence of ionized and PDR gas within the Rho Oph A cloud suggests that similar processes may be occurring around low-mass stars. Finally, the observed correlation between PDRs and ionized gas may offer a method for identifying the low-mass companions of massive stars. These results are consistent with the proposed scenario that low-mass stars form within the outflow cavities generated by massive stars. The resulting low-density environment around the low-mass star allows its low-energy UV photons to generate observable PDRs. This study underscores the significance of observing both ionized and PDR gas to understand the complex interactions between stars and their surroundings. We conclude that PDRs around low-mass stars are a natural outcome of forming inside molecular outflow cavities created by massive stars. Consequently, the distribution of ionized, atomic, and PDR gas around Rho Oph S1 serves as a compelling example of the proposed scenario for massive star formation. The concept of veracity, which encompasses truthfulness, accuracy, and reliability, has gained significant attention due to the proliferation of false information and the need to validate diverse content sources. This surge in interest is largely driven by the Transformer architecture, which has become the leading model for verifying various forms of media. This survey provides a comprehensive review of research on transformer-based approaches for verifying text, images, and video. It outlines the fundamental definitions and tasks associated with veracity, examines the specific roles and applications of transformers in each content type, and analyzes the similarities and distinctions among these areas. Additionally, the survey addresses key challenges and future directions for transformers in veracity research, aiming to offer a holistic perspective on the field. Given the rapid evolution of both transformers and veracity studies, this work is intended to serve as a foundational reference for future research. This study evaluates two factor models designed to forecast mortality rates. The initial model, previously introduced by the authors, employs time-invariant factor loadings, whereas the second model utilizes time-varying factor loadings. The objective of both approaches is to reduce the dimensionality of the standard Lee-Carter model's components. To evaluate their predictive performance, both methods are applied to mortality data from the United States and the United Kingdom. The results indicate that the first model with time-invariant loadings performs comparably to the second model with time-varying loadings. Furthermore, when applied to other countries, the first model yields similar outcomes, suggesting its robustness for practical use. Consequently, the first model is deemed suitable for predicting future mortality rates. Additionally, the authors demonstrate that this approach can effectively predict life expectancies and analyze mortality improvement rates. The paper concludes by discussing the factors influencing the accuracy of these predictions. Finally, given the significant impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on global mortality, the authors apply the first model to predict post-pandemic mortality rates and life expectancies for the UK and US. These predictions are compared against data from the Office for National Statistics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The analysis reveals that, despite the pandemic, life expectancies have not declined in either country. This finding is contrasted with the findings of other researchers who concluded that the pandemic caused a drop in life expectancy. The study also examines the implications of these results for mortality modelling. Finally, the authors suggest that the first model could assist in determining whether the pandemic's effects on mortality are temporary or permanent. The temporal patterns of the estimated factors in both countries indicate a potential long-term impact from the pandemic. However, the authors note that this conclusion is based on a relatively short dataset, which may limit its reliability. They recommend that future research utilize longer time series to validate this finding. Overall, the first model is shown to be highly effective in predicting future mortality rates and life expectancies, even during periods of significant data fluctuations caused by the pandemic. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) offers a promising method for automatically designing neural networks that can rival or surpass hand-crafted architectures in accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. However, the extensive search space required to explore these candidate architectures leads to prohibitively high training costs. To address this, many performance-aware strategies have been developed to reduce the search space by treating candidate architectures as competing entities, similar to concepts in evolutionary algorithms. This paper introduces a novel framework that analyzes and mitigates interference between candidate neural architectures to accelerate the search process. We demonstrate that architectures within the same performance range exhibit distinct weight distributions, a finding that guides our approach to reducing search space complexity. Specifically, we propose a new method, Competitive Weight Distribution Pruning (CWDPrune), which reduces cost by eliminating a portion of the weight space where interference is most likely to occur. Experimental results show that CWDPrune significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 2.5x speedup on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Additionally, we validate the framework's effectiveness on the ImageNet dataset, demonstrating that it successfully identifies high-performance architectures with reduced computational costs. To our knowledge, this represents the first framework to explicitly address and mitigate interference between candidate neural architectures. The code is available at: https://github.com/ChenchenChen1997/CWDPrune.

This paper investigates the properties of "the edge of $X$", defined as $Y := \{x \in X : d(x,\partial X) = 0\}$, within our specific context where $X$ denotes a geodesically complete CAT(0) space. (2) In a geodesically complete CAT(0) space $X$ where every isometry is an involution, $X$ decomposes into a disjoint union of contractible components, each possessing a closed and convex boundary. (3) If $X$ is a geodesically complete CAT(0) space where every isometry is an involution, then $X$ is locally compact if and only if it is locally compact at points within $Y$. We present an exact universal sum rule governing energy deposition across all final states in the scattering of a nonequilibrium quantum state by a many-body system at finite temperature. This rule applies to final equilibrium states as well as to sums over all final states weighted by their unitary transition probabilities. It extends recent sum rules for conserved quantities in closed systems to open systems and many-body contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that sum rules over transition probabilities weighted by $e^{-\beta E_n}$ remain valid when restricted to eigenchannels of energy deposition, which are defined by a specific set of properties. These eigenchannels offer a practical method for calculating total energy deposition, final states, and spectral functions using real-time or quasi-real-time data. Additionally, we illustrate how to derive both equilibrium and non-equilibrium response functions from energy deposition eigenchannels. Finally, we apply these concepts to a tractable model of a two-level system interacting with a bosonic bath. This work establishes a foundation for future research into non-equilibrium many-body scattering processes. In our applications, we employ both exact and approximate numerical techniques. The approximate methods utilized are the same as those applied to large quantum systems in experiments, enabling direct comparison with data obtained via quantum trajectories, quasi-Wigner, and quasi-Wigner-Weyl methods. This allows for the construction of a comprehensive picture of the accuracy of these techniques. We anticipate that our findings will be valuable for interpreting data from quantum simulators and potentially for analyzing responses in quantum materials. To facilitate this, we have made our code publicly available. Additionally, we have developed a sum-rule-based approach for analyzing quantum scattering data that is exact in the limit of a large number of final states. This approach is also accurate when all but one final state are incoherently mixed, a condition that may be approximately satisfied in many experimental scenarios. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by comparing it with exact results in a few cases. This methodology could prove useful for analyzing data from quantum simulators. Finally, we provide a detailed discussion of the relationship between sum rules and conservation laws. Pruning techniques aim to remove redundant components from convolutional networks, thereby revealing the optimal architecture and connection patterns. While recent studies have successfully applied these methods to fully connected networks, their application to convolutional networks remains largely empirical. This work investigates whether a winning lottery ticket within fully connected networks can also be identified through characteristic features derived from pruning. The results indicate that such winning tickets do exist and that the identified connections exhibit significantly lower entropy than the mean. Furthermore, these findings demonstrate that pruning-based feature identification can effectively recover the winning lottery tickets in convolutional networks with superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The study also confirms that these optimal tickets can be located without requiring access to the training labels. Finally, we show that these characteristics are robust across different datasets and can be extrapolated to other datasets. We introduce the concept of \emph{anticipated value}, which evaluates a lottery ticket's worth based on the possibility of reselling it for more than its purchase price. This analysis yields two key findings: first, an existing platform like eBay can function as a viable outlet for lottery tickets; second, an individual should buy a ticket only if the product of its expected value and its expected resale ratio exceeds the purchase cost. Furthermore, we examine how anticipated value influences \emph{lottery addiction} by comparing the selling probability of an addicted player to that of a rational one. Our results indicate that the ratio between these selling probabilities is independent of the specific ticket, relying instead on the players' cost-benefit thresholds. Additionally, we explore the \emph{optimal selling strategy} for an addicted player, identifying an \emph{optimal stopping time} that maximizes the chance of selling a ticket for more than it costs. Finally, through numerical simulations, we assess the practical significance of these findings. Specifically, we demonstrate that a lottery platform like eBay can offer significant value to players, that the probability of buying a ticket is highly sensitive to the product of its expected value and expected resale ratio, and that an optimal selling strategy can substantially increase the likelihood of profiting from a lottery ticket. The valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials is a non-linear, second-harmonic response driven by both electronic-phonon and optical-phonon-valley interactions. While prior investigations have primarily relied on first-principles calculations to investigate the electronic-phonon influence, this study employs a first-principles molecular dynamics approach to simulate the electronic-phonon contribution to valley physics in graphene and borophene. By utilizing ab initio molecular dynamics, we model structural fluctuations inherent to real materials and analyze how these deviations alter valley Hall conductivity. Our findings indicate that structural variations in borophene can diminish valley Hall conductivity by up to 50%, whereas graphene remains unaffected. These results offer essential insights for the experimental realization of valley Hall responses in two-dimensional systems. Additionally, we examine how electron-phonon coupling influences valley splitting in graphene, revealing that mechanisms beyond simple piezoelectricity must be considered. Finally, we explore potential avenues for enhancing electron-phonon contributions to valley Hall responses. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive framework for understanding electron-phonon interactions within two-dimensional materials. Furthermore, our molecular dynamics methodology establishes a robust foundation for simulating electron-phonon coupling in two-dimensional materials, a capability that was previously unattainable. Visualizing high-dimensional data is essential for data analysis, and t-SNE has become a widely adopted method due to its effectiveness. However, its standard formulation relies on Euclidean distance, which renders many resulting visualizations misleading when applied to data residing on a spherical manifold. To address this, we introduce VMF-SNE, a novel algorithm designed to project spherical data onto a 2D plane. This approach utilizes the von Mises-Fisher distribution to define pairwise similarities based on spherical distances. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VMF-SNE outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in producing more accurate and interpretable visualizations. Additionally, we provide an R package to facilitate the application of this method. Our methodology is particularly beneficial for spherical data analysis tasks, including directional data analysis, orientation analysis, and any domain involving data on a spherical manifold. The system comprises a single impurity interacting with a Fermi sea of heavy fermions via a short-range potential. Furthermore, we offer insights into the model's behavior in the intermediate coupling regime. Finally, we discuss potential applications of this framework to ultracold atoms and the Hubbard model. This method combines digital evolution of two-body interactions with continuous analog propagation of one-body terms, utilizing fermionic qubit mapping on qubits alongside fermionization of one-body terms through quantum determinantal methods on quantum gates. This study investigates how remote work impacts Scrum success, specifically examining the correlation between team co-location and project outcomes. Utilizing a multi-method approach, the research combines secondary quantitative data from 1,017 software projects with qualitative insights gathered through 12 in-depth interviews. Findings indicate that remote work does not significantly hinder Scrum project success, suggesting that Scrum teams are capable of delivering successful outcomes in virtual settings. Furthermore, interview responses highlight that while remote environments may pose communication challenges, they simultaneously offer advantages such as reduced daily stand-up times and fewer meetings. These results provide practical guidance for organizations planning to adopt remote work policies. Additionally, the study offers a novel perspective on remote work by analyzing its specific effects on project success, delivery performance, and customer satisfaction. Finally, limitations of this study are outlined to assist other researchers in designing future research on remote work. Ultimately, this work contributes to the growing body of literature on remote work in software engineering and serves as a foundation for further investigation into the topic.

The concept of Gau-Wu (GW) values was introduced by the late Prof. Sien Gau and Dr. Siow-Tuah Wu in 1992 to address the Hermitian eigenvalue problem. Originally, Dr. Wu derived the formula for $3\times 3$ matrices, and subsequent literature has primarily focused on applications within this dimension. This paper extends the concept to select $4\times 4$ and $5\times 5$ arrowhead matrices. We derive explicit formulas for the proposed Gau-Wu values in these higher dimensions. Since the $3\times 3$ formula represents a specific instance of the $4\times 4$ case, our results offer a more generalization of the GW concept. Furthermore, the $4\times 4$ extension demonstrates greater generality and efficiency compared to existing methods found in the literature. These findings may inspire future research into Gau-Wu-like values for broader classes of matrices. The study includes illustrative examples, numerical experiments, and potential application areas. Additionally, the paper provides MATLAB code to demonstrate the computational power of these results. Keywords: Gau-Wu value, Hermitian matrix, Arrowhead matrix, MATLAB. The analysis utilizes the ATLAS detector at the LHC, covering a transverse momentum range of 1.5 to 10 GeV/$c$. The $v_2$ distribution is derived from an asymmetry in the azimuthal angle between the electron and the beam spot, corrected for background electron sources and experimental systematic effects. The results indicate that electrons exhibit a non-zero $v_2$ in Pb-Pb collisions, a finding that aligns with prior ALICE measurements at lower energies. Furthermore, when compared to other heavy-flavor hadron decays, the electron $v_2$ shows a weak dependence on the mother hadron's charge and a strong dependence on its mass. These findings support the hypothesis that the $v_2$ of electrons is primarily determined by the properties of the parent decaying charm hadron. The data also demonstrate a significant suppression of $c$ quarks relative to light quarks, consistent with expectations from energy loss mechanisms in the quark-gluon plasma. This study examines the maximum Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) loss resulting from suboptimal transmit power control in interference networks. Specifically, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of the largest possible GDoF gap between optimal power control and binary power control (which restricts transmission to either zero or full power) within a network of $K$ users. Our findings demonstrate that the extremal GDoF gain achieved through optimal power control is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This result indicates that the maximum potential GDoF loss of binary power control scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ GDoF units, and we provide explicit upper and lower bounds for this loss. Furthermore, we present a closed-form upper bound for the GDoF loss in specific network configurations, demonstrating that this loss remains bounded by $\Theta(K^{1/3})$ GDoF units. We also explore the implications of these results for interference networks with hierarchical channel strength orders. Finally, we extend our analysis to interference channels featuring degraded user groups, proving that the extremal GDoF benefit of optimal power control over binary power control in such settings is also $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This paper introduces a categorization method designed to integrate results from multiple machine learning models to enhance the trustworthiness of automated decision-making systems. The proposed concept, termed the "Adaptable Categorization Process" (ACP), leverages formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer evidence theory. The study demonstrates the ACP's utility through a case study involving the classification of individuals as either "at risk" or "not at risk" for developing type 2 diabetes. The authors introduce a new probabilistic model designed for point pattern generation, named the Creating from the Strauss Process (CSP). This model is built by combining the Poisson process and the Strauss process through a probabilistic choice with parameter $\gamma \in [0,1]$. When $\gamma = 0$, the model simplifies to a Poisson process, while $\gamma = 1$ results in a Strauss process. Beyond these two extremes, the CSP offers a versatile framework capable of capturing a broad spectrum of interaction behaviors, including attraction, repulsion, and independence. The paper provides methods for estimating the model's parameters and evaluates its performance through simulation studies and a real-world application analyzing the locations of US gas stations. Additionally, model selection criteria are introduced to determine the optimal value of $\gamma$ for fitting the process to observed point patterns. Finally, the authors explore a specific parametric family of CSPs to demonstrate the model's flexibility.
Keywords: point patterns, point process, spatial statistics, point pattern simulation, point pattern fitting, clustering, attraction, Poisson process, Strauss process, creating interval, creating from the Strauss process.

This study extends such corrections to the weak-field, non-relativistic regime of quantum gravity. By incorporating these GUP-induced corrections into the Schrödinger equation, we derive modified Galilean transformations that account for quantum gravitational effects. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these corrections remain consistent with the correspondence principle and can be subsumed into a generalized Lorentz transformation. Finally, we calculate the associated energy scale and show that it scales inversely with the cube of the Planck mass. These findings suggest that quantum gravity effects are observable at energy scales significantly below those predicted by string theory. Additionally, we explore the broader implications of these results for cosmology and black hole physics. In conclusion, our results indicate that quantum gravity effects are potentially observable well below the string scale. Instead, such a theory could be validated through cosmological observations or through the study of quantum effects in curved spacetime. We address a multitasking allocation problem where items are shared processing facilities capable of handling multiple users simultaneously, alongside private facilities dedicated to single users. Each user submits a demand specifying the quantity of work to perform at both shared and private locations, while each task requires a specific mode of operation. The objective is to minimize the total time required to complete all tasks. We demonstrate that for any instance, there exists an optimal solution where the completion time at shared facilities does not exceed the second largest time among the three modes for any single task. Based on this property, we propose a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with an approximation ratio of $3.5$. Furthermore, we establish that the problem is AP-hard, meaning no polynomial-time approximation scheme exists unless $P=NP$. Finally, we extend our findings to scenarios where shared facilities have limited capacity, proving that these problems are also AP-hard. Additionally, we consider a variant where each task's mode is selected from a set of options, showing that a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with a ratio of $4$ exists for this case. However, we also prove AP-hardness for this variant when the number of modes is part of the input. Our primary focus remains on the scenario where both shared and private task quantities are fixed constants. In this context, we present a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with a ratio of $2.5$. We also provide an approximation ratio of $2$ for instances with at most two shared processing facilities and show AP-hardness for problems involving three or more shared facilities. These results are complemented by a polynomial-time approximation scheme for cases with a fixed number of shared facilities. Our primary contribution lies in developing a general algorithm for multitasking allocation with shared processing, which serves as the foundation for all our findings. This algorithm is based on a constructive proof of the optimal property and is also utilized to establish the approximation ratio of $3.5$. We further provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance. This paper presents a modeling, simulation, and control enhancement study for a monopod hopping robot operating on deformable terrain. Initially, the dynamics of the robot and the ground are defined, followed by the development of corresponding models. Next, the stability of the hopping motion is analyzed using linearization and multiplier methods. Finally, the study investigates how to enhance hopping performance through the control of the foot's damping coefficient. These advancements were implemented on a laboratory-scale prototype to validate the proposed methods. The results indicate that while the robot can maintain a stable hop, increasing the foot damping coefficient leads to greater hop height and energy efficiency. Consequently, an active control strategy is utilized to adjust the damping coefficient in real-time, thereby improving overall hopping performance. Experimental data collected from the prototype confirms the effectiveness of this approach. Additionally, a method for estimating ground deformation is introduced, and a technique for measuring the foot's contact point is developed to facilitate model parameter identification. Finally, outdoor experiments were conducted to demonstrate the robot's ability to perform stable hopping on uneven terrain. These findings collectively suggest that the proposed modeling and control strategies are effective for achieving stable hopping on variable ground. Furthermore, the ability to estimate foot position and ground deformation enables the robot to adapt to uneven surfaces, marking a significant step toward outdoor applications. The research also identifies limitations, such as the inability to track reference trajectories, and proposes future work to address these challenges. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for developing hopping robots capable of traversing uneven terrain. The methodologies and insights presented here are intended to facilitate future research in this domain. Specifically, the ability to estimate foot position and ground deformation allows the robot to navigate uneven surfaces, representing a crucial advancement toward practical outdoor deployment. Finally, the study outlines several limitations and suggests potential avenues for future investigation. We investigate the multifractal characteristics of eigenstates in one-dimensional interacting fermion systems, focusing on the crossover from many-body localization (MBL) to delocalization. By employing a finite-size scaling approach on the Fock-space non-repeating Green's function, we determine the critical exponent $\tau_2$ governing the second moment across this transition. Our results show that $\tau_2$ remains nearly constant at $0.62 \pm 0.05$ for both the strong MBL and delocalized phases, with no evidence of a critical point between them. This finding contrasts with non-interacting systems, where multifractality evolves continuously from localized to critical to delocalized states. Additionally, we observe a finite-size scaling collapse of the ratio between two- and four-point correlators, which yields a critical exponent for the four-point correlator of $\tau_4 = 1.24 \pm 0.05$. These outcomes are consistent with the random singularity hypothesis, which predicts $\tau_2 = 0.6$ and $\tau_4 = 1.2$ for white multifractals. We also note that our estimated value for $\tau_2$ aligns with recent findings from a different methodology. Finally, we demonstrate that these results hold true for systems with finite density. We conclude that multifractality in interacting many-body systems is governed by a single scale-invariant regime, which persists through the MBL-to-delocalized transition. This contrasts with the critical MBL transition, which is marked by an infinite set of diverging length scales. The presence of a single regime simplifies the analysis of many-body systems and may facilitate the identification of a critical point between the localized and delocalized phases. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for extending this methodology to analyze the fractal dimension of eigenstates in higher dimensions.

Interactive search is a prevalent task in information retrieval, characterized by the ability to engage with a user at each iteration to optimize query efficiency. This study introduces the novel challenge of finding multiple targets within a limited search budget, addressing real-world scenarios such as multi-label image tagging and video content analysis. We present LISA, a new algorithm designed to efficiently identify multiple targets using few queries. Unlike existing methods, LISA is the first to leverage the interdependencies between labels to enhance performance. Extensive experiments on two new Labeled Image Sets demonstrate that LISA surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and query efficiency. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1996/LISA. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive guide to LISA, detailing its design philosophy, implementation specifics, and potential applications. This work aims to foster interest in the field of interactive search for multiple targets. Our hope is that LISA will serve as a strong baseline for future research in this area. Finally, we invite scholars to explore the potential of interactive multiple target search and to establish new state-of-the-art results, thereby advancing the field. We look forward to your contributions.

Universal adversarial examples are designed to deceive machine learning models across various architectures. This study investigates their existence within quantum classifiers. We establish that universal adversarial instances and perturbations do not exist for single-layer quantum classifiers characterized by a linear readout mechanism. Conversely, we demonstrate that these elements can be generated for multi-layer models, specifically those utilizing a quantum perceptron layer. Furthermore, we offer a theoretical analysis of the computational complexity required to construct such adversarial examples. Finally, we examine the existence and generation of universal adversarial instances within models employing the shadow tomography algorithm. Additionally, our experimental results indicate that these instances possess practical utility in evaluating the robustness of quantum neural networks. In this context, we note that the algorithm for generating adversarial instances is not universal and may require adaptation depending on the specific circuit being analyzed.
