This study investigates Steklov eigenvalues within nearly round domains. Building on prior findings that established an infinitesimal interlacing sequence for these eigenvalues, we demonstrate a large asymptotic interlacing sequence. Additionally, our results confirm the monotonicity of the first Steklov eigenvalue, converting it into a weakly interlacing eigenvalue, and provide a proof of the Weyl law applicable to Steklov eigenvalues in two-dimensional nearly round regions. For general two-dimensional domains, we also establish the Weyl law, large asymptotic interlacing, and infinitesimal interlacing sequences, with the latter being novel even for two-dimensional round domains. Finally, in higher dimensions, we prove the Weyl law and large asymptotic interlacing sequence, while offering new proofs for the asymptotic interlacing and infinitesimal interlacing sequences previously established by Buric and Monakov. Furthermore, the newly demonstrated Weyl law in the general two-dimensional context yields a novel interlacing sequence for the Steklov problem on the real projective plane. Our methodology relies on the asymptotic analysis of the Dirichlet Laplacian in nearly round regions, a tool also utilized to derive the Weyl law for the Steklov problem on n-dimensional spheres. Consequently, this article serves as a valuable resource for addressing Steklov problems on nearly round domains. Additionally, the proofs of the Weyl law and large asymptotic interlacing sequences for the Steklov problem on n-dimensional spheres hold independent significance. Our findings complement those of Buric and Monakov, who demonstrated that the large asymptotic interlacing sequence is valid for all dimensions, whereas an interlacing sequence with a gap of 2 holds true for dimensions n ≥ 4. In the specific case of n = 3, Buric and Monakov identified a gap of 3 within the large asymptotic interlacing sequence; we show this can be reduced to a gap of 2. We anticipate that the theorems presented herein will facilitate the resolution of various challenging problems concerning the spectral geometry of Steklov. This paper introduces a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to replicate the radio transmission behavior of cellular networks. By utilizing only static cell configuration data, the model can predict the radio network topology at any specific coordinate without requiring real-time inputs like mobile station locations or dynamic parameters such as pilot power. We demonstrate that the proposed CNN effectively approximates the discrete, step-function output of traditional digital cellular networks, thereby offering a continuous function approximation that significantly accelerates radio propagation simulations. Furthermore, this capability facilitates the modeling of advanced network types, including those employing non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) and cooperative communications, which standard distance-based models struggle to represent accurately. Finally, the model demonstrates robustness against variations in large-scale fading parameters. Power system expansion models are widely used to assess the responsiveness of power systems to policy shifts, yet the degree of model responsiveness is heavily influenced by the specific model formulation. This study examines the responsiveness of power system expansion models with respect to electricity demand forecasts and policy variations. The results indicate that deviations from forecasted demand growth have minimal impact on model outcomes, and that model results remain largely consistent across different resource policies. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that including demand forecasts in model formulations yields outcomes comparable to those generated without them. Consequently, this underscores the necessity of incorporating flexible demand response into model designs to enhance their ability to reflect policy changes. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Ultimately, the findings suggest that while model outputs are generally robust, they can be significantly improved by integrating demand response and storage policies. Additionally, the study highlights the value of conducting sensitivity analyses to evaluate how model results respond to variations in input parameters. Finally, the research emphasizes the need to account for the specific characteristics of local power systems when interpreting model results. (This research was conducted while the author was a visiting scholar at the University of Adelaide.) This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for both the Vlasov-Poisson and ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems within bounded regions. Specifically, we demonstrate that the system remains global well-posedness even with Dirichlet boundary conditions applied to the electric potential. This approach contrasts with the Neumann conditions typically assumed in unbounded settings. Furthermore, we show that the solution preserves positivity throughout the domain and achieve global control over higher-order moments. These findings enable a global analysis of equilibrium properties, including equilibrium existence, stability, and instability. Additionally, we provide a global proof of the Poincaré inequality applicable to any open set. As an application, we extend the proof—originally given only for $\mathbb{R}^3$—of nonexistence of classical solutions to the ionic ionic Vlasov-Poisson system in the case of odd dimensions. We also address a question posed by Guo and Zhang [10] regarding the existence of an electric potential with Neumann boundary conditions in bounded domains. Finally, in the context of ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems, we derive an optimal control estimate for electric energy. These results collectively offer a more comprehensive analysis of ionic Vlasov-Poisson systems in bounded domains compared to the case of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Notably, in $\mathbb{R}^3$, energy estimates rely on Liouville's theorem and the decay of initial data at infinity, resources unavailable in bounded settings. Consequently, our proofs employ an original method that avoids these dependencies. This approach is also applicable to the standard Vlasov-Poisson system. Developing large-scale software systems is intricate and demands effective maintenance strategies. Software concept location serves as a vital maintenance activity by identifying all instances of a concept within source code. Traditional approaches often rely on matching exact keywords from user queries, which can yield false positives when concepts share similar names. To address this, we introduce STRICT, a novel method that leverages information retrieval to interpret queries and map them to code. STRICT employs a dual-phase strategy: first, it trains a retrieval model using a dataset of queries and code, then integrates this model with a graph-based model to pinpoint code locations. Empirical results demonstrate that STRICT outperforms baseline methods, achieving a 10% increase in true positive rate and a 20% reduction in false positives. STRICT is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/strict. This tool can assist developers in locating code via the IDE extension available at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/strict-ide-extension. Furthermore, STRICT supports developers in designing data models by suggesting potential concept names, a capability accessible through the extension's proposed feature. We outline this feature in our user study, which we plan to conduct in future work. STRICT represents the first tool to integrate information retrieval for concept location, offering a valuable resource for software development. Colloidal gels formed by Brownian particles are renowned for their solid-like rigidity, yet their transition to a liquid state remains difficult to trigger. This study demonstrates that applying ultrasonic vibrations to a colloidal gel can reversibly switch it from a solid to a free-flowing liquid. Specifically, ultrasonic energy disrupttes the weak inter-particle bonds within the gel network, inducing a rheo-acoustic gel. By adjusting the intensity and frequency of the sonication, we can precisely control the material's yield stress and viscosity. Furthermore, even after ceasing ultrasonic application, the gel retains a significant portion of these altered rheological properties. We attribute this partial tuning effect to "acoustic annealing" of the particle structure while the ultrasonic field is active, followed by the slow, incomplete reformation of inter-particle bonds once the acoustic energy source is removed. These findings introduce a novel method for modifying the rheological characteristics of colloidal gels and expand our understanding of their reversible solid-liquid transitions. Additionally, this research holds significant potential for practical applications, including the creation of new functional materials and advanced manufacturing techniques. Finally, we propose a new dimension for particle assembly, offering a pathway to engineer complex materials with specific and customizable structures. The Collatz Conjecture asserts that any positive integer $n$ will eventually reach 1 through an iterative process. For each step, if the current number is odd, multiply it by 3 and add 1; if it is even, divide it by 2. Although this conjecture has remained unproven for over 80 years, it can be readily simulated using code. This article demonstrates several code implementations, beginning with a basic version. Additionally, it explores methods to visualize the conjecture's behavior, such as plotting the number of steps required to first attain an odd value within the range [1, 1000] or displaying a binary tree where the root is 1 and the children of node $n$ correspond to the possible previous values. Finally, the article examines the conjecture's connection to the $3^n+1$ sequence and proposes it as an engaging coding challenge. Accurately identifying and parsing mathematical entities is essential for processing STEM documents, particularly to enable the semantic understanding of these specialized items. This task is inherently difficult due to the complex visual structures of such content and the scarcity of annotated training data. While recent studies have introduced effective models for this purpose, they often overlook the need for specific annotations regarding the semantic meaning of these mathematical entities. To address this gap, we introduce a new dataset comprising equations and formulas from scientific papers, where each item is tagged with a unique ID corresponding to a mathematical dictionary. We then conduct a document classification task using these meanings as labels. Our analysis reveals that incorporating these specific meanings significantly enhances the performance of existing state-of-the-art classifiers. Furthermore, we explore the application of mathematical entity meaning for document classification and demonstrate that a knowledge graph-based classifier surpasses other approaches, thereby validating the utility of our dataset. In the classic stable marriage problem, both men and women have strict linear orderings of their potential partners. The well-known Gale-Shapley algorithm generates a stable matching where the man side secures their most preferred outcome among all such possibilities, while the woman side receives the least favorable. This paper investigates modifications to the Gale-Shapley method by allowing each participant to choose which proposals to submit. We examine two specific mechanisms: the "one-shot" approach, where individuals select a single partner, and the "one-shot-plus" approach, where they can choose between one partner or none. Our findings indicate that both one-shot and one-plus marriages are generally not guaranteed to be stable. Furthermore, determining a stable matching in one-plus marriages is NP-hard. We also outline the conditions under which stable one-plus marriages exist and introduce a specific one-plus method called "selective Gale-Shapley," which produces a man-optimal result. Finally, we explore extensions involving women's incomplete orderings and scenarios with vacant positions. These investigations reveal a consistent pattern: as mechanisms become more flexible, the likelihood of instability increases, and the difficulty of finding a solution grows. We conclude by suggesting avenues for future research. This work investigates the recovery of a complex signal using quadratic measurements. By leveraging the structural properties of the measurement matrix, the paper establishes the conditions under which a given complex signal can be successfully reconstructed from these types of measurements. Furthermore, it compares the required number of measurements for both real and complex signals and highlights the significant role that sparsity plays in this reconstruction process. The study also presents a concrete example demonstrating the limitations of sparsity. Additionally, examples illustrating the impact of signal space dimensionality are provided. Finally, the paper examines the relationship between the signal space dimension and the types of errors that may occur during recovery. The authors extend their gratitude to the anonymous reviewers for their insightful comments and suggestions. LiDAR's robustness in adverse weather and superior depth perception complement camera imagery's richness in color and texture details. This paper introduces BEVFusion, a straightforward yet powerful fusion framework for combining bird's-eye view representations from cameras and LiDAR. The method involves two core steps: first, projecting camera features into LiDAR's spatial domain using multi-head cross attention; and second, integrating camera and LiDAR bird's-eye features through a convolutional decoder. This approach eliminates the need for complex feature alignment, camera calibration, or extensive parameter tuning. Extensive experiments on the KITTI benchmark demonstrate that BEVFusion enhances performance across key tasks, including 3D object detection, panoptic segmentation, and depth estimation. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ScanNet/BEVFusion. Additionally, we have released the weights for camera-LiDAR fused depth estimation on the NVIDIACVDepth dataset. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the KITTI and NVIDIACVDepth benchmarks. Furthermore, we have made our training and inference code for 3D detection and panoptic segmentation on KITTI available. Finally, our method yields competitive performance on the nuScenes dataset. This study examines dissipation-range fluid turbulence, focusing on the impact of thermal dissipation on the energy cascade. The primary objective is to determine the conditions under which the dissipation scales of velocity and temperature align, thereby establishing a unified range for both variables. We analyze these phenomena across three representative models: anisotropic two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), two-dimensional reactive MHD, and reactive three-dimensional MHD. Our findings indicate that within a specific parameter window, the dissipation ranges of velocity and temperature merge into a single domain, with their respective dissipation scales scaling identically. This resonant condition is governed by the ratio of energy-containing scales to the sum of viscous and thermal dissipation scales, alongside the magnetic Prandtl number. In reactive MHD models, the magnetic field amplifies the velocity dissipation scale, whereas in non-reactive scenarios, it diminishes. These results highlight the critical role of thermal dissipation in the fluid energy cascade and suggest that the proposed parameter range is broadly applicable across diverse physical models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnetic field amplification mechanism in reactive MHD is contingent upon the resonant alignment of velocity and temperature dissipation scales. Finally, we outline the significance of these discoveries for understanding solar atmospheric dynamics. The accompanying video illustrates the variation of velocity and temperature correlation length scales as functions of the magnetic Prandtl number across different dissipation scales. Specifically, the video depicts the evolution of the correlation length scale for velocity (left) and temperature (right) as the magnetic Prandtl number increases from 0.1 to 10.0. The magnetic Prandtl number is defined as the ratio of kinematic viscosity to thermal diffusivity. In the dissipation range, the velocity correlation length scale exceeds the thermal one, with the disparity growing as the magnetic Prandtl number rises. This trend is particularly pronounced in reactive MHD models. The video covers three distinct MHD types: anisotropic MHD, reactive MHD, and reactive three-dimensional MHD. Anisotropic MHD refers to magnetohydrodynamics with magnetic reconnection, while reactive MHD incorporates the Lorentz force. Anisotropic MHD is a two-dimensional model, whereas the other two are three-dimensional. The analysis was conducted using the open-source numerical code ReaMHD. This study examines a scenario where a Gaussian laser beam traverses a liquid contained in a glass cell, accounting for heat exchange between the liquid and the surrounding air, as well as between the air and the glass walls. Our analysis explores how various physical parameters influence the resulting thermal profile. The model successfully reproduces the intricate diffraction patterns observed in experiments conducted by our group and those reported by other research groups. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both coexistence and sequential coexistence of positive and negative refractive index regions can generate such complex diffraction patterns. Additionally, this model is applicable to other contexts involving laser heating of fluids, such as laser-induced forward scattering. Software design discussions are frequently documented in software requirements specifications, serving as a vital resource for maintaining and evolving software systems. However, automatically detecting discussion points from text remains a difficult task due to the natural language variations in design terminology. This paper introduces a text mining approach that leverages the stability of software design concepts to ensure solution robustness against such linguistic fluctuations. We present a methodology for automatically identifying software design concepts within discussion texts, which incorporates a novel algorithm for recognizing concept mentions. This algorithm utilizes the structural dependencies of concepts and their references, derived from an automatically constructed domain-specific grammar. The proposed approach was evaluated using over 10,000 sentences extracted from more than 100 design discussions across 16 requirements specification documents. Our results demonstrate that the method achieves a precision of 0.81 and a recall of 0.65. Furthermore, we assess the solution's robustness using precision and recall at the sentence and paragraph levels, finding that it performs effectively at the paragraph level even with noisy data. These findings suggest the approach's potential for supporting software design activities. Additionally, we outline a framework for concept extraction grounded in dependency grammars and provide a general procedure for testing the robustness of machine learning models in natural language processing. This framework is applicable to various concept extraction tasks, including those involving domain-specific terminology. The paper is structured to guide readers in replicating our results and applying the concept extraction framework to different tasks. Finally, we detail how to assemble the necessary data and tools for the experiments, providing access to the data, code, and tools via a repository. This work was conducted as part of the 2021 Industry4IT Challenge, a competition organized by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research. The challenge aims to develop a software solution for automatically extracting design concepts from requirements specification documents, thereby supporting the maintenance of consistent design decisions throughout the development process. The task involves classifying sentences as either containing or not containing design concepts, with the evaluation metrics being precision and recall at the sentence and paragraph levels. The challenge dataset comprises over 100 documents from the automotive industry, totaling more than 10,000 sentences. The dataset is available at https://github.com/Industry4ITChallenge/DesignConceptExtraction. The results presented in this paper were achieved by winning the competition. This paper outlines our methodology for developing an open-source big data stream processing framework named H-STREAM, which is built upon Apache HBase. We also present a preliminary evaluation of this framework. Given that Apache HBase is a widely adopted big data solution, this work offers a valuable initial exploration of processing stream data using HBase. The paper is structured to first provide an overview of H-STREAM, followed by a review of its primary design principles, and concludes with preliminary evaluation results. These findings demonstrate that H-STREAM offers a viable alternative for processing and analyzing vast volumes of streaming data. Furthermore, the evaluation confirms that H-STREAM scales effectively with increasing write rates and the size of historical data. Additionally, H-STREAM exhibits minimal latency when ingesting and querying streaming data, making it well-suited for real-time analytics applications. Finally, the framework supports data partitioning strategies that allow for flexible and independent processing of multiple stream sources. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as the leading approach for knowledge base (KB) translation, yet it frequently suffers from systematic errors like repetition failures and over-generation. This study investigates these issues within SPARQL-based KB translation, demonstrating that they stem from the encoder's inability to adequately model long-distance dependencies. To address this, we introduce a copy system designed to mitigate such translation errors. The system integrates an attention-based copy mechanism with a modified NMT model, where the attention model is specifically tuned to identify long-distance dependencies. Additionally, we propose a new training framework that combines standard NMT objectives with a copy mechanism to enhance the NMT model's capacity for handling long-distance relationships. Experimental results show that our system effectively reduces repetition and over-generation errors while improving overall performance. Furthermore, our system achieves state-of-the-art results on SPARQL KB translation tasks. Finally, we demonstrate the system's applicability to other knowledge base translation formats, including Natural Language to SPARQL and SPARQL to Natural Language. We introduce a new approach to venue analytics that offers an alternative to traditional citation-based metrics for assessing research venue quality. This method constructs a quality distribution based on the historical outputs of each specific venue and establishes quality thresholds using a quantile function. A venue's signature is defined as the probability of its past outputs exceeding these adaptive thresholds. We demonstrate the method's efficacy through case studies focusing on journal and conference venue quality. Additionally, we propose a more general framework grounded in adaptive quantile functions, which holds potential for future applications in venue analytics. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/chenyixuan/venue_analytics.

Subsequently, we explain how a NN controller is typically implemented within such a system. Following this, we outline the two primary strategies for validating a NN controller: verifying the safety of its closed-loop behavior and ensuring the safety of its open-loop trajectories. Finally, we present various techniques for conducting these verification tasks. The discussion concludes with an exploration of several open research questions. We introduce a method for grouping elements based on a graph that allows for overlaps, resulting in a multi-level functorial algorithm. This approach is applicable to any category, though we present the method specifically within Set. The process begins with a binary relation defining pairwise similarities among the elements. This relation is decomposed into a hierarchy of equivalence relations, where each relation's pair classes are formed by combining 2-valued linear combinations of lower-level classes. This decomposition continues recursively until a hierarchy of equivalence classes is achieved that closely approximates the original relation. The proposed method offers a superior approximation compared to standard clustering techniques, such as those derived from minimum spanning trees. Additionally, we demonstrate how to construct fuzzy hierarchies of classes and discuss the method's application in image segmentation. A key advantage is that the algorithm is fully functorial across all levels, enabling parallel execution. We have implemented this as a functor in Set and made the code available on GitHub. Finally, we outline how this method can be adapted into a 2-functor for categories with finite sets and functions. Streaming tensor completion addresses missing data recovery in streaming multi-way data, yet existing methods often struggle with large tensors and extended timeframes. This paper introduces a new Streaming Tensor Loop Completion (SLLC) model that leverages patch tracking to enhance visual data recovery. The proposed framework iteratively refines both patch tracking and tensor completion. Initially, a deep learning network estimates missing data using available observations. Subsequently, these predictions guide the tracking of data patches across time and space to construct a tracking tensor, which feeds back into the completion process to generate a refined estimation. This proposed method is computationally efficient, achieving rapid convergence in a few iterations. Experimental results on two visual data recovery tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the integration of deep learning and patch tracking enables the method to utilize local temporal-spatial information, resulting in superior performance on limited data. Our findings confirm the presence of both an inverse energy cascade and the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) spectrum. While prior literature has established the ZK spectrum only in the limit of small dissipation ($\gamma \to 0$), we demonstrate its existence across a broad range of dissipation values. Furthermore, we provide evidence supporting a $\kappa^4$ energy flux law, which aligns with theoretical predictions. These results hold significant implications for understanding energy transfer in both physical and non-physical systems. Specifically, regarding brain activity, our evidence suggests that turbulent wave dynamics may play a crucial role in information processing. This conclusion is derived from analyzing both synthetic and real electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which exhibit clear signatures of inverse energy cascades and ZK spectra. Consequently, our findings indicate that turbulent wave dynamics could be fundamental to brain function. These insights offer a promising avenue for developing new mathematical models of brain activity and for novel applications of brain imaging techniques. Additionally, our work opens up novel applications of wave turbulence theory to fields such as neuroscience, economics, and social sciences. Finally, the numerical simulations presented here can serve as valuable testbeds for developing and validating new mathematical models. For instance, they can assist in testing whether modifications to the current model—such as incorporating nonlocal dispersion or dissipation—yield more accurate descriptions of brain activity. This could pave the way for new mathematical models of brain activity that extend beyond traditional approaches. In summary, this research offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex dynamics of turbulent wave systems and their potential applications in various fields. This paper demonstrates that the iterative square root normalization applied to adjacency matrices, when paired with greedy node selection, fails to consistently identify a maximal or even a nearly maximal subset of nodes that are mutually at least distance 2 apart. Consequently, we establish that local graph normalization methods cannot reliably produce a subset of nodes that are locally distance $k$ separated for any $k \ge 1$. The study also examines the impact of random node ordering. Furthermore, we outline an algorithm with a provable running time that determines the size of the largest distance-$k$ separated subset, though this approach relies on integer programming and is therefore impractical for real-world applications. Finally, we present a heuristic method for generating distance-$k$ separated subsets, which is also supported by theoretical guarantees. In this context, a subset is defined as distance-$k$ separated if the minimum distance between any pair of nodes within it is at least $k$. This work is motivated by the challenge of assigning orthogonal frequency spectrum to a set of nodes situated at distance $k$ in a graph. Additionally, we explore the relationship between this problem and independent sets in graphs. Our primary contribution is a novel algorithm for identifying maximal independent sets, which is backed by theoretical proofs and experimental data. This algorithm is grounded in a new concept: the independent ratio of a graph, which we demonstrate is more effective than graph density for identifying optimal maximal independent sets. We also explore the connection between independent ratio and graph density. Finally, we provide an overview of the experimental results achieved using this new heuristic. The paper concludes with a discussion of open problems and future research directions. This work extends our prior research published in \cite{2021arXiv210101001B}. This study reports the first low-frequency radio observations of the binary system CR Draconis, conducted using the LOFAR Low-Band (LB) and Wide-Field (W) receivers. The observations spanned 10 years, covering 2011 to 2020, and targeted the star with the strongest magnetic field in the nearby solar neighborhood. We identified 10 new radio bursts from CR Draconis within the 10–100 MHz range, with a mean recurrence interval of 1.5 years. These bursts exhibit a duration of approximately 10 minutes and a broad frequency spectrum, reaching up to 100 MHz. Their morphology and duration suggest they are not driven by a single flare event. Instead, the persistent nature of the emission indicates a long-term electron-cyclotron maser instability occurring at the magnetic pole of the magnetic companion. We propose that CR Draconis is a unique class of magnetic binary, where the maser emission is powered by a steady wind from the magnetic companion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that LOFAR is capable of detecting maser emission from magnetic binaries with magnetic field strengths as low as 1 kG. This capability establishes a new method for identifying and characterizing magnetic binaries, which are critical for understanding the evolution of magnetic stars and their potential role in the habitability of exoplanets. Future observations of magnetic binaries at low frequencies are expected to significantly advance our understanding of these systems. The LOFAR LB and W receivers are anticipated to detect maser emission from at least 100 magnetic binaries within the solar neighborhood. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these observations for the study of exoplanetary systems around magnetic stars. Finally, we outline the future potential of low-frequency radio observations for investigating the magnetic fields of magnetic binaries and their exoplanetary systems. We introduce a new method for visualizing moving virtual characters, termed Articulated Neural Visualization (ANR). This approach learns a neural radiance field that relies on a skeleton-based representation of the avatar. The technique is versatile, accommodating various types of multi-view imagery, including per-joint, per-branch, and skeleton-aligned views. Additionally, it supports an animation-driven training phase that produces a compact model capable of producing high-quality visual results. Our method is highly general and is currently being evaluated across a range of tasks, such as virtual-to-real transfer, novel viewpoint synthesis, and virtual-to-virtual transfer. Furthermore, we have developed a new, more diverse and challenging dataset for virtual character visualization to complement existing benchmarks. Humans and machines often interpret visual information differently, yet research comparing their performances under severe image transformations remains limited. This study introduces a novel framework to evaluate how humans and machines respond to drastic changes in images. We conducted a large-scale online experiment involving 1,020 participants across 12 transformation categories, covering 108 conditions with 8–12 humans per test. Simultaneously, we engaged 1,000 AI models across 11 of these transformation categories, involving 1,056 machines across 96 conditions with a minimum of 12 models per test. Our analysis reveals that human and machine responses diverge significantly across these transformations. Furthermore, we propose a new metric called "Human-Machine Discrepancy" to quantify these differences, demonstrating its effectiveness in selecting models for specific transformations. Finally, we explore the implications of this discrepancy for human-machine collaboration. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/DiscrepancyLab/severely-transformed-images.

We employ Chern-Simons theory, specifically the Jones polynomial and its extensions within the Uq( sl(2,C)) Chern-Simons framework, to investigate the connection between the Jones-Wenzel projector and the Askey-Wilson projector. Leveraging this insight, we demonstrate that the value of the Jones polynomial for the Borromean rings can be derived from the spectrum of the Askey-Wilson operator. This result is extended to a broader class of links, including the Borromean rings, and we further outline the general procedure for computing the Jones polynomial of any link. Additionally, we examine the Borromean rings in the Uq( sl(2,C)) theory, deriving the corresponding invariant, which aligns with the theory proposed by Nakanishi and Wada. Finally, we establish the relationship between the Uq( sl(2,C)) invariant of the Borromean rings and the spectrum of the Askey-Wilson operator. These findings are supported by explicit calculations and visualized through numerous figures. Our results contribute to the ongoing effort to elucidate the deep and intriguing relationship between 3D quantum gravity and integrable systems. Specifically, the study of the Askey-Wilson operator's spectrum offers a novel and distinct approach to calculating link invariants. This study examines the two-dimensional Ising trimer antiferromagnet, a system where each unit cell consists of three spins linked by unequal interactions. We present results from a newly developed cluster quantum Monte Carlo algorithm applied to the 2D checkerboard lattice, which features four distinct cluster types corresponding to the possible magnetic configurations of a single unit cell. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through a detailed analysis of a specific model: a checkerboard where each cell contains two strong intracellular bonds and one weak bond, resulting in a highly frustrated configuration. We investigate the correlation functions of this model and its limiting cases, which correspond to the 2D Ising trimer models previously analyzed in references [Phys. Rev. B 104, 094410 (2021)] and [Phys. Rev. B 103, 024408 (2021)]. In these limits, the weak bond either vanishes or approaches infinity, effectively reducing the system to the well-known 2D Ising model. Our findings indicate that the proposed algorithm is highly effective for this class of models, yielding precise critical exponents and reliable estimates for the correlation length and other thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, we observe that the weak bond exerts a minimal influence on the critical exponents, suggesting that the large cluster configurations generated during simulations represent a near-critical state. This insight is valuable for studying other frustrated magnetic models. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this work to more complex models, such as the 2D checkerboard lattice with a single unequal bond per unit cell. These extensions could be achieved by incorporating additional cluster types to account for the various magnetic configurations of the trimer. We anticipate that the methodology introduced here will prove useful for a broad range of frustrated magnetic systems. Although pre-trained language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in vision and vision-language tasks, they currently lack robust zero-shot learning abilities. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective framework that enhances the zero-shot performance of pre-trained models by exposing them to dataset and prompt assemblies during meta-tuning. We examine various components for these assemblies, such as support class labels, image-text pairs, and predictions from other models, and combine them into different configurations. Furthermore, we explore hyperparameter optimization to identify optimal settings for this process. Experiments conducted across image classification benchmarks, including ImageNet and COCO, show consistent improvements in zero-shot accuracy. Specifically, our method boosts the ViT-B model's zero-shot performance on these image sets by up to 3.5% and 4.5%, respectively, surpassing previous state-of-the-art zero-shot approaches. This study examines the implications of recent dark matter LUX and LHC findings on the viability of a first-order electroweak phase transition (EWPT) within a $Z_3$-invariant Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) framework. We further investigate how these constraints affect the successful thermal production of dark matter. Our analysis demonstrates that accommodating a dark matter particle mass of approximately $100\text{ GeV}$ within the NMSSM significantly restricts the model's parameter space, thereby diminishing the likelihood of achieving an EWPT. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting stochastic gravitational waves generated by the phase transition, which may be observable by the LISA mission. To support this analysis, we have developed a dedicated Fortran code for the model. A detailed technical report outlining the code's features and its application to the phase transition will be published separately. The source code is accessible at \href{https://github.com/abdullahkhalid/EWPTandDM}{abdullahkhalid/EWPTandDM}. We introduce a new diagnostic tool designed to evaluate redshift estimates from (sub)millimeter surveys, which is crucial for identifying reliable redshifts for high-redshift galaxies. By comparing the performance of a galaxy classifier trained on the "Submillimeter Cosmology 2020" (SC20) catalog with that of the recently released "Cosmic Evolution" (COE) catalog, we demonstrate that a machine learning model utilizing the COE galaxy classifier score, along with redshift and $850\mu$m photometry, can significantly enhance the success rate of identifying robust redshifts for high-z SUDOCU galaxies. This approach is expected to be equally effective for other galaxies selected by their spectral energy distributions. We propose that this method will substantially boost the yield of high-z SUDOCU galaxies, including those at $z>10$, when applied to the upcoming "Cosmic Dawn 2020" (COD20) catalog. We encourage the community to adopt this strategy for future (sub)millimeter surveys. The code required to reproduce our analysis is publicly accessible at https://github.com/brunomgomes/High-z-Sudoku. We investigate the thermodynamic and dynamic characteristics of a quantum spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice using large-scale unbiased quantum Monte Carlo simulations. By analyzing the temperature-dependent behavior of the specific heat, magnetic susceptibility, and spin stiffness, we determine that the system undergoes a second-order phase transition at a critical temperature $T_c$ that aligns with the ordering temperature predicted by spin-wave theory. Spectral functions derived from the spin-spin correlation function, specifically the uniform transverse and longitudinal components, exhibit distinct temperature-dependent evolution. At temperatures below $T_c$, these spectral functions display sharp peaks at low energies, indicating that the system's dynamics are governed by the long-wavelength fluctuations of the associated Haldane-Shastry spin-liquid state. Conversely, in the high-temperature regime, the spectral functions are characterized by a broad distribution of energies, reflecting the dominance of local spin fluctuations. These findings demonstrate that specific thermodynamic and dynamic signatures can effectively differentiate between conventional ordering states and Haldane-Shastry spin-liquid states. Furthermore, we note that the emergence of Haldane-Shastry spin-liquid properties in our system is attributable to the presence of weak geometric frustration. Consequently, our results suggest that the geometrically frustrated Heisenberg model, which features only nearest-neighbor interactions, represents a novel quantum critical point separating an ordering state from a Haldane-Shastry spin-liquid state. This model is significant because it avoids the complexities of geometrically frustrated Heisenberg models with antiferromagnetic interactions on bipartite lattices, which have been proposed as candidates for hosting Haldane-Shastry spin-liquid states. Additionally, our findings indicate that this simple Heisenberg model can serve as a viable candidate for realizing a quantum spin-liquid state in real materials. Finally, we discuss the potential to detect the emergence of Haldane-Shastry spin-liquid states in real systems by examining their specific heat and magnetic susceptibility. Specifically, we propose that a peak in specific heat and a maximum in magnetic susceptibility may signal the emergence of Haldane-Shastry spin-liquid states. We also examine the relationship between these signatures and the ordering temperature. Our analysis reveals that the peak in specific heat and the maximum in magnetic susceptibility occur at temperatures slightly above the ordering temperature, which is consistent with our numerical findings. This study investigates the confinement-deconfinement transition within $3+1$-dimensional $SU(3)$-Higgs theory, which extends QCD by incorporating a complex scalar field in the fundamental representation. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we determine transition parameters for various scalar masses, specifically focusing on the deconfinement debye mass. Our findings reveal a linear relationship between this deconfinement debye mass and the scalar mass, a result that contrasts with expectations for pure QCD. These observations align with recent lattice QCD studies concerning debye mass in pure QCD and the presence of a scalar in the adjoint representation. Additionally, we analyze the string tension and its dependence on the deconfinement debye mass, finding that the confinement-dedeconfinement shift exhibits a linear dependence on this mass. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for QCD phase structure, particularly regarding the search for a deconfined low-temperature state in QCD with a scalar in the fundamental representation. This search is motivated by the potential to address the strong-CP problem via a solution analogous to the "axiglon" approach. Furthermore, we highlight the relevance of these findings to future collider experiments, such as those at the Future Circular Collider, which aim to investigate the properties of a scalar in the fundamental representation. Finally, we compare our results with those obtained using the Polyakov loop and the Creutz ratio. While the Polyakov loop yields similar results, the Creutz ratio indicates a non-linear dependence of the deconfinement debye mass on the scalar mass. We conclude that the string tension calculated via the Creutz formula may be influenced by string excitations, leading to a significant string tension gap between the confined and deconfined phases. Consequently, the string tension derived from the Polyakov loop is deemed more reliable. Finally, we discuss the potential for a scalar with a mass linearly proportional to the string tension to exist within QCD. This scenario could be explored through measurements of the debye mass, string tension, and other relevant quantities. Such measurements could be conducted using both lattice QCD and future collider experiments. Specifically, we suggest that the debye mass, calculable via two-point correlation functions of temporal gauge fields, could be measured at the Future Circular Collider. Additionally, we propose that the string tension could be determined through measurements of jet deflection caused by the medium. These measurements would provide a means to test the hypothesis that a scalar with a linear mass dependence on the string tension

The antiferromagnetic phase transition in the face-centered-tetragonal (fct) structure of Cr$_2$Al was investigated using neutron powder diffraction. This transition occurs at $T_{\rm N} = 315$ K, where the paramagnetic state transforms into a commensurate antiferromagnetic state characterized by the propagation vector $\mathbf{k} = (1/2, 1/2, 1/2)$. The observed magnetic arrangement corresponds to a ferromagnetic chain model along the $c$-axis, linked to a nearest-neighbor exchange interaction $J_1$ that is antiferromagnetic in nature. Additionally, a tetragonal distortion of the fct unit cell was detected, shifting from $a = b = 5.902$ \AA\ and $c = 11.804$ \AA\ in the paramagnetic phase to $a = b = 5.896$ \AA\ and $c = 11.806$ \AA\ in the antiferromagnetic phase. This distortion is attributed to the Jahn-Teller effect, which arises from the partially filled $e_g$ orbitals of the Cr$^{2+}$ ions. Furthermore, a second exchange interaction, $J_2$, connecting fourth nearest neighbors along the $c$-axis, was determined to be ferromagnetic. This $J_2$ interaction is derived from the lowest energy state of a classical spin Hamiltonian that accounts for the experimentally observed magnetic structure. Finally, the temperature dependence of the magnetization was analyzed using the Arrott-Noakes method, yielding a critical exponent of $\beta = 0.36$. This value indicates that Cr$_2$Al belongs to the 3D-Heisenberg universality class. These findings are supported by the calculated density of states. Additionally, the study examines the influence of the magnetic structure on the electronic properties of Cr$_2$Al. Notably, the electronic structure of Cr$_2$Al is closely related to that of the superconducting variant, Nb$_3$Al. Consequently, this work provides a foundation for future research into the relationship between magnetism and superconductivity in these materials. The sample used for the measurements was prepared via a solid-state reaction.

This study examines various gas kinetic models, incorporating a relaxation-time (RT) model with velocity-dependent collision frequency alongside its traditional constant relaxation-time counterpart. These models are evaluated against the Boltzmann equation and numerical solutions derived from the discrete-ordinate (DN) method. The results indicate that the proposed RT model with velocity-dependent frequency offers a significant improvement over the standard RT model with constant relaxation frequency, showing strong agreement with both Boltzmann solutions and DN numerical outcomes. This enhanced performance is particularly evident in the rarefied regime and under conditions involving substantial temperature gradients. Furthermore, the RT model with velocity-dependent collision frequency accurately captures the physics of rarefied gas flows. Finally, the RT model with $\omega^{1/2}$ velocity-dependent collision frequency is demonstrated to effectively represent the influence of the intermolecular potential within rarefied gas flows. These findings are supported by various numerical examples. Additionally, the two newly proposed RT models are shown to be consistent with the generalized Chapman-Enskog solutions. Collectively, these results validate the proposed RT models for practical applications. The research was conducted using the open-source Boltzmann solver, BOLOM. HD58260 is a rapidly rotating, metal-poor star that exhibits strong magnetic fields, making it a prime candidate for studying the interplay between stellar rotation and magnetism. This study utilizes high-resolution spectropolarimetry to investigate the star's surface magnetic field. By analyzing emission lines of neutral iron and titanium, we detected a significant negative longitudinal magnetic field value of $-1200 \pm 300$ G, indicating a dominant pole oriented toward the observer. We also observed a substantial spectropolarimetric signal in the emission line $\textrm{Fe~I}$~$6166$ \AA, which displays a strong inverse Zeeman signature. This finding suggests that the line originates in the upper photosphere or lower chromosphere, where the magnetic field is oriented away from the observer. These results are consistent with a large-scale dipolar field configuration, a conclusion supported by the mean magnetic field derived from Stokes V profiles of absorption lines. Furthermore, the spectropolarimetric behavior of the $\textrm{Fe~I}$~$6166$ \AA\ emission line aligns with a large-scale radial magnetic field. These observations provide compelling evidence for a magnetic field structure resembling that of a rapidly rotating, metal-poor Ap star. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the evolution of magnetic fields in metal-poor stars. The data utilized in this study can be accessed at www.esac.esa.int/apstar. This paper establishes the free boson representation of the Dong-HeHe intertwinning operator within the one-dimensional Heisenberg-Dunkl algebra. It provides explicit expressions for both the generalized Dunkl operator and the HeHe intertwinning operator in terms of free bosons, along with their Hermitian conjugates. Furthermore, an explicit formula for the normal ordering of the generalized Dunkl operator using free bosons is derived. The results demonstrate that the HeHe intertwinning operator maps any Hermitian Dunkl operator (with $z=0$) to a standard annihilation operator. Finally, the intertwinning operator is expanded into a series of products of creation and annihilation operators, and the first few terms of this expansion are calculated explicitly. This research expands upon the authors' prior work regarding the $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$ group and Heisenberg algebra. The findings may prove beneficial for further investigations into the quantum harmonic oscillator, Heisenberg algebra, and related fields. Additionally, the methodology employed here can be utilized to derive the free boson representation of the generalized Dunkl operator in $d$ dimensions, where $d$ is a positive integer. The resulting $d$-dimensional HeHe intertwinning operator will transform any Hermitian Dunkl vector into an $d$-tuple of annihilation operators. This approach also offers a novel method for deriving the normal ordering of the $d$-dimensional Dunkl operator, thereby extending previous findings by the first author. The applications of these results are expected to be significant across various scientific disciplines.

Keywords: Heisenberg-Dunkl algebra, Dunkl intertwinning operator, boson representation, normal ordering.

We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in NGC 5253, a low-metallicity galaxy known for its intense star formation. The data reveal a galaxy-wide H30$\alpha$ emission with a luminosity of 1.1 $\pm$ 0.2 $\times$ 10$^{37}$ erg s$^{-1}$, which aligns with emission detected in the galaxy's core. By comparing these findings with observations of the H28$\alpha$ and H31$\alpha$ lines, we demonstrate that the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a reliable tracer for star formation rates in this galaxy. This line offers a distinct advantage over H$\alpha$ emission, as it remains detectable in regions where H$\alpha$ is heavily extinguished by dust. Our results indicate that H30$\alpha$ is detectable in approximately 10% of the galaxy's area, whereas H$\alpha$ is only observable in the core. Additionally, we present H31$\alpha$ observations that show the H31$\alpha$/H30$\alpha$ ratio is consistent with theoretical predictions across the regions where both lines are detected. These findings suggest that the H30$\alpha$ line is a robust star formation indicator in low-metallicity galaxies like NGC 5253, capable of penetrating dust-obscured regions that remain inaccessible to H$\alpha$ observations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the H30$\alpha$/H28$\alpha$ ratio can be utilized to determine the star formation timescale in this galaxy. Finally, we conclude that H30$\alpha$ is a valuable tool for studying star formation in galaxies with metallicities as low as 0.2 solar values. This makes it a complementary indicator to H$\alpha$, particularly for studying the most metal-poor galaxies in the local universe. This study introduces the concept of ergodic conditional expectation operators, offering a general framework for their mathematical analysis. We demonstrate the consistency of the Nadaraya-Watson and conditional mean decomposition estimators under specific regularity conditions. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between ergodic conditional expectation operators and Markov kernels, proving that these operators are strictly positive, bounded linear operators that act as probability-preserving positive contractions on $L^p$ spaces for $1 \leq p \leq \infty$. These theoretical findings facilitate the estimation of both ergodic conditional expectation operators and associated ergodic Markov kernels, for which we derive the convergence rate of the Nadaraya-Watson estimator. Finally, we validate these results using simulated data, illustrating the operators' utility in modeling the conditional mean and variance of time series. Additionally, we apply these ergodic operators to analyze the daily closing prices of the S&P 500 index. This study addresses the task of creating reduced-order filters for a standard SIR epidemic model. The process dynamics are observed via a reduced-order filter created using the sliding mode observer technique originally proposed by Z. Man. This approach was selected for its robustness against model uncertainties and its ability to handle non-smooth dynamics. The paper presents stability results for the filter design and includes a numerical simulation to demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Additionally, the application of this reduced-order filter within an epidemic prediction framework is explored. Given the critical nature of accurate and reliable information in managing the COVID-19 pandemic, the authors believe this work holds significant potential for future research. Furthermore, the proposed methodology is versatile and can be extended to various other models, such as SEIR or other standard epidemic models, as well as to other observation models. Finally, the authors intend to investigate the application of this approach in the context of epidemic control. Keywords: SIR model, sliding mode observer, reduced-order observer, filter design, epidemic prediction, reduced-order filter, epidemic control.

Recent years have seen significant research interest in applying machine learning to semantic knowledge graphs, particularly for linking entities across different subgraphs. This paper introduces a novel Resource-Conscious Asynchronous Online Federated Learning (RC-AOL) framework designed for nonlinear regression. The core objective is to minimize regression error while accounting for resource usage, specifically communication costs, within distributed environments where data arrives continuously and online. To achieve this, we propose a new objective function that balances local regression performance against communication expenses. We demonstrate that solving this optimization problem is equivalent to executing a specific filtering process. Leveraging this insight, we develop an efficient Asynchronous Online Federated Learning (ASOL) algorithm. Subsequently, we extend ASOL into the RC-AOL algorithm by incorporating a virtual node that acts as a rate limiter to reduce communication overhead. Finally, we evaluate the performance of RC-AOL through numerical simulations and experimental data fitting. The results indicate that while ASOL achieves lower regression errors than synchronous federated learning methods, it simultaneously increases communication costs; in contrast, RC-AOL successfully mitigates this issue without compromising performance. Furthermore, compared to existing rate-limited online federated learning approaches, RC-AOL delivers superior regression accuracy. Numerical testing confirms the robustness of RC-AOL across various scenarios, including those with heterogeneous data distributions. Ultimately, RC-AOL offers a practical solution for nonlinear regression in distributed online settings where data sources face communication constraints. The findings suggest that this approach is applicable to diverse real-world problems, such as forecasting nonlinear trends in energy consumption, traffic flow, and weather patterns. Additionally, we plan to extend RC-AOL to address classification tasks in the near future. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of rate limiting to asynchronous federated learning. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/RC-AOL}.

The optical absorption characteristics of silicon films featuring a three-dimensional photonic band gap were evaluated across various thicknesses, widths, and refractive index contrast levels. For thin thin-film silicon, the photonic band gap structure functions as a highly efficient back reflector, boosting total light absorption in the forward direction. In the thin film regime, this photonic crystal back reflector can achieve near-total absorption across the entire solar spectrum. Conversely, for ultrathin silicon films, the photonic band gap acts as a front reflector, significantly enhancing absorption in the forward direction. Although the photonic band gap structure occupies a larger volume than bulk silicon, it requires less material to reach the same level of absorption. This is particularly advantageous for thin silicon films with high refractive index contrast, such as nanowire arrays, which can substantially reduce material usage while maintaining high absorption efficiency. Furthermore, these findings can be applied to other thin film absorbers equipped with photonic band gap structures. By strategically positioning the photonic band gap either in front of or behind the thin film, one can effectively tune the absorption spectrum. This work provides a theoretical foundation for the design and optimization of thin and ultrathin silicon-based photonic devices. Additionally, the developed model is applicable to other thin film absorbers, enabling the design of devices with tunable absorption spectra and minimal material consumption. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/Si-Photonic-Crystal-Reflectors. This paper presents a straightforward methodology employing basic calculus to derive asymptotic solutions for the exponential equation involving natural logarithms and polynomial terms. The study utilizes these solutions to explain how to determine the tower function's order, power tower degrees, and the number of iterations required for various logistic map functions to achieve statistical stability. Additionally, it provides insights into the solution sets of the exponential equation, including instances where no solutions or infinitely many solutions exist. The approach is further demonstrated through several combinatorics and number theory problems. Finally, numerical examples are provided to illustrate the accuracy of the derived solutions. This research serves as a continuation of our prior collaborative work on estimating prime numbers and factorials. Our objective is to make fundamental calculus a valuable instrument for solving problems across diverse disciplines. Given the scarcity of literature on this subject, we anticipate our findings will be valuable to graduate students and researchers in mathematics and related fields. The paper is structured into seven sections, with the first offering a brief introduction, the second describing the proposed approach, the third applying it to find the order of tower functions, and the fourth applying it to degrees of power towers. The study investigates the magnetic properties of a novel, previously unexplored single crystal of the centered honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$. This work expands the range of known magnetoelectric materials and offers new perspectives on honeycomb antiferromagnets. Graph representation learning has gained significant traction recently, with node embedding techniques being particularly prominent. These methods typically transform nodes into low-dimensional vectors to facilitate downstream applications, such as predicting links in scientific co-authorship networks. However, the performance of these techniques in sparse networks is often suboptimal. This paper identifies the primary cause: existing node embedding methods are primarily designed for dense graphs, causing them to fail to generalize effectively to sparse environments. To address this limitation, we introduce Sparse to Sparse Neighbors Embedding (SSNE), a node embedding algorithm specifically tailored for sparse graphs. Our approach incorporates a novel regularization term that explicitly accounts for graph sparsity. We validate the efficacy of this regularization through numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we assess the overall performance of SSNE in the link prediction task, demonstrating its superiority over current state-of-the-art node embedding methods. Detecting wildfires and smoke plumes is crucial for safeguarding human life, property, and the environment. While current methods often rely on fusing infrared and visible light images, they frequently fail to account for the specific challenges posed by wildfire scenarios. To address this, we introduce a new deep learning-based infrared-visible integration approach specifically tailored for these images. Our method generates a novel infrared-visible integration image that enhances key wildfire features, such as flames and smoke, thereby improving the efficacy of subsequent detection algorithms. We have developed a new deep learning architecture named FIRe-GAN, which employs a generator network to produce integration images from visible and infrared inputs and a discriminator network designed to identify whether an image is a real infrared capture or a synthetic one. Extensive experiments were conducted on a newly established dataset, the Los Angeles Wildfire Dataset, to evaluate our approach. The results demonstrate that FIRe-GAN significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving an accuracy of 99.99% and a 20.5% increase in AUC compared to the second-best approach. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/FIRe-GAN. Furthermore, we have launched a new web-based image integration tool, FIRe-GAN Online, available at https://chenyi2000.github.io/FIRe-GAN/. This tool allows users to input their own infrared and visible images to automatically generate integration images using our method. We anticipate that this tool will be valuable for researchers and practitioners working on wildfire imagery integration. Our paper and tool are expected to benefit the broader computer vision community. Additional details can be found in our blog post at https://chenyi2000.github.io/FIRe-GAN/. We welcome any feedback or inquiries. Our team consists of Chenyi Shen (chenyishen@cs.ucsb.edu), Yi Zhang (yishy2000@cs.ucsb.edu), and Chenyang Liu (chenyangliu@cs.ucsb.edu). This study introduces a newly compiled dataset designed for automatically identifying indicators of depression in social media content. The dataset was developed through a two-stage labeling process: first, psychological experts examined Facebook posts to detect signs of depression, and second, linguistics students annotated the same posts to detect stigmatizing language. Subsequently, the postgraduate researchers utilized both the expert and student labels to train machine learning models to recognize both positive and negative depictions of depression. Finally, the researchers employed these trained models to manually annotate additional Facebook posts to evaluate their efficacy. The findings indicate that human annotators achieved high accuracy in detecting signs of depression using the proposed method, with precision rates of 90.5% for positive signs and 86.8% for stigmatizing signs. These results suggest that the method effectively identifies signs of depression, potentially aiding individuals at risk of depression or suicide. Furthermore, the approach could assist in reducing the stigma surrounding mental health conditions. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions.

This study investigates the influence of coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole excitations on these resonances in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. To achieve this, we developed a microscopic framework that incorporates both quadrupole excitations and the coupling between them. By utilizing a deformed shell model, we calculated the energy-weighted strength distributions for the isoscalar monopole and quadrupole responses, as well as the isoscalar monopole-quadrupole coupled strength. The results demonstrate that this coupling significantly alters the strength distribution, leading to a substantial reduction in the isoscalar monopole strength. Furthermore, the calculated energy-weighted sum rules remain consistent with the classical hydrodynamic model, which treats nuclei as incompressible fluids. These findings align with experimental data, confirming the validity of our theoretical approach. Consequently, this work underscores the critical role of isoscalar monopole-quadrupole coupling in shaping the strength distribution of the isoscalar giant monopole resonance. Additionally, the proposed model offers a valuable tool for analyzing giant resonances in other nuclei. Finally, we provide insights into the impact of this coupling on the width of the isoscalar giant monopole resonance. The code used in this study is accessible at \url{https://github.com/abhishekkumar1997/iso-scalar-giant-monopole-resonance}. This work examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence within feedback-controlled motion systems featuring Coulomb friction. Theoretical predictions regarding convergence or limit cycle formation are validated through numerical simulations and experimental data. The presented model and control approach are applicable to various systems, including robotic manipulators and linear motion guides. Furthermore, the implications of these findings for motion system design are explored. A key contribution of this research is its demonstration of the potential benefits of carefully selected discontinuous control laws, which can either accelerate convergence or mitigate chattering. The proposed control law is continuous from below, ensuring that the actuator reaches its maximum speed or force output as soon as the desired trajectory becomes unreachable. This strategy prevents the system from entering a "quasi-stable" state, such as sticking at an intermediate position, which could cause prolonged or even indefinite convergence delays. Numerical results indicate that incorporating such a control law can reduce convergence time by a factor of 2 to 3. Additionally, it can eliminate chattering in systems that would otherwise exhibit limit cycles, or significantly reduce their amplitude. To validate the approach, a simple experimental setup was constructed, and the proposed control law was implemented on a real robotic arm. The resulting experimental data aligns well with numerical predictions. The authors acknowledge that the proposed control law is not always feasible, as it may require actuator forces exceeding physical limits. However, these constraints can be incorporated into the analysis, as demonstrated in this paper. When such limitations are present, the system may still exhibit stick-slip behavior, though with a reduced slip frequency. The paper concludes by discussing the resulting convergence properties and their impact on trajectory planning. Finally, the proposed control law is noted for its simplicity, making it suitable for real-time implementation. In contrast, existing methods for generating stick-slip-free trajectories rely on complex, often non-convex optimization problems that are difficult to solve online. Consequently, the authors suggest that future research should focus on developing efficient online algorithms to design slip-free trajectories. Furthermore, the influence of parameter uncertainties on convergence and limit cycles warrants investigation, as this work assumes nominal parameter values. Finally, while the focus here is on one-dimensional systems, the approach is readily extendable to higher-dimensional cases, such as planar robotic manipulators. Extending the analysis to multi-degree-of-freedom systems is left for future work. The authors thank the reviewers for their valuable comments and suggestions. This paper introduces Deep Bellman Insurance (DBI), a new reinforcement learning approach designed for sequential decision-making under risk aversion. DBI operates by solving a Bellman equation that incorporates risk preferences into the dynamics of a Markov decision process. The method is validated across three contexts: a simulated investment portfolio allocation scenario, a stylized model of health insurance demand, and an empirical examination of actual insurance market data. The findings indicate that DBI outperforms competing algorithms in all cases, achieving superior risk-adjusted returns and a more equitable distribution of risk. Additionally, the stylized health insurance application demonstrates that DBI can be utilized for policy evaluation. Overall, this research establishes a robust framework for learning risk-averse policies, a capability that is especially valuable for applications such as portfolio management, resource allocation, and policy assessment. Sequential recommenders are prevalent in real-world applications due to their ability to enhance user experience and boost system revenue. However, a key challenge remains: determining which items to suggest and the optimal timing. To address this, we introduce a new approach that leverages a user's purpose to generate recommendations. Our method, latent user purpose modeling (LUPM), learns a finite set of purposes from historical user sessions and predicts the most suitable purpose given the current context. We evaluate this technique on the Yahoo! News recommendation task, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art sequential recommenders. The source code is available at https://github.com/leehyuk98/LUPM. This project was developed as a Kaggle competition entry on Sequential Recommendation. Additionally, the paper explores the relationship between user purpose modeling and sequential recommenders, offering insights into future research directions. The reducible double confluent Heun equation, originally derived by Jess and Miki as a generalization of the Heun equation, serves as a powerful analytical tool for describing bound states in one-dimensional potentials featuring two types of singularities. This paper demonstrates that the reducible double confluent Heun equation can be viewed as the Lie point symmetry generator associated with a one-parameter family of singular potentials. This family includes two distinct singular models at its boundaries, representing the maximal and minimal unfolding. This perspective offers a novel approach to the problem of classifying potentials solvable via the Heun equation. Furthermore, the double confluent Heun equation is linked to a symmetric unfolding of the source term in a nonhomogeneous heat equation. This connection provides a fresh physical interpretation for the Heun classification, which was previously established by the authors in the context of classifying singular Sturm-Liouville problems. Additionally, this unfolding yields a symmetric formulation of the source term within Sturm-Liouville problems that possess a specific symmetry under spatial reflection. This outcome reinforces the connection between Heun's classification and classifying reflectionally symmetric Sturm-Liouville problems, a link that was previously identified by the authors in a different context. The paper concludes with a discussion of the reducible double confluent Heun equation as a degenerate case of the general double confluent Heun equation. In this analysis, we examine the reducible symmetric unfolding of the source term and its relationship to a symmetric unfolding of the potential, a connection that was previously established in a broader context. Finally, the paper includes an appendix detailing the unfolding of the double confluent Heun equation itself. This appendix presents a comprehensive description of the unfolding process, covering both the differential equation and the Sturm-Liouville problem, and offers a unified treatment of the unfolding for all three types of double confluent Heun equations. The appendix also provides a unified discussion of the classification of all three unfolded forms of the double confluent Heun equation. This work contributes to the ongoing effort to elucidate the intricate web of connections linking Heun's classification, the solvability of the heat equation, and the classification of symmetric Sturm-Liouville problems. Ultimately, these findings contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of Heun's classification. The research was conducted within the framework of the project "Unified treatment of Heun's classification," supported by grant no. 20-21038S from the Czech Science Foundation. We investigate the estimation of a low-rank matrix from noisy, potentially missing observations, where the signal strengths and error variances vary by row. This framework encompasses groupwise heteroskedasticity and enables more efficient estimation than previous methods. Our analysis establishes the fundamental limits for both estimation error and matrix recovery, demonstrating that a simple entrywise estimator is optimal for achieving the best possible estimation error. Furthermore, we show that specific existing techniques, including nuclear norm minimization, are suboptimal. For construction, we develop a computationally efficient procedure that matches the derived lower bounds on estimation error, contrasting with other approaches that are either suboptimal or lack explicit error rate guarantees. We also present a lower bound on computational complexity, indicating that our proposed method resides within this limit. Finally, we illustrate the benefits of our approach through a case study on estimating the mean matrix of a multi-group Gaussian tensor. In this application, our method surpasses a recent tensor mean estimator, offering superior upper bounds on estimation error while maintaining comparable computational costs. To our knowledge, these theoretical results represent the first of their kind for this problem. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/lowrank.

This work investigates the intrinsic topological model for interacting spin-1/2 fermions on a honeycomb lattice without reliance on symmetry. The interaction Hamiltonian comprises the Majorana model proposed by Hasan and Meng, characterized by a tunable parameter. The resulting topological phase diagram includes a non-symmetry-protected topological phase and an energy gap that vanishes at the boundary between trivial and topological states. Furthermore, the Majorana zero mode at the hexagon corner is identified through the determinant of the matrix $M_{ij} = \langle i | \hat{n}_j | i \rangle$, where $|i\rangle$ represents the ground state and $\hat{n}_j$ denotes the $j$-th component of the spin operator. This mode is confirmed through the local charge distribution function and the charge distribution around the zero mode. Additionally, the charge distribution function exhibits a step-like feature, demonstrating sensitivity to variations in the model's parameter. Finally, the stability of the Majorana zero mode is analyzed in relation to the system's energy gap. These findings offer valuable insights for the topological quantum computation community. The theoretical framework developed here is applicable to various coupled hexagon-based systems, such as graphene and Kagome lattices. Consequently, this research provides a novel theoretical foundation for advancing topological quantum computing. The model is realized through a hexagon-based circuit, which can be fabricated using standard lithography techniques. This represents a significant step toward the experimental validation of the theoretical predictions. The proposed circuit holds potential for topological quantum computing applications. Recent anomalies in semi-inclusive lepton flavor invariance ratios regarding $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions are investigated. By analyzing the difference between these two ratios, many hadronic uncertainties are eliminated. The analysis reveals that semi-inclusive hadronic effects within the Standard Model are sufficiently large to account for the observed discrepancies. Furthermore, a new theoretical framework is introduced to address these issues, which is also applicable to other flavor anomalies. Finally, the study examines the impact of potential new physics operators, specifically those associated with right-handed currents. The results indicate that a pure right-handed current scenario is excluded at the 95% confidence level, whereas models featuring mixed left-right currents remain viable. Additionally, the influence of interference terms between left and right operators is explored. These findings suggest that future measurements of these ratios could uncover evidence of new physics, potentially characterized by right-handed currents. This research was conducted using Python and the Pythia8 simulation package. The accompanying Python code is available at: https://github.com/abdullahkaya17/semi-inclusive-lepton-flavor-invariance-ratios. Pythia8 was utilized to generate event samples for the analysis.
